## Statement

Assume AC. Let $p_0\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ be a probability density with compact support $K$, a finite union of intervals. Suppose $J=\int_{\{p_0>0\}}(p_0'')^2/p_0<\infty$ and there are $a,c>0$ such that $P_0(I)\ge c\lambda(I)^a$ for every interval $I\subseteq K$. Let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is a finite nonzero measure with continuous strictly positive density on a neighborhood of $K$, and independently let $S\sim G$ for any probability measure $G$ on $(0,\infty)$. Suppose $n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2}$ for $0<a_2<a_1<1$, and put $\sigma=\sigma_nS$. Then for constants $C_1,C_2>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$ \Pi_n\left\{\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_{F,\sigma})\le C_1\sigma_n^4,\quad P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_{F,\sigma}}\right]^2\le C_1\sigma_n^4\right\}\ge\exp\{-C_2\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}. $$
Consequently, for $d_n=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\sigma_n^2\}$, the same two local quantities are at most $C_1d_n^2$ on a set of prior mass at least $e^{-C_3nd_n^2}$. Logarithmic integrands vanish where $p_0=0$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and all hypotheses of the Statement.

[F1] Gaussian convolution of this truth has KL and log-square error at most $(4/9)\sigma^4J$. [[lem-gaussian-convolution-kl-and-log-square-second-order-bound]]

[F2] A compactly supported mixing law in an interval of length at most a fixed multiple of $\tau$ has a discrete normal-mixture approximation at scale $\tau$ with $O(\log(e/\eta))$ atoms, $L^1$ error at most $\eta$ and supremum error at most $\eta/\tau$. [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-finite-support-approximation]]

[F3] For a finite partition with interval-cell base masses in $[c\eta^2,1]$ and $N\eta\le1/4$, a DP finite vector has probability at least $C\exp\{-c'N\log(e/\eta)\}$ of having total target-weight discrepancy plus residual mass at most $3\eta$; the constants are uniform when the residual-cell base mass ranges in a fixed compact subset of $(0,m]$. [[lem-dirichlet-process-simplex-small-ball]]

[F4] The mixture density is jointly measurable, positive and finite. [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-density-well-defined]]

[F5] The Gaussian kernel has formula $\phi_\sigma(x)=(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]

## Proof

1.1 Choose $0<s_-<s_+<\infty$ with $g:=G([s_-,s_+])>0$, possible because these compact intervals exhaust $(0,\infty)$. Set $b_n=\sigma_n$, $\tau=s_-b_n$, $B=a+6$ and $\eta=b_n^B$. For all large $n$, partition each nondegenerate component of $K$ into equal consecutive Borel intervals of lengths in $[\tau/8,\tau/4]$: use $\lceil4\ell/\tau\rceil$ pieces for a component of length $\ell$. Endpoints can be assigned arbitrarily because $P_0$ has a density. The support of a continuous density has no isolated points, so there are no isolated support components to treat. There are $O(b_n^{-1})$ coarse cells $I_k$, each of mass at least $c' b_n^a$. Translate the conditional probability $P_0(\cdot\mid I_k)$ to an interval centered at zero, apply [F2] at scale $\tau$, and translate back. Multiplying by $P_0(I_k)$ and summing gives a finite probability $F_n$ with at most $C b_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$ atoms in the closures of these cells, each carrying its original coarse-cell label, and $\|p_{F_n,\tau}-p_{P_0,\tau}\|_\infty\le\eta/\tau$. The total weight of atoms with label $k$ is exactly $P_0(I_k)$. [F2, given, choose, construct]

1.2 Put $\delta=\eta\tau$. Move each atom to a nearest point of the global lattice of mesh $\delta$ and merge atoms at the same location. Preserve its fractional label weights when merging. The resulting distinct locations $z_j$ are separated by at least $\delta$, with weights $w_j$ summing to one, and still number $N\le Cb_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$. Let $U_j=[z_j-\delta/4,z_j+\delta/4)$ and $U_0=\mathbb R\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^NU_j$. These are disjoint partition cells. The base density is bounded above and below on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, so $c_0\eta\tau\le\alpha(U_j)\le C_0\eta\tau\le1$ eventually. Since $B>1$, $\eta\tau\ge c_1\eta^2$ and $N\eta\to0$. Also $\sum_j\alpha(U_j)\le C N\delta\to0$, so, writing $m=\alpha(\mathbb R)>0$, we have $\alpha(U_0)\in[m/2,m]$ eventually. [given, step 1.1, construct, algebra]

1.3 Apply [F3] with tolerance $\eta$ to get an event $E_n$ on which $\sum_j|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta$ and $\Pi_{DP}(E_n)\ge\exp\{-C b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}$. Its constants can be taken uniform in $n$: in the proof of [F3] the only residual-parameter factors are $\Gamma(m)/\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))$ and a lower bound $(\eta^2/2)^m$ for the residual power. The gamma ratio is bounded below on the fixed compact interval $[m/2,m]$, and the latter power already has fixed exponent $m$. The remaining constants use only the fixed bound $c_1\eta^2\le\alpha(U_j)\le1$. Finally $\log(e/\eta)\le C\log n$ by the polynomial lower bandwidth bound. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

2.1 For $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$, the original discrete approximation still satisfies $\|p_{F_n,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\eta/b_n$. Indeed the Gaussian convolution identity $\phi_u*\phi_v=\phi_{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}$ follows by completing the square and integrating; convolution with a probability kernel contracts the supremum norm by the triangle inequality. Use $u=\tau$, $v=\sqrt{\sigma^2-\tau^2}$, treating equality by the original approximation. Differentiating [F5] gives $\|\phi_\sigma'\|_\infty\le C\sigma^{-2}$. Atom relocation by at most $\delta/2$ therefore changes the mixture by at most $C\delta/\sigma^2\le C\eta/b_n$. For $F\in E_n$, replacing each $F|_{U_j}$ by its mass at $z_j$ costs at most the same derivative bound times $\delta/4$; the weight discrepancies and residual mass cost at most $3\eta\|\phi_\sigma\|_\infty$. Consequently, uniformly over $F\in E_n$ and $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$, one has $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\eta/b_n$. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 For any $x\in K$ choose a coarse cell whose closure contains $x$. Its length is at most $\tau/4$, so every original atom with that label, and every associated relocated atom-cell, lies in $[x-\tau,x+\tau]$ eventually. Let $J_x$ be the set of relocated atom indices carrying a positive fraction of this label's weight. Merging preserves the full label weight, so $\sum_{j\in J_x}w_j\ge P_0(I_k)\ge c' b_n^a$. The vector discrepancy on $E_n$ implies $F([x-\tau,x+\tau])\ge\sum_{j\in J_x}F(U_j)\ge c'b_n^a-3\eta\ge c'b_n^a/2$. On this neighborhood, [F5] is at least $c''/b_n$ for every $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$. Thus $p_{F,\sigma}(x)\ge c'''b_n^{a-1}$. The same argument directly with the coarse-cell mass under $P_0$ gives $p_{P_0,\sigma}(x)\ge c'''b_n^{a-1}$, after decreasing the constant. [F4, F5, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Put $q=p_{P_0,\sigma}$ and $r=p_{F,\sigma}$. The mean-value theorem for the logarithm and steps 2.1–2.2 give $\sup_{x\in K}|\log(q(x)/r(x))|\le C\eta b_n^{-a}=Cb_n^6$. By [F1], $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert Q)\le Cb_n^4$ and $P_0[\log(p_0/q)]^2\le Cb_n^4$ uniformly in these scales. Adding the bounded log perturbation proves $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_{F,\sigma})\le Cb_n^4+Cb_n^6\le C'b_n^4$. The inequality $(u+v)^2\le2u^2+2v^2$ similarly gives $P_0[\log(p_0/r)]^2\le C'b_n^4$. All integrals exist by the displayed bounds, and integrands vanish off $\{p_0>0\}$. [F1, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra]

3.2 The scale event $S\in[s_-,s_+]$ has fixed probability $g>0$ and is independent of $F$. Therefore $E_n$ times this event is contained in the displayed KL/log-square set and has probability at least $g\exp\{-C b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}$. Increase $C_2$ to absorb $g$. Since $nd_n^2\ge b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2$ and $d_n^2\ge b_n^4$, the consequent local-radius form follows as well. This proves all assertions without a unimodality hypothesis. [given, step 1.3, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be a bounded probability density supported on a compact
set $K\subset\mathbb R$. Let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure with a
continuous density bounded below by a positive constant on a neighborhood of
$K$. Assume
$$h(p_0,p_0*\phi_\sigma)\le C\sigma^2$$
for all sufficiently small $\sigma>0$, where $\phi_\sigma$ is the centered
normal density with standard deviation $\sigma$. Let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$ and
let $S\sim G$ be independent, where $G$ is any probability measure on
$(0,\infty)$. Suppose $n^{-a_1}\lesssim\sigma_n\lesssim n^{-a_2}$ for
$0<a_2<a_1<1$. Set $\sigma=\sigma_nS$ and
$$\delta_n:=\max\{(n\sigma_n)^{-1/2}\log n,\ \sigma_n^2\log n\}.$$
Then, for some constant $C_1>0$ and all sufficiently large $n$,
$$\Pi_n\!\left\{(F,\sigma):\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_{F,\sigma})\le C_1\delta_n^2,\quad
P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_{F,\sigma}}\right]^2\le C_1\delta_n^2\right\}
\ge e^{-C_1n\delta_n^2}.$$
Here $p_{F,\sigma}$ is the density of [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-density-well-defined]],
and all logarithmic integrands are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC; the compactly supported bounded density $p_0$; the stated Gaussian-convolution Hellinger bound; the finite base measure $\alpha$ with a positive continuous density near $K$; the independent priors $F\sim DP(\alpha)$ and $S\sim G$; and the polynomial bounds on $\sigma_n$.

[A1] AC supplies $DP(\alpha)$ and the directional KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]

[F1] [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-density-well-defined]]: $p_{F,\sigma}(x)=\int\phi_\sigma(x-z)F(dz)$ is a positive finite-valued jointly measurable density.

[F2] [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-finite-support-approximation]]: a probability mixing law on a compact interval has a discrete approximation with logarithmically many atoms and controlled $L^1$ and supremum mixture errors.

[F3] [[lem-dirichlet-process-simplex-small-ball]]: for a finite partition whose interval-cell base masses are bounded below by $c\eta^2$, a DP vector has probability at least $e^{-c'N\log(e/\eta)}$ of being within $O(\eta)$ of any target weight vector while every interval-cell mass is at least $\eta^2/2$; its constants are uniform when the residual-cell base mass $\alpha(U_0)$ ranges in a fixed compact subset of $(0,m]$.

[F4] [[lem-hellinger-ratio-controls-kl-moments]]: if $h^2(p,q)$ is small and $\|p/q\|_\infty\le R<\infty$, then $\mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q)\le Ch^2(1+\log^+R)$ and $P[(\log(p/q))^2]\le Ch^2(1+\log^+R)^2$.

[F5] [[def-dirichlet-process]] and [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]]: the finite evaluation vector of $F$ on a measurable partition has the Dirichlet law with parameters given by $\alpha$.

[F6] [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and [[lem-hellinger-distance-controls-l1-and-total-variation]]: $h$ is the root-L2 distance between square-root densities, satisfies the triangle inequality, and $h^2(p,q)\le\int|p-q|d\lambda$.

[F7] [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]: $\phi_\sigma(x-z)=\sigma^{-1}\phi((x-z)/\sigma)$ for the standard normal density $\phi$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Since $G$ is a probability on $(0,\infty)=\bigcup_{m\ge1}[1/m,m]$, choose $0<s_-<s_+<\infty$ with $g:=G([s_-,s_+])>0$. Put $\sigma_-=s_-\sigma_n$. By [F2] applied to the law $P_0$ at scale $\sigma_-$, there is a finite discrete probability $F_n$ supported on $K$ with at most $C\sigma_n^{-1}\log n$ atoms and $\|p_{F_n,\sigma_-}-p_{P_0,\sigma_-}\|_1\le\eta_n$, where $\eta_n:=\sigma_n^8$. [F2, given, choose]

1.2 Choose a compact interval $D$ whose interior contains $K$ and on which the density of $\alpha$ is bounded above and below by positive constants. Moving an atom by at most $\eta_n\sigma_-$ changes its normal mixture by at most $C\eta_n$ in $L^1$: differentiating [F7] gives $\|\partial_z\phi_{\sigma_-}(\cdot-z)\|_1=E|Z|/\sigma_-\le1/\sigma_-$, since $2|Z|\le1+Z^2$ and $E Z^2=1$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Move each atom of $F_n$ to a nearest point of a lattice of mesh $\eta_n\sigma_-$ and merge coincident atoms; distinct relocated locations are separated by at least $\eta_n\sigma_-$. Around each relocated atom take a centered cell of length $\ell_n=\eta_n\sigma_-/2$; these cells are disjoint. Each gap of length $g\ge\ell_n$ between the atom-cells, including the two end gaps in $D$, is split into $q=\lceil2g/\sigma_-\rceil$ equal subintervals. If $q=1$, their length is $g\ge\ell_n$; if $q\ge2$, then $g>\sigma_-/2$ and $q\le4g/\sigma_-$, so each length lies in $[\sigma_-/4,\sigma_-/2]$. Thus the resulting Borel partition $U_1,\ldots,U_N$ of $D$ has every cell length between $c\eta_n\sigma_-$ and $\sigma_-/2$, every atom-cell diameter at most $2\eta_n\sigma_-$, and $N\le C(m_n+\sigma_-^{-1})\le C\sigma_n^{-1}\log n$, where $m_n$ is the number of atoms. Let $w_j=F_n(U_j)$, so $\sum_jw_j=1$. For all large $n$, the base density bounds give $c\eta_n\sigma_n\le\alpha(U_j)\le1$. Since $\eta_n=\sigma_n^8$, we have $c\eta_n\sigma_n\ge c'\eta_n^2$ eventually, and $N\eta_n\le C\sigma_n^7\log n\to0$ using $\sigma_n\le Cn^{-a_2}$. Apply [F3] with parameters $a=c'$, $b=2$, and $\eta=\eta_n$ to obtain an event $E_n$ with $\Pi_{DP}(E_n)\ge e^{-C N\log(e/\eta_n)}\ge e^{-C\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2},$ on which $F(D^c)\le C\eta_n$, $\sum_j|F(U_j)-w_j|\le C\eta_n$, and $F(U_j)\ge\eta_n^2/2$ for every $j$. [A1, F3, F5, F7, given, construct]

2.1 For $F$ in $E_n$, compare $p_{F,\sigma}$ with $p_{F_n,\sigma}$, uniformly for $s_-\sigma_n\le\sigma\le s_+\sigma_n$. The [F7] location derivative bound and atom-cell diameter at most $2\eta_n\sigma_-$ make the within-cell $L^1$ error at most $C\eta_n$; the gap cells and $D^c$ have total $F$-mass at most $C\eta_n$, and the cell-weight discrepancies sum to at most $C\eta_n$. Since each normal density has $L^1$ norm one, these terms give $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F_n,\sigma}\|_1\le C\eta_n$. For $u,v>0$, completing the square gives $\int\phi_u(y)\phi_v(x-y)\,dy=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(u^2+v^2)}}e^{-x^2/(2(u^2+v^2))}=\phi_{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}(x),$ since $y^2/u^2+(x-y)^2/v^2=((u^2+v^2)/(u^2v^2))(y-u^2x/(u^2+v^2))^2+x^2/(u^2+v^2)$. Also, for any densities $f,g,k$, Tonelli and the triangle inequality give $\|f*k-g*k\|_1\le\int\!\int|f(y)-g(y)|k(x-y)\,dy\,dx=\|f-g\|_1$. Apply these identities with $u=\sigma_-$ and $v=\sqrt{\sigma^2-\sigma_-^2}$ to obtain $\|p_{F_n,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_1\le C\eta_n$. Thus [F6] gives $h(p_{F,\sigma},p_{P_0,\sigma})\le C\sqrt{\eta_n}$, and the assumed bias bound gives $h(p_0,p_{F,\sigma})\le C(\sigma_n^2+\sqrt{\eta_n})\le C\sigma_n^2$. [F1, F2, F6, F7, given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 For every $x\in K$, the interval $[x-\sigma_-,x+\sigma_-]$ contains a full cell $U_j$ because $D$ contains a fixed neighborhood of $K$ and all cells have length at most $\sigma_-/2$. On this interval $\phi_\sigma(x-z)\ge c/\sigma$ for $s_-\sigma_n\le\sigma\le s_+\sigma_n$. Therefore [F1] and the cell-mass lower bound in step 1.2 give $p_{F,\sigma}(x)\ge c\eta_n^2/\sigma_n$. Since $p_0$ is bounded and vanishes outside $K$, this implies $R_n:=\|p_0/p_{F,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\sigma_n\eta_n^{-2}=C\sigma_n^{-15}$. The polynomial lower bound on $\sigma_n$ makes $1+\log^+R_n\le C\log n$. Applying [F4] to the Hellinger bound in step 2.1 yields both local KL quantities at most $C\sigma_n^4(\log n)^2\le C\delta_n^2$. [F1, F4, F6, F7, given, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The scale event $S\in[s_-,s_+]$ has probability $g>0$ and is independent of $F$. Thus the subset $E_n\times\{S\in[s_-,s_+]\}$ is contained in the displayed local KL/log-square set and has prior probability at least $g e^{-C\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2}$. By the definition of $\delta_n$, $n\delta_n^2\ge\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2$, so increasing $C_1$ absorbs $g$ and proves the required lower bound. [given, step 1.2, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $p_0$ be supported on a compact interval $I=[L,U]$ with
$L<U$, let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$ for a finite nonzero base measure whose
density is bounded below on a neighborhood of $I$, and let $S\sim G$ be
independent with $\sigma=\sigma_nS$. Put $R=(U-L)/2$ and, for $d>0$,
$I_d=[L-d,U+d]$.
Observe IID data from $p_0$ under the location-mixture density
$p_{F,\sigma}$. Let $\epsilon_n,\delta_n>0$ with
$n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$ and $n\delta_n^2\to\infty$. Suppose the local KL
and log-square prior-mass condition gives a denominator event
$$P_0^n\{D_n\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}\}\longrightarrow1,$$
where $D_n=\int\prod_i p_{F,\sigma}(X_i)/p_0(X_i)\,\Pi_n(dF,d\sigma)$.
Choose $s_n\to0$ and put $q_n=2\Phi(-R/s_n)$, where $\Phi$ is the
standard normal distribution function. If
$$nq_n-(C_0+2)n\delta_n^2\to\infty,\qquad
n\epsilon_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}\to0,$$
then the posterior complement of
$$\mathcal S_n:=\{(F,\sigma):\sigma\le s_n,\ F(I_d^c)\le\epsilon_n^2\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC; compactly supported truth; positive continuous base density near its support; the DP normal-mixture model and independent scale prior; the denominator event; and the two displayed asymptotic conditions.

[A1] Full AC supplies the DP construction and the directional KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]

[F1] [[thm-dirichlet-process-posterior-update]]: conditionally on latent IID locations $\theta_{1:n}\mid F\sim F^{\otimes n}$, the posterior law of $F$ is $DP(\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{\theta_i})$.

[F2] [[thm-dirichlet-process-polya-urn-predictive-law]]: conditionally on all latent locations except $\theta_i$, the prior predictive law of $\theta_i$ is $(\alpha+\sum_{k\ne i}\delta_{\theta_k})/(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1)$, by exchangeability.

[F3] [[thm-dirichlet-process-posterior-update]] and [[thm-dirichlet-process-polya-urn-predictive-law]]: under the posterior $DP(\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{\theta_i})$, the next latent location has predictive probability $(\alpha(A)+\sum_i\mathbf1_A(\theta_i))/(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)$; because its conditional law given $F$ is $F$, this is the posterior mean of $F(A)$.

[F4] [[lem-iid-posterior-denominator-lower-bound-from-kl-mass]]: the local KL/log-square prior-mass condition gives the displayed lower bound for $D_n$ with probability tending to one.

[F5] [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]: the latent observation likelihood is $\phi_\sigma(x-\theta)=(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}e^{-(x-\theta)^2/(2\sigma^2)}$.

[F6] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative likelihood numerators may be integrated in either order.

[F7] [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]: for a nonnegative random variable $Y$ and $a>0$, $P(Y\ge a)\le E[Y]/a$.

[F8] [[def-dirichlet-process]] and [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]]: $DP(\alpha)$ is an evaluation-measurable random probability measure with the stated Dirichlet finite-partition laws.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The latent representation is $\theta_i\mid F\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}\sim F$ and $X_i\mid\theta_i,\sigma\sim N(\theta_i,\sigma^2)$ independently. Use the test $\varphi_n=\mathbf1\{\text{some }X_i\notin I\}$. Its type-I error is zero. For fixed $\theta$ and $\sigma$, set $g(\theta)=P(\theta+\sigma Z\in I)=\Phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)-\Phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)$. Then $g'(\theta)=\sigma^{-1}\left[\phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)-\phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)\right].$ For $\theta\le(L+U)/2$, $|L-\theta|\le|U-\theta|$, so $g'(\theta)\ge0$ because the standard normal density decreases with absolute value; for $\theta\ge(L+U)/2$ the inequality reverses and $g'(\theta)\le0$. Thus $g$ is maximized at the midpoint, where the component leakage is $2\Phi(-R/\sigma)$. Every component with $\sigma>s_n$ therefore puts probability at least $q_n=2\Phi(-R/s_n)$ outside $I$, and $P_{F,\sigma}^n(\varphi_n=0)\le(1-q_n)^n\le e^{-nq_n}$. [A1, F5, given, construct]

1.2 By [F8] the latent DP model is a measurable prior law. Introduce the latent locations $\theta_{1:n}$. Given these locations, $X_{1:n}$ and $\sigma$, the observation likelihood is independent of $F$, so [F1] gives the conditional law $DP(\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{\theta_i})$. Given this updated $F$, the next latent location has conditional law $F$; applying [F3] to that predictive draw gives $E[F(A)\mid\theta_{1:n},X_{1:n},\sigma]=\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_i\mathbf1_A(\theta_i)}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n}$ for every Borel set $A$. With $A=I_d^c$, conditional Markov inequality yields $\Pi_n(F(A)>\epsilon_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})\le\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_iP(\theta_i\in A,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})}{\epsilon_n^2(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)}.$ [F1, F3, F7, F8, given, algebra]

1.3 Fix an index $i$ and condition on $\theta_{-i},X_{1:n},\sigma$. The latent vector is exchangeable because its conditional law given $F$ is IID. Reordering $\theta_i$ last and applying [F2] shows its prior predictive law given $\theta_{-i}$ is $H_i=(\alpha+\sum_{k\ne i}\delta_{\theta_k})/(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1)$. Bayes' formula multiplies this measure by the likelihood $\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)$. Almost surely $X_i\in I$. On $A=I_d^c$, $|X_i-t|\ge d$, so the likelihood numerator is at most $C\sigma^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. For $\sigma\le s_n$, the denominator is at least the base-measure contribution $\frac{1}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1}\int_{X_i-\sigma}^{X_i+\sigma}\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)\,\alpha(dt)\ge\frac{c}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1},$ because the base density is bounded below near $I$ and $[X_i-\sigma,X_i+\sigma]$ lies there for all sufficiently large $n$. Consequently $P(\theta_i\in A\mid\theta_{-i},X_{1:n},\sigma)\le Cn\sigma^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2\sigma^2)}\le Cn s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)},$ where $s^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s^2)}$ is increasing on $0<s<d$. [A1, F2, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 Let $N_n^H$ be the likelihood-ratio numerator integrated over $\{\sigma>s_n\}$. By change of density and [F6], $E_0[(1-\varphi_n)N_n^H]\le e^{-nq_n}$. On the denominator event, [F7] therefore gives, for every $\zeta>0$, $P_0^n\{\Pi_n(\sigma>s_n\mid X_{1:n})>\zeta\}\le o(1)+\zeta^{-1}e^{(C_0+2)n\delta_n^2-nq_n}\longrightarrow0.$ [F4, F6, F7, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Substitute the step 1.3 bound into step 1.2 and use $\alpha(A)\le\alpha(\mathbb R)$. The resulting upper bound is $\frac{\alpha(\mathbb R)}{\epsilon_n^2(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)}+Cn\epsilon_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}+\Pi_n(\sigma>s_n\mid X_{1:n}),$ which tends to zero by $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, the second premise, and step 2.1. Thus the posterior probability of $F(I_d^c)>\epsilon_n^2$ tends to zero. Combining with step 2.1 proves the sieve-complement claim. [F4, F7, step 2.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, given, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For $A\ge1$, $\tau>0$, and $0<\epsilon<1/4$, let
$$\mathcal P_{A,\tau}:=\{p_{F,\sigma}:F([-A,A])=1,\ \tau\le\sigma\le2\tau\}.$$
There is a universal constant $C$ such that
$$\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal P_{A,\tau},h)\le C(A/\tau\vee1)\left[\log\!\left(\frac{C(A/\tau\vee1)}{\epsilon}\right)\right]^2.$$
The same bound, with a changed universal constant, holds for
$$\mathcal P_{A,\tau,\rho}:=\{p_{F,\sigma}:F([-A,A]^c)\le\rho,\ \tau\le\sigma\le2\tau\}$$
whenever $0\le\rho\le c\epsilon^2$ for a sufficiently small universal $c>0$.
Here $N$ is the covering number in the stated metric.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** $A\ge1$, $\tau>0$, $0<\epsilon<1/4$, AC, and the mixture density of [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-density-well-defined]].

[A1] Assume AC for the normal-density and finite-support approximation interfaces. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[lem-dirichlet-normal-mixture-finite-support-approximation]]: a mixture with mixing law on $[-A,A]$ is within $L^1$ error $\eta$ of a discrete mixture with at most $C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$ atoms.

[F2] [[lem-hellinger-distance-controls-l1-and-total-variation]]: for probability densities, Hellinger distance is a metric and $h^2(p,q)\le\int|p-q|d\lambda$.

[F3] [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]: $\phi_\sigma(x-z)=\sigma^{-1}\phi((x-z)/\sigma)$, with $\phi$ the standard normal density.

[F4] [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]]: the Hellinger metric used here is the root-L2 distance between square-root densities.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Put $K:=\lceil C_0(A/\tau\vee1)\log(e/\epsilon)\rceil$. By [F1], every $p_{F,\sigma}\in\mathcal P_{A,\tau}$ is within $L^1$ distance $\epsilon^2/C_1$ of a mixture with at most $K$ atoms, for a fixed sufficiently large $C_1$. Pad shorter mixtures by zero-weight atoms. [A1, F1, given, choose]

2.1 Differentiating the density in [F3] gives $\|\partial_z\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)\|_1=\sigma^{-1}E|Z|\le\sigma^{-1}$, since $2|Z|\le1+Z^2$ and $E Z^2=1$, and $\|\partial_\sigma\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)\|_1=\sigma^{-1}E|Z^2-1|\le2\sigma^{-1}$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Integrating these derivatives along the location and scale segments yields $\|\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)-\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z')\|_1\le |z-z'|/\sigma$ and $\|\phi_\sigma-\phi_{\sigma'}\|_1\le2|\sigma-\sigma'|/(\sigma\wedge\sigma')$. Now choose a scale grid in $[\tau,2\tau]$ and a location grid in $[-A,A]$, each with mesh at most $c_2\tau\epsilon^2$, and an $L^1$ grid on the $K$-simplex of mesh at most $c_2\epsilon^2$. Replacing the scale, locations and weights changes the mixture density in $L^1$ by at most $C c_2\epsilon^2$; choose $c_2$ so this plus the approximation from step 1.1 is at most $\epsilon^2/4$. Thus the resulting finite set is an $L^1$ cover of radius $\epsilon^2/4$, hence an $h$-cover of radius $\epsilon/2$ by [F2]. [A1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, given, construct]

3.1 The scale grid has at most $C\epsilon^{-2}$ points and the location grid at most $C(1+A/(\tau\epsilon^2))$ points. Rounding each of the first $K-1$ weights down to a mesh proportional to $\epsilon^2/K$ leaves the last weight nonnegative after setting it to make the sum one, gives at most $(CK/\epsilon^2)^K$ weight vectors, and changes their $L^1$ distance by at most $2c_2\epsilon^2$. Therefore the logarithm of the cover size is at most $C\log(e/\epsilon)+K\left[\log\!\left(\frac{C(A/\tau\vee1)}{\epsilon^2}\right)+\log\!\left(\frac{CK}{\epsilon^2}\right)\right]\le C(A/\tau\vee1)\left[\log\!\left(\frac{C(A/\tau\vee1)}{\epsilon}\right)\right]^2.$ The constructed finite set is an $h$-net of radius $\epsilon/2$, hence also a net of radius $\epsilon$; its cardinality therefore bounds the covering number and proves the first bound. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 If $r:=F([-A,A]^c)=0$, then $F$ already belongs to the compact-location class. If $0<r\le\rho<1$, let $F_A$ and $F_{A^c}$ be the normalized restrictions to $[-A,A]$ and its complement. Then $p_{F,\sigma}=(1-r)p_{F_A,\sigma}+r p_{F_{A^c},\sigma}$, so $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F_A,\sigma}\|_1\le2r$. By [F2], $h(p_{F,\sigma},p_{F_A,\sigma})\le\sqrt{2r}$; the triangle inequality in [F4] then transfers the compact cover to the tail-constrained class. For sufficiently small universal $c$, $\rho\le c\epsilon^2$ makes the truncation error at most $\epsilon/2$, so the radius-$\epsilon/2$ cover from steps 2.1–2.2 becomes a radius-$\epsilon$ cover after the constant rescaling used in the entropy bound. [A1, F2, F4, step 2.1, step 3.1, given, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://diamhomes.ewi.tudelft.nl/~avandervaart/books/bayesianstatistics"

## Statement

Assume AC, let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure of total mass $m$, and
let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$. Consider a finite partition
$(U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_N)$ with $\alpha(U_0)=0$ or
$0<\alpha(U_0)\le m$. Write $\alpha_j=\alpha(U_j)$ for $j\ge1$, and assume
$$a\eta^b\le\alpha_j\le1\quad(1\le j\le N),\qquad 0<\eta<1/4,qquad N\eta\le1/4,$$
for fixed $a,b>0$. For every $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_N)$ in the probability
simplex, there are constants $c,C>0$ depending only on $a,b,m,\alpha(U_0)$
such that
$$\Pr\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^N|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta,\quad
\min_{1\le j\le N}F(U_j)\ge\eta^2/2\right\}\ge C\exp\{-cN\log(e/\eta)\}.$$
For any compact $J\subset(0,m]$, the constants may instead depend only on
$a,b,m,J$ and are uniform over $\alpha(U_0)\in J$.
When $\alpha(U_0)=0$, the zero-base cell has $F(U_0)=0$ almost surely and is
omitted from the Dirichlet vector.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, a finite nonzero base measure, the stated finite partition, and $w$ in the $N$-simplex.

[A1] Full AC supplies the normalized-gamma Dirichlet-process existence interface and implies Countable Choice for the finite-dimensional Dirichlet density. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] [[def-dirichlet-process]] and [[thm-existence-of-dirichlet-process-by-normalized-gamma-poisson-random-measure]]: the finite-partition mass vector has the Dirichlet law with parameters $\alpha(U_j)$; zero-base cells have mass zero.

[F2] [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]: with positive parameters $(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_N)$, the simplex density is $\Gamma(m)\prod_{j=0}^Nx_j^{a_j-1}/\prod_{j=0}^N\Gamma(a_j)$, where $m=\sum_j a_j$; the zero-coordinate case is omitted.

[F3] The Euler Gamma values are positive and finite for positive arguments, and $\Gamma(s+1)=s\Gamma(s)$ for $s>0$. [[def-real-gamma-function-by-the-euler-integral]] [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]] [[thm-real-gamma-functional-equation]]

[F4] The real Gamma function is continuous and positive on $(0,\infty)$. [[thm-real-gamma-is-smooth]] [[thm-real-gamma-euler-integral-convergence]]

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 By [F1]–[F2], if $\alpha(U_0)>0$ the vector $(X_0,X_1,\ldots,X_N):=(F(U_0),F(U_1),\ldots,F(U_N))$ has the displayed Dirichlet density; if $\alpha(U_0)=0$, set $X_0=0$ and use the $N$-coordinate Dirichlet density. Choose an index $i_*$ with $w_{i_*}=\max_jw_j\ge1/N$. For every $j\ne i_*$ restrict $x_j$ to $[\max(w_j-\eta^2,\eta^2/2),\min(w_j+\eta^2,1)]$, an interval of length at least $\eta^2/2$. If $\alpha(U_0)>0$, also restrict $x_0$ to $[\eta^2/2,\eta^2]$ and define $x_{i_*}=1-x_0-\sum_{j\ne i_*}x_j$; if $\alpha(U_0)=0$, define $x_{i_*}=1-\sum_{j\ne i_*}x_j$. The deviations of the coordinates other than $i_*$ sum to at most $N\eta^2$, so $|x_{i_*}-w_{i_*}|\le N\eta^2$. Consequently the total event deviation is at most $2N\eta^2+\eta^2\le3\eta$; and $x_{i_*}\ge1/N-N\eta^2\ge\eta^2/2$ because $N\eta\le1/4$. These choices lie in the simplex, satisfy the event, and their integration region has coordinate volume at least $(\eta^2/2)^N$ when $\alpha(U_0)>0$ and $(\eta^2/2)^{N-1}$ when $\alpha(U_0)=0$. [A1, F1, F2, given, choose, construct]

2.1 For $0<a_j\le1$, split the Euler integral for $\Gamma(1+a_j)$ at $1$. On $(0,1]$, $t^{a_j}\le1$, and on $[1,\infty)$, $t^{a_j}\le t$, so $\Gamma(1+a_j)\le1+\int_1^\infty te^{-t}\,dt=1+2/e$. The functional equation in [F3] gives $\Gamma(a_j)\le(1+2/e)/a_j$. Put $c_\Gamma=(1+2/e)^{-1}$. When $\alpha(U_0)>0$, the normalizing coefficient in [F2] is at least $[\Gamma(m)/\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))]c_\Gamma^N\prod_{j=1}^N a_j$; when $\alpha(U_0)=0$ and $N\ge2$, it is at least $\Gamma(m)c_\Gamma^N\prod_{j=1}^N a_j$. These Gamma factors are positive by [F3]. On the region from step 1.1, each interval coordinate satisfies $x_j^{a_j-1}\ge1$. If $\alpha(U_0)>1$, its factor is at least $(\eta^2/2)^{m}$; if $0<\alpha(U_0)\le1$, it is at least one. For $\alpha(U_0)>0$, integrating the density over that region is therefore at least $[\Gamma(m)/\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))](c_\Gamma a/2)^N\eta^{(b+2)N}$, multiplied by $(\eta^2/2)^m$ when $\alpha(U_0)>1$. For $\alpha(U_0)=0$ and $N\ge2$, the coordinate volume $(\eta^2/2)^{N-1}\ge(\eta^2/2)^N$ gives a lower bound $\Gamma(m)(c_\Gamma a/2)^N\eta^{(b+2)N}$. If $\alpha(U_0)$ ranges in a compact $J\subset(0,m]$, [F4] bounds $\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))$ above uniformly, so $\Gamma(m)/\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))$ is uniformly bounded below; all other Gamma factors here are fixed and positive. Since $a,b$ are fixed, $(c_\Gamma a/2)^N\eta^{(b+2)N}\ge\exp\{-c_1N\log(e/\eta)\}$ for some $c_1>0$. When present, the residual factor $(\eta^2/2)^m$ is at least $\exp\{-c_2N\log(e/\eta)\}$ because $m$ is fixed and $N\ge1$. Combining these bounds gives $C\exp\{-cN\log(e/\eta)\}$ with constants depending only on $a,b,m,\alpha(U_0)$, uniformly when $\alpha(U_0)\in J$. If $\alpha(U_0)=0$ and $N=1$, then $F(U_1)=w_1=1$ almost surely, so the event has probability one and satisfies the claimed bound after taking $C\le1$. The resulting probability is the one in the Statement by [F1]. [A1, F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra, cases] ∎

## Statement

Assume countable choice for the $L^2$ prior construction, with the full posterior kernel supplied as in [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Fix a finite set $J$ of wavelet coordinates in the product white-noise model of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Suppose $\varphi$ is bounded and continuous at each normalized truth coefficient $r_j=\theta_{0,j}/\sigma_j$, with $\varphi(r_j)>0$. Let $\widetilde\Pi_{n,J}$ be the conditional posterior law of $\sqrt n(\theta_J-X_J)$ given the full data. If $J=\varnothing$, both laws are the unique probability on the zero-dimensional one-point space. For nonempty $J$, the posterior and Gaussian densities $p_{n,J}$ and $\phi_J$ on $\mathbb R^{|J|}$ satisfy

$$\int_{\mathbb R^{|J|}}|p_{n,J}(u\mid X)-\phi_J(u)|\,du\longrightarrow0$$

in probability under the true white-noise law. Consequently $d_{\rm TV}(\widetilde\Pi_{n,J},N_{|J|}(0,I))\to0$, where $d_{\rm TV}(\mu,\nu):=\sup_A|\mu(A)-\nu(A)|$ and $N_{|J|}(0,I)$ is the product of $|J|$ standard normal laws.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]: The posterior marginal on every finite coordinate set is the product of the coordinate Bayes densities.

[F2] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: Pointwise convergence under an integrable dominating function gives convergence of the integrals.

[F3] [[thm-finite-and-countable-subadditivity-of-measures]]: The probability of a countable union of events is at most the sum of their probabilities.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable choice is used for the $L^2$ prior construction; the full posterior kernel is supplied as model input in [F1], and the finite-dimensional density limit is choice-free.

**Given:** Countable choice, a fixed finite coordinate set $J$, the coordinate prior densities and white-noise observations, boundedness of $\varphi$, and its continuity and strict positivity at each $r_j$.

## Proof

1.1 Fix one coordinate $j=(l,k)$ and write $r=\theta_{0,j}/\sigma_j$. Under the true law, $X_j/\sigma_j=r+Z_j/(\sqrt n\sigma_j)\to r$ in probability, and $b_n=(\sqrt n\sigma_j)^{-1}\to0$. By [F1], under [A1], the posterior density of $U_n=\sqrt n(\theta_j-X_j)$ is $p_n(u\mid X_j)=\frac{e^{-u^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nu)}{c_n(X_j)},\qquad c_n(X_j)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-v^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nv)\,dv.$ For any deterministic sequence $x_n/\sigma_j\to r$, boundedness of $\varphi$ and [F2] give $c_n(x_n)\to\varphi(r)\sqrt{2\pi}>0$. [A1, F1, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Along such a deterministic sequence, $p_n(u\mid x_n)\to(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}$ pointwise and is eventually bounded by a constant multiple of $e^{-u^2/2}$. A second application of [F2] gives convergence in $L^1(du)$, hence convergence in total variation. Since $X_j/\sigma_j\to r$ in probability, if the total-variation convergence in probability failed, some subsequence would have error probability bounded below. Select a further subsequence for which $\mathbb P(|X_j/\sigma_j-r|>2^{-q})\le2^{-q}$ at its $q$th term; [F3] bounds each union of tail events by the corresponding geometric tail, which tends to zero, so the further subsequence converges almost surely to $r$, contradicting the deterministic conclusion. [F2, F3, step 1.1, choose, algebra]

3.1 For finite nonempty $J$, [F1] makes the scaled posterior and its Gaussian target product measures. Telescope the difference of their product densities one coordinate at a time. Integrating the absolute value of each term gives the $L^1$ distance of that coordinate pair, since every other coordinate density integrates to $1$. Thus the joint $L^1$ distance is at most the sum of the finitely many coordinate $L^1$ distances, which tends to zero in probability by step 2.1. For each measurable event $A$, the absolute difference of its probabilities is at most this $L^1$ distance, so the total-variation conclusion follows. [F1, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m>0$, $B=\sum_j\beta_j$, and let $Z_j$ be independent $\operatorname{Gamma}(\beta_j,1)$ variables. Put $S=\sum_j Z_j$. Then $\omega=(Z_j/S)_j$ is $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$, and $S$ is $\operatorname{Gamma}(B,1)$, with mean $B$ and variance $B$. Each $Z_j$ has mean $\beta_j$, variance $\beta_j$, and moment-generating function $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=(1-u)^{-\beta_j}$ for every real $u<1$. For real $q_j$ satisfying $|q_j|\le b$, put $T(q)=\sum_jq_j(Z_j-\beta_j)$ and $V=\sum_j\beta_jq_j^2$. If $V>0$, then for $x>0$,
$$\Pr\{|T(q)|>x\}\le2\exp\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2(V+bx)}\right\}.$$
If $V=0$, $T(q)=0$ almost surely. Sums of disjoint groups of the $Z_j$ are independent Gamma variables with their respective summed shapes.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Full AC, the positive finite shape vector, and the weights in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-gamma-distribution-shape-rate]] and [[lem-gamma-density-normalization]] supply the normalized density $z^{a-1}e^{-z}/\Gamma(a)$, $z>0$, for $a>0$.

[F2] [[def-dirichlet-distribution]] specifies the normalized density $\Gamma(B)\prod_j\omega_j^{\beta_j-1}/\prod_j\Gamma(\beta_j)$ on the simplex, and the point mass at one for $m=1$.

[F3] Finite product laws and nonnegative changes of variables are supplied by [[thm-sigma-finite-product-measure-exists-is-rectangular-and-is-unique]] and [[thm-c-one-change-of-variables-for-nonnegative-lebesgue-measurable-functions]].

[F4] [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]] gives the exponential tail bound.

[F5] [[lem-uniqueness-of-a-multivariate-exponential-transform]] identifies laws having the same finite moment-generating transform near zero under AC.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 The product Gamma law exists by [F3]. In its density make the substitution $z_j=s\omega_j$, $\omega_m=1-\sum_{j<m}\omega_j$. Its Jacobian is $s^{m-1}$: factor $s$ from the proportion columns of the derivative matrix and add its first $m-1$ rows to the last; the remaining last row has first entry one and all other entries zero. The resulting density factors as $s^{B-1}e^{-s}/\Gamma(B)$ times the simplex density in [F2]. Integrating either normalized factor proves both distributional assertions. For $m=1$, $\omega_1=1$ directly. [F1, F2, F3, given, algebra, cases]

1.2 Substituting $y=(1-u)z$ in the Euler Gamma density gives $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=(1-u)^{-\beta_j}$ for $u<1$. Its first two derivatives at zero yield mean $\beta_j$ and variance $\beta_j$; differentiation is justified by an exponential majorant with any fixed parameter in $(0,1)$. Independence makes the joint transform of disjoint group sums the product $\prod_h(1-u_h)^{-\sum_{j\in I_h}\beta_j}$, which is the transform of the corresponding product Gamma law. By [F5], these are the same laws. In particular $S$ has the asserted mean and variance, also following from step 1.1. [F1, F3, F5, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 For $|\lambda|b<1$, independence and step 1.2 give $\log\mathbb E e^{\lambda T(q)}=\sum_j\beta_j[-\log(1-\lambda q_j)-\lambda q_j]\le\lambda^2 V/[2(1-|\lambda|b)]$. Indeed the convergent logarithm series gives $-\log(1-u)-u\le\sum_{r\ge2}|u|^r/r\le u^2/[2(1-|u|)]$ for $|u|<1$. If $V>0$, set $\lambda=x/(V+bx)$; exponential Markov then bounds the upper tail by $\exp[-x^2/(2(V+bx))]$. Apply the same calculation to $-q$ and sum the bounds. If $V=0$, positivity of all $\beta_j$ forces every $q_j=0$, so $T(q)=0$. [F4, step 1.2, algebra, cases] ∎

## Statement

Assume AC. Let $p\in C^2(\mathbb R)$ be a nonnegative compactly supported probability density and suppose
$$ J:=\int_{\{p>0\}}\frac{(p''(x))^2}{p(x)}\,dx<\infty. $$
For $\sigma>0$, set $q_\sigma=p*\phi_\sigma$, where $\phi_\sigma$ is the centered normal density with standard deviation $\sigma$. Then
$$ \int\frac{(p-q_\sigma)^2}{q_\sigma}\,dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q_\sigma)\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \int p\left[\log\frac p{q_\sigma}\right]^2dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J. $$
The logarithmic integrands are zero where $p=0$. No unimodality or uniform bound on $p/q_\sigma$ is assumed.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** AC and the density and integrability hypotheses of the Statement.

[F1] The normal kernel is $\phi_\sigma(x)=(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}$ and integrates to one. [[lem-normal-location-scale-density]]

[F2] Cauchy–Schwarz bounds an integral of a product by the product of its two $L^2$ norms. [[cor-cauchy-schwarz-inequality-for-l-two]]

[F3] Nonnegative product integrals may be taken in either order. [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]

[F4] The directional KL divergence of two densities with absolute continuity is the integral of their log ratio under the first law. [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]

## Proof

1.1 At every zero of the nonnegative differentiable function $p$, $p'=0$. At each accumulation point of its zero set, differentiation along zeros of $p'$ gives $p''=0$; isolated zeros form a countable set. Thus $p''=0$ almost everywhere on $\{p=0\}$. Put $r=p''/p$ on $\{p>0\}$ and zero elsewhere. Then $p''=rp$ almost everywhere, $\int r^2p=J$, and [F2] gives $\int|p''|\le\sqrt J$. Both $p$ and $p''$ are continuous and compactly supported. [F2, given, algebra]

1.2 Let $P_t f=f*\phi_{\sqrt t}$ for $t>0$. Direct differentiation of [F1] gives $\partial_t\phi_{\sqrt t}=\tfrac12\partial_x^2\phi_{\sqrt t}$. Differentiation under the compactly supported $p$ integral and two integrations by parts therefore give $\partial_tP_t p=\tfrac12P_t p''$. The boundary terms vanish because $p,p'$ have compact support. Gaussian approximate identities converge uniformly on continuous compactly supported functions: split their convolution integral at $|z|\le\delta$, where uniform continuity controls the integrand difference, and its complement, whose normal mass tends to zero by scaling and integrability of [F1]. Integrating the derivative from a positive $\varepsilon$ to $t$ and letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ consequently yields $p-P_t p=-\tfrac12\int_0^tP_s p''\,ds$ pointwise. [F1, step 1.1, algebra]

2.1 Fix $t>0$ and put $q=P_t p$, which is positive everywhere. For $0<s\le t$, the Gaussian formula gives $\phi_{\sqrt t}(z)\ge\sqrt{s/t}\,\phi_{\sqrt s}(z)$ for every $z$, hence $q\ge\sqrt{s/t}P_s p$. Applying [F2] inside the convolution and then [F3] gives $|P_s p''|^2\le(P_s p)P_s(r^2p)$ and therefore $\int |P_s p''|^2/q\le\sqrt{t/s}\int P_s(r^2p)=\sqrt{t/s}J$. These inequalities remain valid if one of the pointwise nonnegative integrals is infinite. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Apply [F2] to the time integral in step 1.2 with weights $w(s)=(t/s)^{1/4}$. Since $\int_0^t w(s)ds=4t/3$, it gives $|p-q|^2\le\tfrac14(4t/3)\int_0^t w(s)^{-1}|P_s p''|^2ds$. Divide by $q$, integrate and use [F3] and step 2.1. The result is $\int(p-q)^2/q\le\tfrac14(4t/3)J\int_0^t(t/s)^{1/4}ds=(4/9)t^2J$. In particular all these weighted integrals are finite. [F2, F3, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.1 For $u>0$, $\log u\le u-1$ gives $u\log u-u+1\le(u-1)^2$. Also write $u=e^{2v}$. The inequality $|v|\le|\sinh v|$, obtained by integrating $\cosh v\ge1$, gives $u(\log u)^2\le(u-1)^2$. At $u=0$, both inequalities extend by their finite limits, with $u\log u=u(\log u)^2=0$. Apply these pointwise bounds to $u=p/q$ and integrate against $q$. Since $p,q$ integrate to one, [F4] identifies the first integral as KL; its negative part is integrable because $u\log u\ge-e^{-1}$. Both requested logarithmic quantities are at most the chi-square integral from step 2.2. Taking $t=\sigma^2$ proves the Statement. [F1, F4, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

id: lem-hellinger-ratio-controls-kl-moments
kind: lemma
title: "A bounded likelihood ratio controls KL and log-square moments by Hellinger distance"
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: bayesian-computational-statistics-62
dependency_level: 1
deps:

sources:

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1885"
    - title: "Subhashis Ghosal and Aad W. van der Vaart, Fundamentals of Nonparametric Bayesian Inference, Lemma 6.13"
      url: "https://diamhomes.ewi.tudelft.nl/~avandervaart/books/bayesianstatistics"

## Statement

Let $p,q$ be probability densities relative to one measure $\mu$, assume
$p\,d\mu\ll q\,d\mu$, let
$h^2:=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2d\mu$, and suppose
$R:=\operatorname*{ess,sup}_{q\,d\mu}(p/q)<\infty$, with $p/q=0$ on
$\{q=0,p=0\}$. Then $p\ll q$ and for a universal constant $C$,
$$\mathrm{KL}(p\,d\mu\Vert q\,d\mu)\le C h^2(1+\log^+R),\qquad \int p\left[\log(p/q)\right]^2d\mu\le C h^2(1+\log^+R)^2.$$
The logarithm is assigned value zero on $\{p=0\}$; the moment integrand is
also set to zero there.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Two probability densities $p,q$ relative to one measure, $p\,d\mu\ll q\,d\mu$, and finite $R$ as in the Statement.

[A1] Assume AC for the library directional KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]

[F1] [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]]: $h^2=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2d\mu$.

[F2] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]: when $p\,d\mu\ll q\,d\mu$, the directional KL divergence is the integral of $\log(p/q)$ against $p\,d\mu$.

[F3] [[def-natural-logarithm]] and [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]: $\log$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)$, and $\log x\to0$ as $x\to1$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Put $u=p/q$ on $\{q>0\}$. The explicit absolute-continuity premise gives $p=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{q=0\}$. Define $g(u)=(\sqrt u-1)^2$ and $a(u)=(u\log u-u+1)/g(u)$, $b(u)=u(\log u)^2/g(u)$ for $u\ne1$, with their limiting values at $u=1$ and $u=0$. These limits are finite: at $u=1$ the Taylor expansions of $\sqrt u$ and $\log u$ give $a(1)=2$, $b(1)=4$, while $u\log u\to0$ and $u(\log u)^2\to0$ as $u\downarrow0$. Thus $a,b$ are continuous on $[0,2]$ and bounded there by [F3]. [A1, F3, given, algebra]

2.1 For $u\ge2$, $g(u)=u(1-u^{-1/2})^2\ge u(1-2^{-1/2})^2$, while $0\le u\log u-u+1\le u\log u$ and $u(\log u)^2$ retain their displayed forms. Hence $a(u)\le C\log u$ and $b(u)\le C(\log u)^2$ for a universal $C$. Combining with step 1.1, for every $0\le u\le R$, $u\log u-u+1\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R),\qquad u(\log u)^2\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R)^2.$ [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Integrating the first inequality in step 2.1 against $q\,d\mu$ gives the KL bound, since $\int q(u\log u-u+1)d\mu=\int p\log(p/q)d\mu$ by $\int p=\int q=1$ and [F2]. Integrating the second gives the log-square bound. Finally $\int qg,d\mu=h^2$ by [F1], so both right sides have the claimed factors of $h^2$. [A1, F1, F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

      url: "https://arxiv.org/pdf/0708.1885"
    - title: "Subhashis Ghosal, Jayanta K. Ghosh and Aad W. van der Vaart, Convergence rates of posterior distributions, Theorem 2.1 and Lemma 8.1"
      url: "https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1016218228"

## Statement

Assume AC. For each $n$, let $\Pi_n$ be a prior on a measurable parameter
space $\Theta_n^*$, and let $p_\theta$ be a jointly measurable family of finite-valued densities
against one sigma-finite measure, and let $p_0$ be the true density for IID
data $X_1,\ldots,X_n$. Let $\epsilon_n,\delta_n>0$ satisfy
$\delta_n\le\epsilon_n$, $n\delta_n^2\to\infty$, and
$n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$. Suppose for a constant $C_0>0$ that
$$\Pi_n\!\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\delta_n^2,\quad
P_0\left[\log\frac{p_0}{p_\theta}\right]^2\le\delta_n^2\right\}\ge e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}.$$
Let $S_n\subseteq\Theta_n^*$ be a measurable sieve with
$\Pi_n(S_n^c\mid X_{1:n})\to0$ in $P_0^n$-probability. Partition it into
countably many measurable sets $S_{n,j}$, put $\pi_{n,j}=\Pi_n(S_{n,j})$,
and let $N_{n,j}=N(\epsilon_n,\{p_\theta:\theta\in S_{n,j}\},h)$ be the
finite covering number as defined in [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]], with centers in that density class, whenever $\pi_{n,j}>0$. If
$$e^{-n\epsilon_n^2}\sum_{j:\pi_{n,j}>0}\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\longrightarrow0,$$
then for every sufficiently large fixed $M$, the posterior mass of
$$\{\theta:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n\}$$
converges to zero in $P_0^n$-probability.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** A dominated IID model with a jointly measurable density family, AC, the displayed local prior mass, a measurable sieve with vanishing posterior complement, and a countable measurable partition satisfying the weighted entropy condition.

[A1] Assume AC for the directional KL convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]] [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]]

[F1] [[lem-iid-posterior-denominator-lower-bound-from-kl-mass]]: if the local KL and log-square set has prior mass at least $e^{-C_0n\delta_n^2}$, then, except with probability at most $(n\delta_n^2)^{-1}$, the normalized likelihood denominator is at least $e^{-(C_0+2)n\delta_n^2}$.

[F2] [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]]: $h^2(P,Q)=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2d\mu$ and $\int\sqrt{pq}d\mu=1-h^2(P,Q)/2$.

[F3] [[lem-hellinger-distance-controls-l1-and-total-variation]]: Hellinger distance is a metric and event-supremum total variation is bounded by Hellinger distance, including for finite product laws.

[F4] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: nonnegative measurable likelihood-ratio integrands may be integrated in either order.

[F5] [[def-dominated-statistical-experiment]] and [[def-likelihood-density]]: all densities are relative to the same fixed sigma-finite measure; the supplied family is jointly measurable, so likelihood-ratio integrals are measurable.

[F6] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]] and [[thm-factorization-of-expectations-for-independent-variables]]: disjoint finite blocks of an IID sample are independent, and expectations of products of nonnegative functions of those blocks factor.

[F7] [[cor-markov-inequality-for-random-variables]]: for a nonnegative random variable $Y$ and $a>0$, $P(Y\ge a)\le E[Y]/a$.

[F8] [[def-probability-measure]] and [[def-measure-with-density]]: $P_0$ and each model law are probability measures represented by their displayed densities; integrating $p_\theta/p_0$ under $P_0$ gives $\int_{\{p_0>0\}}p_\theta\,d\mu\le1$.

[F9] [[def-covering-packing-bracketing-number-and-metric-entropy]]: $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,h)$ is the least finite number of centers from $\mathcal F$ whose closed Hellinger balls of radius $\epsilon$ cover $\mathcal F$.

## Proof

**Given:** The hypotheses in the Statement.

1.1 Put $x_n=n\epsilon_n^2$, $y_n=n\delta_n^2$, and let $D_n$ be the likelihood denominator relative to $p_0^n$. By [F1], on an event $\Omega_n$ with $P_0^n(\Omega_n^c)\le y_n^{-1}$, $D_n\ge e^{-(C_0+2)y_n}$. [A1, F1, given]

1.2 Write $T_n=\sum_j\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}$ and $s_n=e^{-x_n}T_n$, so $s_n\to0$. Fix $K>2(C_0+3)$ and split indices into active $J_n^+=\{j:\pi_{n,j}\ge e^{-Kx_n}\}$ and small-mass $J_n^-$. Since $N_{n,j}\ge1$, $\sum_{J_n^-}\pi_{n,j}\le e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n=e^{(1-K/2)x_n}s_n$. For active $j$, $\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\le T_n=e^{x_n}s_n$, hence $\log(N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j})\le(2+2K)x_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$. [given, algebra]

1.3 Fix a sufficiently large constant $M$. If $M\epsilon_n\ge\sqrt2$, then the alternative is empty because Hellinger distance is at most $\sqrt2$, and the desired posterior mass is zero for this $n$. For the remaining $n$, choose, by [A1], a finite $\epsilon_n$-cover with centers in each active stratum's density image, as allowed by [F9]. For every center $q$ within $\epsilon_n$ of a density $p_\theta$ satisfying $h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n$, the triangle inequality gives $h(q,p_0)>(M-1)\epsilon_n$. Set $m_n=\left\lceil\frac{2\log 8}{(M-1)^2\epsilon_n^2}\right\rceil$. On a block of $m_n$ observations define $T_q=\mathbf1\{\prod_iq(X_i)>\prod_i p_0(X_i)\}$. On rejection, $p_0^{\otimes m_n}\le\sqrt{p_0^{\otimes m_n}q^{\otimes m_n}}$, so its type-I error is at most the product affinity; on acceptance, $q^{\otimes m_n}\le\sqrt{p_0^{\otimes m_n}q^{\otimes m_n}}$, so its type-II error under $q$ has the same bound. By [F2], this affinity is $(1-h^2(q,p_0)/2)^{m_n}\le e^{-m_nh^2(q,p_0)/2}\le1/8$. [A1, F2, F9, given, construct]

2.1 If $h(p_\theta,q)\le\epsilon_n$, product affinity gives $h^2(P_\theta^{m_n},Q^{m_n})=2\left[1-\left(1-h^2(p_\theta,q)/2\right)^{m_n}\right]\le m_n\epsilon_n^2$, using $1-(1-u)^m\le mu$ for $u\in[0,1]$; [F3] bounds their total variation by $\sqrt{m_n}\epsilon_n$. Since $M\epsilon_n<\sqrt2$, $\epsilon_n^2<2/M^2$ and $m_n\epsilon_n^2\le\frac{2\log8}{(M-1)^2}+\frac{2}{M^2}\le1/64$ for sufficiently large $M$. The total variation is then at most $1/8$. Therefore the block test in step 1.3 rejects with probability at least $3/4$ under every $p_\theta$ in the alternative and at most $1/8$ under $p_0$. [F2, F3, step 1.3, algebra]

3.1 Divide $L_n=\lfloor n/m_n\rfloor$ disjoint blocks and let $Y_k$ be their block-test indicators. Under each IID law the indicators are independent by [F6]; their means are at most $a=1/8$ under $P_0$ and at least $b=3/4$ under every alternative by step 2.1. For independent Bernoulli variables with means at most $a$, exponential Markov [F7] gives $P_0(L_n^{-1}\sum Y_k\ge t)\le e^{-L_nD(t\Vert a)}$; with means at least $b$, the negative-exponential bound gives $P_\theta(L_n^{-1}\sum Y_k<t)\le e^{-L_nD(t\Vert b)}$, where $D(t\Vert u)=t\log(t/u)+(1-t)\log((1-t)/(1-u))$. These bounds follow by bounding each moment generating function by $1-u+ue^\lambda$ (using $u=a$ for $\lambda>0$, $u=b$ for $\lambda<0$) and optimizing over $\lambda$. [F6, F7, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The function $D(t\Vert a)-D(t\Vert b)$ is affine and strictly increasing on $[a,b]$, is negative at $a$, and equals $D(b\Vert a)>0$ at $b$. Let $t_*$ be its unique zero. By AC [A1], for each active $j$ choose $t_j\in[t_*,b]$ such that $L_n\{D(t_j\Vert a)-D(t_j\Vert b)\}=\log(N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j})$. This is possible after increasing $M$: writing $A=2\log 8$, $M\epsilon_n<\sqrt2$ implies $A/((M-1)^2\epsilon_n^2)>2$ for sufficiently large $M$, so the ceiling in $m_n$ costs at most a fixed factor; since $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, the floor in $L_n$ also costs at most a fixed factor eventually. Hence $L_n\ge cM^2x_n$ for a universal $c>0$, while step 1.2 bounds the right side by $(2+2K)x_n$. Define $\phi_{n,j}$ as the maximum of the block-majority tests over its $N_{n,j}$ centers, using threshold $t_j$. Continuity on $[t_*,b]$ and positivity of both divergences at $t_*$ give a constant $c_*>0$ such that $(D(t\Vert a)+D(t\Vert b))/2\ge c_*$ there. The null union bound and step 3.1 give $P_0^n(\phi_{n,j}=1)\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}$; the same Chernoff bound for a center within $\epsilon_n$ of each alternative gives $\sup_{\theta\in S_{n,j}:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n}P_\theta^n(\phi_{n,j}=0)\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}$ by step 2.1. [A1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 Let $\phi_n$ be one on the countable union of the rejection events of $\phi_{n,j}$ over $j\in J_n^+$ and zero otherwise; it is measurable as a countable union of measurable events. The union bound and step 4.1 give $P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. For the tested likelihood numerator on an active stratum, Tonelli [F4], the jointly measurable likelihood interface [F5] and change of density give $E_0[(1-\phi_n)\int_{\{\theta\in S_{n,j}:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n\}}\prod_i\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi_n(d\theta)]\le\pi_{n,j}\sup_{\theta\text{ in the set}}P_\theta^n(1-\phi_{n,j})\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}.$ [F4, F5, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Write $d_n=e^{-(C_0+2)y_n}$. For the active numerator $R_n^+$, step 5.1 gives $P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$ and $E_0[(1-\phi_n)R_n^+]\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. Thus, for every fixed $\zeta>0$, $P_0^n(R_n^+/D_n>\zeta)\le P_0^n(D_n<d_n)+T_ne^{-c_*L_n}+\zeta^{-1}d_n^{-1}T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. This tends to zero for sufficiently large $M$, since $T_n=e^{x_n}s_n$, $y_n\le x_n$, $L_n\ge cM^2x_n$, and $s_n\to0$. For the small-mass numerator $R_n^-$, [F8] and Tonelli give $E_0[R_n^-]\le\sum_{J_n^-}\pi_{n,j}\le e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n$; hence its posterior mass tends to zero in probability by Markov and the denominator event, because $e^{(C_0+2)y_n}e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n\le s_ne^{(C_0+3-K/2)x_n}\to0$ when $K>2(C_0+3)$. [F7, F8, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 The posterior outside the $M\epsilon_n$-ball is the union of its active-stratum part, its small-mass-stratum part, and the sieve complement. Step 6.1 sends the first two parts to zero in probability, and the sieve-complement term tends to zero by hypothesis. [given, step 6.1] ∎

## Statement

Let $Q_n$ be data-indexed probability measures on $M_0(w)$ and let $G$ be a fixed probability measure on this space. For the projections $P_J$ of [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]], suppose that for every fixed $J$,
$$\beta_{BL}(Q_n\circ P_J^{-1},G\circ P_J^{-1})\to0$$
in probability, and that for every $\varepsilon,\eta>0$,
$$\lim_{J\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P\left\{Q_n(\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon)>\eta\right\}=0.$$
Then $\beta_{BL}(Q_n,G)\to0$ in probability.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The $M_0(w)$ norm and projections, the bounded-Lipschitz metric, and the finite-projection and posterior-tail assumptions in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]: $M_0(w)$ has the weighted supremum norm and consists of coefficient sequences whose normalized level maxima vanish.

[F2] [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]]: $P_Jx\to x$ in $M_0(w)$ for every $x\in M_0(w)$.

[F3] [[thm-continuity-from-above-for-measures]]: if measurable sets decrease and the first has finite measure, their measures decrease to the measure of their intersection.

## Proof




1.1 For any probability measure $Q$ on $M_0(w)$ and any bounded $1$-Lipschitz function $h$, $|h(x)-h(P_Jx)|\le\min(2,\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)})$. Splitting at $\varepsilon>0$ and taking the supremum over such $h$ gives $\beta_{BL}(Q,Q\circ P_J^{-1})\le\varepsilon+2Q(\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon)$. Applying this to $Q_n$ and $G$, then using the triangle inequality, bounds $\beta_{BL}(Q_n,G)$ by the two projection errors and the fixed-$J$ distance between projected laws. [F1, given, algebra]

2.1 For each $x\in M_0(w)$, [F2] gives $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$. Thus the events $\{x:\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon\}$ decrease to the empty set, and [F3] makes their $G$-probabilities tend to zero. Given any target error, first choose $\varepsilon$ small, then choose $J$ large so this $G$-tail and the limiting posterior-tail probability are small; for that fixed $J$, the projected-law distance tends to zero in probability by assumption. Step 1.1 then implies $\beta_{BL}(Q_n,G)\to0$ in probability. [F2, F3, given, step 1.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The finite level sets $K_l$, weights $w_l\ge1$, and the vanishing-tail definition of $M_0(w)$.

[F1] [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]: $\|x\|_{M(w)}=\sup_l w_l^{-1}\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|$, and membership in $M_0(w)$ means this normalized maximum tends to zero.

## Proof

1.1 Let $(x^{(m)})$ be Cauchy in $M_0(w)$. Each coordinate is Cauchy because $|x^{(m)}_{lk}-x^{(n)}_{lk}|\le w_l\|x^{(m)}-x^{(n)}\|_{M(w)}$. Let $x_{lk}$ be its scalar limit. The uniform Cauchy bound passes to every finite collection of coordinates and then to the supremum, so $x^{(m)}\to x$ in the weighted supremum norm. To see $x\in M_0(w)$, fix $\varepsilon>0$, choose $m$ with $\|x-x^{(m)}\|_{M(w)}<\varepsilon$, then choose $J$ so the normalized tail of $x^{(m)}$ is below $\varepsilon$; for $l>J$ the normalized tail of $x$ is at most $2\varepsilon$. Thus $M_0(w)$ is complete. [F1, given, choose, algebra]

1.2 Finite-support sequences with rational coordinates are countable and dense: first choose $J$ to make the tail of any $x\in M_0(w)$ small, then approximate its finitely many coordinates through level $J$ by rationals. Hence $M_0(w)$ is separable. The formula for the norm shows $P_J$ is a contraction, and the defining tail limit gives $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$. [F1, given, choose, algebra]

2.1 If $x\in\ell^2$, then $w_l\ge1$ implies $w_l^{-1}\max_k|x_{lk}|\le(\sum_k|x_{lk}|^2)^{1/2}$. The right side tends to zero because its squares are level blocks of a convergent nonnegative series. Its supremum is at most $\|x\|_{\ell^2}$, so $x\in M_0(w)$. [F1, given, algebra] ∎

id: lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs
kind: lemma
title: The multiscale primitive map is continuous into C[0,1]
status: draft
origin: pipeline
pipeline_run: bayesian-computational-statistics-62
deps:

sources:

      url: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1310.2484
    - title: Giné and Nickl, Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models, proof of Theorem 7.3.20
      url: https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf
dependency_level: 2

## Statement

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a compactly supported wavelet basis of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The Haar basis with its finite scaling coordinate, as specified in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], is also allowed. Assume each level-$l$ wavelet for $l\ge l_0$ has zero integral, uniformly bounded overlap, support length at most $C_0 2^{-l}$, and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Let $M_0(w)$ be as in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and suppose
$$S_w:=\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}<\infty.$$
For $x\in M_0(w)$ define
$$Jx(t):=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle 1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle_{L^2},\qquad 0\le t\le1.$$
Then this series converges absolutely and uniformly in $t$, $Jx\in C([0,1])$, and $\|Jx-Jy\|_\infty\le C S_w\|x-y\|_{M(w)}$ after adding the finite coarsest-level constant to $C S_w$. If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, then $Jx(t)=\int_0^t f(u)\,du$.

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** The wavelet geometry, summability condition, and multiscale space in the Statement.

[F1] [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]]: $\|x\|_{M(w)}=\sup_l w_l^{-1}\max_k|x_{lk}|$.

[F2] [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]: $(\psi_{lk})$ is a complete orthonormal basis of $L^2([0,1])$; finite orthogonal projections converge in $L^2$.

## Proof




1.1 For fixed $t$ and level $l\ge l_0$, a wavelet whose support lies wholly on one side of $t$ contributes zero: it is either disjoint from $[0,t]$ or its entire support is integrated and its mean is zero. Only supports meeting $t$ can contribute. Uniformly bounded overlap bounds their number by a constant, and each coefficient has magnitude at most $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Thus $\sup_t\sum_k|\langle1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_1 2^{-l/2}$. The finitely many coarsest levels have a finite uniform sum as well. [given, algebra]

2.1 By [F1] and step 1.1, the absolute sum of all terms at levels $l\ge l_0$ is at most $C_1\|x\|_{M(w)}\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}$, uniformly over $t$. Its tails tend uniformly to zero because $S_w<\infty$. Each finite-level sum is continuous in $t$, since $t\mapsto\int_0^t\psi_{lk}(u)du$ is continuous for an $L^1$ function. The uniform limit is continuous. Applying the same estimate to $x-y$ proves the stated operator-norm bound. [F1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 If $x_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ for $f\in L^2$, the finite orthogonal projections converge to $f$ in $L^2$ by [F2]. The map $f\mapsto\int_0^t f(u)du=\langle f,1_{[0,t]}\rangle$ is a continuous $L^2$ functional because $\|1_{[0,t]}\|_2\le1$. Applying it to the finite projections shows that their coefficient sums converge to $\int_0^t f$, while step 2.1 identifies the same limit with $Jx(t)$. [F2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

id: lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law
kind: lemma
title: The product-prior posterior factors by coordinates
status: draft
origin: pipeline
dependency_level: 1
deps:
  - lem-wavelet-product-prior-is-l2-valued
  - def-countable-choice
  - def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables
  - thm-dynkin-pi-lambda
  - thm-rectangle-criterion-for-independent-random-elements
proof_strategy: direct
provenance:

verification:
  precheck: pass
sources:
  references:
    - title: "Castillo and Nickl, Nonparametric Bernstein–von Mises theorems in Gaussian white noise, §3.1, printed pp. 2013–2014"
      url: https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/AOS1133.pdf
    - title: "Giné and Nickl, Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models, §7.3.3, printed pp. 583–585"
      url: https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf
---

## Statement

Assume countable choice for the $L^2$-valued prior construction. Let the wavelet product prior have independent coefficients $\theta_{lk}=\sigma_l\xi_{lk}$, where the $\xi_{lk}$ are IID with density $\varphi$. Observe the independent Gaussian sequence

$$X_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}+n^{-1/2}Z_{lk},$$

where the $Z_{lk}$ have the standard normal density and are independent of the prior. Assume a data-indexed posterior kernel for the $L^2$-valued prior is supplied as part of this model. In the product white-noise model, for every finite set $J$ of coefficient indices its conditional law of $(\theta_j)_{j\in J}$ given the full data sequence $(X_j)$ is the product of the one-coordinate densities

$$p_{j,n}(t\mid X_j)=\frac{e^{-n(t-X_j)^2/2}\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t/\sigma_j)}{\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-n(s-X_j)^2/2}\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(s/\sigma_j)\,ds},\qquad j\in J.$$

Here $j$ abbreviates a pair $(l,k)$ and $\sigma_j=\sigma_l$. For $J=\varnothing$, the formula denotes the unit law on the zero-dimensional one-point space. Each denominator is strictly positive and finite: the Gaussian factor is everywhere positive and at most $1$, while the prior density integrates to $1$.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]: The prior coefficients are mutually independent and have a common law; scaling by the fixed positive $\sigma_l$ preserves coordinate independence.

[F2] [[thm-rectangle-criterion-for-independent-random-elements]]: Independence of random elements is equivalent to factorization of probabilities on all finite measurable rectangles.

[F3] [[thm-dynkin-pi-lambda]]: If a lambda-system contains a generating pi-system, it contains the generated sigma-algebra.

[L1] [[lem-wavelet-product-prior-is-l2-valued]]: The wavelet prior coefficients define an $L^2$-valued random element under the stated scale and finite-second-moment conditions.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable choice is used only for the $L^2$-valued prior construction supplied by [L1]; the finite-coordinate factorization argument itself uses no choice axiom.

[A2] The full data-indexed posterior kernel on $L^2$ is supplied as part of the model. We use the version whose finite-coordinate marginals are the displayed densities; the proof verifies their conditional-law identities under the prior-predictive model. This item does not claim a general full-kernel existence theorem.

**Given:** Countable choice, the product prior, the independent Gaussian coordinate experiment, and the supplied posterior kernel [A2]. The coordinate marginal formula is verified below.

## Proof

1.1 For each coordinate $j$, the pair $(\theta_j,X_j)$ is a measurable function of the independent pair $(\xi_j,Z_j)$. Thus the coordinate pairs are independent: finite rectangle probabilities factor by [F1] and [F2]. Fix finite $J$. For any cylinder event $B$ depending on finitely many observations outside $J$, the random vector $(\theta_J,X_J)$ is independent of $B$ by that same factorization. The events in $\sigma(X_{J^c})$ for which this independence identity holds form a lambda-system containing the outside-coordinate cylinder pi-system; [F3] extends it to all outside-data events. Hence conditioning on $X_{J^c}$ adds no information about $\theta_J$ once $X_J$ is known. [F1, F2, F3]

2.1 For finite $J$, the joint prior density of $\theta_J$ is the product of $\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t_j/\sigma_j)$, and the likelihood of $X_J=x_J$ is proportional to $\prod_{j\in J}e^{-n(x_j-t_j)^2/2}$. Each one-dimensional normalizer is at most $1$ and is positive: the Gaussian factor is bounded by $1$, is strictly positive everywhere, and the prior density integrates to $1$. Thus the normalized product density is $\prod_{j\in J}p_{j,n}(t_j\mid x_j)$. Integrating it over rectangles in $\theta_J$ and $X_J$ verifies the conditional-law identity for these coordinates. The prior is a Borel probability on $L^2$ by [L1] under [A1], and [A2] supplies the full posterior kernel; step 1.1 extends the finite-coordinate identity to the full observation sequence. [A1, A2, F1, F2, step 1.1, L1, algebra]

3.1 The product of the one-coordinate conditional densities in step 2.1 is exactly the stated finite-dimensional posterior marginal, so the posterior factors by coordinates for every finite index set $J$. [step 2.1] ∎

id: lem-product-prior-posterior-second-moment-in-negative-sobolev-space

      url: https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/AOS1133.pdf
    - title: "Giné and Nickl, Mathematical Foundations of Infinite-Dimensional Statistical Models, Theorem 7.3.12 and proof, printed pp. 584–586"
      url: https://www.statslab.cam.ac.uk/~rn289/Site/__files/FULLPDF.pdf
---

## Statement

Use the wavelet product-prior white-noise model of [[lem-wavelet-product-prior-is-l2-valued]] and [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]], with $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, $\alpha>0$, and $2^l$ coefficients at level $l\ge0$. Let $\theta_{0,lk}$ be the coefficients of a fixed $f_0\in L^2([0,1])$. Assume countable choice for the $L^2$ prior construction, with the full posterior kernel supplied by [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]], and suppose

$$\sup_{l,k}\left|\frac{\theta_{0,lk}}{\sigma_l}\right|\le M<\tau,$$

where the common prior density $\varphi$ satisfies $\varphi(u)\le C_\varphi$ for all $u$, $\varphi(u)\ge c_\varphi>0$ for $|u|<\tau$, and $m_2:=\int u^2\varphi(u)\,du<\infty$. For every $\delta>1/2$ there is a constant $C_\delta<\infty$, independent of $n$, such that

$$\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}\int\|f-f_0\|_{H(\delta)}^2\,\Pi_n(df\mid X^{(n)})\le\frac{C_\delta}{n}.$$

No continuity assumption on $\varphi$ is needed for this moment estimate.

## Facts & Assumptions

[F1] [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]: $\|u\|_{H(\delta)}^2=\sum_{l,k}w_l^\delta|u_{lk}|^2$, where $w_l^\delta=a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ and $\sum_{l,k}w_l^\delta<\infty$ for $\delta>1/2$.

[F2] [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]: Given the data coordinate $X_{lk}$, the posterior density of $\theta_{lk}$ is proportional to $e^{-n(\theta-X_{lk})^2/2}\sigma_l^{-1}\varphi(\theta/\sigma_l)$; finite coordinate marginals factor.

[F3] [[thm-monotone-convergence-for-the-integral]]: Expectations of nonnegative partial sums increasing pointwise to a limit increase to the expectation of that limit.

[F4] [[thm-tonelli-theorem-for-sigma-finite-product-spaces]]: For the nonnegative Gaussian-integral integrand, expectation and Lebesgue integration may be interchanged on the sigma-finite product of the normal probability space and $\mathbb R$.

[A1] The true normalized coordinates $r_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}/\sigma_l$ satisfy $|r_{lk}|\le M<\tau$, and $\varphi$ has the boundedness, local positivity, and second-moment properties in the statement.

[A2] [[def-countable-choice]]: Countable choice is used for the $L^2$ prior construction. The full posterior kernel is supplied as model input in [F2]; the coordinate moment estimates below require no further choice.

**Given:** Countable choice, the white-noise observations $X_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}+n^{-1/2}Z_{lk}$ with independent standard normal coordinates, the prior, and its coordinate posterior law. The expected posterior loss bound in the Statement is to be proved.

## Proof

1.1 Fix $(l,k)$ and abbreviate $\sigma=\sigma_l$, $\theta_0=\theta_{0,lk}$, $r=\theta_0/\sigma$, and $\lambda=\sqrt n\,\sigma$. Under the true law write $X=\theta_0+n^{-1/2}Z$, where $Z$ has density $(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-z^2/2}$. If $B_{lk}(X)=\int(\theta-\theta_0)^2\,\Pi_n(d\theta_{lk}\mid X)$, change variables $v=\sqrt n(\theta-\theta_0)$ in [F2] to obtain $nB_{lk}(X)=\frac{N_\lambda(Z)}{D_\lambda(Z)},\quad D_\lambda(z)=\frac1\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-v^2/2+zv}\varphi(r+v/\lambda)\,dv,\quad N_\lambda(z)=\frac1\lambda\int_{\mathbb R}v^2e^{-v^2/2+zv}\varphi(r+v/\lambda)\,dv.$ All integrands are nonnegative and the denominator is positive. The posterior kernel is the $L^2$ model supplied by [F2] under [A2]. [A1, A2, F2, given, algebra]

2.1 Set $h=(\tau-M)/2>0$. If $\lambda\le S_0$ for a fixed $S_0>0$, then $|r+v/\lambda|<\tau$ whenever $|v|\le h\lambda$. Substituting $v=\lambda t$ and pairing $t$ with $-t$ gives $D_\lambda(z)\ge c_\varphi\int_{-h}^h e^{-\lambda^2t^2/2+z\lambda t}\,dt=2c_\varphi\int_0^h e^{-\lambda^2t^2/2}\cosh(z\lambda t)\,dt\ge 2hc_\varphi e^{-h^2\lambda^2/2}\ge d_0:=2hc_\varphi e^{-h^2S_0^2/2}>0,$ because $\cosh(x)\ge1$ and $e^{-\lambda^2t^2/2}\ge e^{-h^2\lambda^2/2}$ on $[0,h]$. Completing the square in the standard normal density gives $\mathbb E e^{Zv}=e^{v^2/2}$; hence, by the substitution $u=r+v/\lambda$, $\mathbb E N_\lambda(Z)=\frac1\lambda\int v^2\varphi(r+v/\lambda)\,dv=\lambda^2\int(u-r)^2\varphi(u)\,du\le2\lambda^2(m_2+M^2).$ Here [F4] justifies the exchange of expectation and the nonnegative $v$-integral. Therefore $\mathbb E B_{lk}(X)\le C\lambda^2/n=C\sigma_l^2\le CS_0^2/n$ in this range. [A1, given, step 1.1, F4, algebra]

2.2 If $\lambda\ge S_0$, let $R=hS_0$. For $|v|\le R$ one has $|r+v/\lambda|<\tau$, so $D_\lambda(z)\ge\frac{c_\varphi e^{z^2/2}}\lambda I_R(z),\qquad N_\lambda(z)\le\frac{C_\varphi e^{z^2/2}}\lambda J(z),$ where $I_R(z)=\int_{-R}^{R}e^{-(v-z)^2/2}\,dv$ and $J(z)=\int_{\mathbb R}v^2e^{-(v-z)^2/2}\,dv=\sqrt{2\pi}(1+z^2)$. Thus $nB_{lk}(X)\le(C_\varphi/c_\varphi)J(Z)/I_R(Z)$. For $|z|\le R$, integrate $I_R$ over the half-interval nearest $z$; for $|z|>R$, integrate over the half-interval adjacent to the nearer endpoint. These choices give the common lower bound $I_R(z)\ge\frac R2\exp\left(-\frac{R^2}{2}-\frac{(|z|-R/2)_+^2}{2}\right).$ Consequently $\mathbb E[J(Z)/I_R(Z)]$ is finite: after multiplying by the standard normal density, its integrand is bounded on $|z|\le R/2$ and is at most a constant times $(1+z^2)e^{-R|z|/2}$ on $|z|>R/2$. Hence $\mathbb E B_{lk}(X)\le C/n$ also when $\lambda\ge S_0$, with $C$ independent of $(l,k,n)$. [A1, given, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The two ranges in steps 2.1 and 2.2 cover every $\lambda>0$; since $\sigma_l^2\le S_0^2/n$ in the first range, there is a single constant $C$ for which $\sup_{l,k}\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}B_{lk}(X)\le C/n$. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 By [F1], the posterior squared loss is the nonnegative series $\sum_{l,k}w_l^\delta B_{lk}(X)$. Apply monotone convergence [F3] to its finite partial sums and use step 3.1 to obtain $\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}\int\|f-f_0\|_{H(\delta)}^2\,\Pi_n(df\mid X)=\sum_{l,k}w_l^\delta\mathbb E_{f_0}^{(n)}B_{lk}(X)\le\frac Cn\sum_{l,k}w_l^\delta.$ The trace on the right is finite for $\delta>1/2$ by [F1], proving the bound. [A1, F1, F3, step 3.1] ∎
