citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let K be a finite kernel from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$, in particular a probability kernel, or a uniformly sigma-finite kernel with the specified exhaustion of the kernel definition. For every nonnegative $\Sigma\otimes\Tau$-measurable function $f:S\times T\to[0,\infty]$, the function
$$I_f(s)=\int_T f(s,t)\,K(s,dt)$$
is $\Sigma$-measurable, with infinity allowed. For a real product-measurable f, the set $D=\{s:I_{|f|}(s)<\infty\}$ is measurable, and its signed integral on D, extended by zero on $S\setminus D$, is a measurable real function. No assertion here is made for a general kernel lacking a common measurable finite-mass exhaustion.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

derivations.claim: The kernel $K$ in [F2] is a probability kernel because, for fixed $(F,\sigma,x)$, $A\mapsto F(A)$ is a probability measure, while for fixed Borel $A$, $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto F(A)$ is measurable by the evaluation sigma-algebra. The integrand $(\sigma,x,z)\mapsto(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}\exp(-(x-z)^2/(2\sigma^2))$ is continuous on $(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R^2$ and hence product-measurable. Therefore [F3] makes its integral against $K$ jointly measurable.

The integrand is strictly positive, so its integral against a probability measure is positive. It is bounded above by $(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$, so the integral is finite and has the stated upper bound.

By [F4], $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R}\left(\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-(x-z)^2/(2\sigma^2)}\,dx\right)F(dz)=\int_{\mathbb R}1\,F(dz)=1,$ where the inner integral is one by [F1] and $F$ has total mass one. Thus $p_{F,\sigma}$ is a probability density.

The **monic probabilists' Hermite polynomials** are the polynomials $H_m\in\mathbb R[x]$ defined by
$$H_0=1,\qquad H_1(x)=x,\qquad xH_m(x)=H_{m+1}(x)+m\,H_{m-1}(x)\quad(m\ge1).$$
The recurrence is solved for the higher polynomial, $H_{m+1}(x)=xH_m(x)-mH_{m-1}(x)$, so it determines $H_m$ uniquely by induction on $m$. Each $H_m$ is monic of degree $m$: $H_2=x^2-1$, $H_3=x^3-3x$ and $H_4=x^4-6x^2+3$; in general $H_m(x)=m!\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}\frac{(-1/2)^j x^{m-2j}}{j!\,(m-2j)!}$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

$$ \int\frac{(p-q_\sigma)^2}{q_\sigma}\,dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \mathrm{KL}(p\Vert q_\sigma)\le\frac49\sigma^4J,\qquad \int p\left[\log\frac p{q_\sigma}\right]^2dx\le\frac49\sigma^4J. $$
The logarithmic integrands are zero where $p=0$. No unimodality or uniform bound on $p/q_\sigma$ is assumed.

support points and
$$\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_1\le\eta,\qquad
\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_\infty\le\eta/\sigma.$$

$$\Pr\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^N|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta,\quad
\min_{1\le j\le N}F(U_j)\ge\eta^2/2\right\}\ge C\exp\{-cN\log(e/\eta)\}.$$

For all large $n$, partition each nondegenerate component of $K$ into equal consecutive Borel intervals of lengths in $[\tau/8,\tau/4]$: use $\lceil4\ell/\tau\rceil$ pieces for a component of length $\ell$. Endpoints can be assigned arbitrarily because $P_0$ has a density. The support of a continuous density has no isolated points, so there are no isolated support components to treat. There are $O(b_n^{-1})$ coarse cells $I_k$, each of mass at least $c' b_n^a$. Translate the conditional probability $P_0(\cdot\mid I_k)$ to an interval centered at zero, apply [F2] at scale $\tau$, and translate back. Multiplying by $P_0(I_k)$ and summing gives a finite probability $F_n$ with at most $C b_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$ atoms in the closures of these cells, each carrying its original coarse-cell label, and $\|p_{F_n,\tau}-p_{P_0,\tau}\|_\infty\le\eta/\tau$. The total weight of atoms with label $k$ is exactly $P_0(I_k)$.

Put $\delta=\eta\tau$. Move each atom to a nearest point of the global lattice of mesh $\delta$ and merge atoms at the same location. Preserve its fractional label weights when merging. The resulting distinct locations $z_j$ are separated by at least $\delta$, with weights $w_j$ summing to one, and still number $N\le Cb_n^{-1}\log(e/\eta)$. Let $U_j=[z_j-\delta/4,z_j+\delta/4)$ and $U_0=\mathbb R\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^NU_j$. These are disjoint partition cells. The base density is bounded above and below on a fixed compact neighborhood of $K$, so $c_0\eta\tau\le\alpha(U_j)\le C_0\eta\tau\le1$ eventually. Since $B>1$, $\eta\tau\ge c_1\eta^2$ and $N\eta\to0$. Also $\sum_j\alpha(U_j)\le C N\delta\to0$, so, writing $m=\alpha(\mathbb R)>0$, we have $\alpha(U_0)\in[m/2,m]$ eventually.

Apply [F3] with tolerance $\eta$ to get an event $E_n$ on which $\sum_j|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta$ and $\Pi_{DP}(E_n)\ge\exp\{-C b_n^{-1}(\log n)^2\}$. Its constants can be taken uniform in $n$: in the proof of [F3] the only residual-parameter factors are $\Gamma(m)/\Gamma(\alpha(U_0))$ and a lower bound $(\eta^2/2)^m$ for the residual power. The gamma ratio is bounded below on the fixed compact interval $[m/2,m]$, and the latter power already has fixed exponent $m$. The remaining constants use only the fixed bound $c_1\eta^2\le\alpha(U_j)\le1$. Finally $\log(e/\eta)\le C\log n$ by the polynomial lower bandwidth bound.

For $\tau\le\sigma\le s_+b_n$, the original discrete approximation still satisfies $\|p_{F_n,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_\infty\le C\eta/b_n$. Indeed the Gaussian convolution identity $\phi_u*\phi_v=\phi_{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}$ follows by completing the square and integrating; convolution with a probability kernel contracts the supremum norm by the triangle inequality. Use $u=\tau$, $v=\sqrt{\sigma^2-\tau^2}$, treating equality by the original approximation. Differentiating [F5] gives $\|\phi_\sigma'\|_\infty\le C\sigma^{-2}$. Atom relocation by at most $\delta/2$ therefore changes the mixture by at most $C\delta/\sigma^2\le C\eta/b_n$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $p,q$ be probability densities relative to one measure $\mu$, assume

probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the

$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$

$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

derivations.claim: Since $G$ is a probability on $(0,\infty)=\bigcup_{m\ge1}[1/m,m]$, choose $0<s_-<s_+<\infty$ with $g:=G([s_-,s_+])>0$. Put $\sigma_-=s_-\sigma_n$. By [F2] applied to the law $P_0$ at scale $\sigma_-$, there is a finite discrete probability $F_n$ supported on $K$ with at most $C\sigma_n^{-1}\log n$ atoms and $\|p_{F_n,\sigma_-}-p_{P_0,\sigma_-}\|_1\le\eta_n$, where $\eta_n:=\sigma_n^8$.

Choose a compact interval $D$ whose interior contains $K$ and on which the density of $\alpha$ is bounded above and below by positive constants. Moving an atom by at most $\eta_n\sigma_-$ changes its normal mixture by at most $C\eta_n$ in $L^1$: differentiating [F7] gives $\|\partial_z\phi_{\sigma_-}(\cdot-z)\|_1=E|Z|/\sigma_-\le1/\sigma_-$, since $2|Z|\le1+Z^2$ and $E Z^2=1$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Move each atom of $F_n$ to a nearest point of a lattice of mesh $\eta_n\sigma_-$ and merge coincident atoms; distinct relocated locations are separated by at least $\eta_n\sigma_-$. Around each relocated atom take a centered cell of length $\ell_n=\eta_n\sigma_-/2$; these cells are disjoint. Each gap of length $g\ge\ell_n$ between the atom-cells, including the two end gaps in $D$, is split into $q=\lceil2g/\sigma_-\rceil$ equal subintervals. If $q=1$, their length is $g\ge\ell_n$; if $q\ge2$, then $g>\sigma_-/2$ and $q\le4g/\sigma_-$, so each length lies in $[\sigma_-/4,\sigma_-/2]$. Thus the resulting Borel partition $U_1,\ldots,U_N$ of $D$ has every cell length between $c\eta_n\sigma_-$ and $\sigma_-/2$, every atom-cell diameter at most $2\eta_n\sigma_-$, and $N\le C(m_n+\sigma_-^{-1})\le C\sigma_n^{-1}\log n$, where $m_n$ is the number of atoms. Let $w_j=F_n(U_j)$, so $\sum_jw_j=1$. For all large $n$, the base density bounds give $c\eta_n\sigma_n\le\alpha(U_j)\le1$. Since $\eta_n=\sigma_n^8$, we have $c\eta_n\sigma_n\ge c'\eta_n^2$ eventually, and $N\eta_n\le C\sigma_n^7\log n\to0$ using $\sigma_n\le Cn^{-a_2}$. Apply [F3] with parameters $a=c'$, $b=2$, and $\eta=\eta_n$ to obtain an event $E_n$ with $\Pi_{DP}(E_n)\ge e^{-C N\log(e/\eta_n)}\ge e^{-C\sigma_n^{-1}(\log n)^2},$ on which $F(D^c)\le C\eta_n$, $\sum_j|F(U_j)-w_j|\le C\eta_n$, and $F(U_j)\ge\eta_n^2/2$ for every $j$.

For $F$ in $E_n$, compare $p_{F,\sigma}$ with $p_{F_n,\sigma}$, uniformly for $s_-\sigma_n\le\sigma\le s_+\sigma_n$. The [F7] location derivative bound and atom-cell diameter at most $2\eta_n\sigma_-$ make the within-cell $L^1$ error at most $C\eta_n$; the gap cells and $D^c$ have total $F$-mass at most $C\eta_n$, and the cell-weight discrepancies sum to at most $C\eta_n$. Since each normal density has $L^1$ norm one, these terms give $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F_n,\sigma}\|_1\le C\eta_n$. For $u,v>0$, completing the square gives $\int\phi_u(y)\phi_v(x-y)\,dy=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi(u^2+v^2)}}e^{-x^2/(2(u^2+v^2))}=\phi_{\sqrt{u^2+v^2}}(x),$ since $y^2/u^2+(x-y)^2/v^2=((u^2+v^2)/(u^2v^2))(y-u^2x/(u^2+v^2))^2+x^2/(u^2+v^2)$. Also, for any densities $f,g,k$, Tonelli and the triangle inequality give $\|f*k-g*k\|_1\le\int\!\int|f(y)-g(y)|k(x-y)\,dy\,dx=\|f-g\|_1$. Apply these identities with $u=\sigma_-$ and $v=\sqrt{\sigma^2-\sigma_-^2}$ to obtain $\|p_{F_n,\sigma}-p_{P_0,\sigma}\|_1\le C\eta_n$. Thus [F6] gives $h(p_{F,\sigma},p_{P_0,\sigma})\le C\sqrt{\eta_n}$, and the assumed bias bound gives $h(p_0,p_{F,\sigma})\le C(\sigma_n^2+\sqrt{\eta_n})\le C\sigma_n^2$.

For every $x\in K$, the interval $[x-\sigma_-,x+\sigma_-]$ contains a full cell $U_j$ because $D$ contains a fixed neighborhood of $K$ and all cells have length at most $\sigma_-/2$. The scale event $S\in[s_-,s_+]$ has probability $g>0$ and is independent of $F$. citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ be the probability measures on the Borel sets of
$\mathbb R$, equipped with the evaluation sigma-algebra, and let $\sigma>0$.
For $F\in\mathcal P(\mathbb R)$ define
$$p_{F,\sigma}(x):=\int_{\mathbb R}\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-z)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)F(dz).$$
Then $(F,\sigma,x)\mapsto p_{F,\sigma}(x)$ is jointly measurable,
$0<p_{F,\sigma}(x)\le(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})^{-1}$ for every $(F,\sigma,x)$,
and $\int_{\mathbb R}p_{F,\sigma}(x)\,dx=1$. In particular it is the
Lebesgue density of the convolution of $F$ with $N(0,\sigma^2)$.

There is a universal constant $C$ such that, for $A,\sigma>0$,
$0<\eta<1/2$, and every probability measure $F$ supported on $[-A,A]$,
there is a discrete probability measure $F'$ on $[-A,A]$ with at most
$$C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$$
support points and
$$\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_1\le\eta,\qquad
\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_\infty\le\eta/\sigma.$$

Assume AC, let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure of total mass $m$, and
let $F\sim DP(\alpha)$. Consider a finite partition
$(U_0,U_1,\ldots,U_N)$ with $\alpha(U_0)=0$ or
$0<\alpha(U_0)\le m$. Write $\alpha_j=\alpha(U_j)$ for $j\ge1$, and assume
$$a\eta^b\le\alpha_j\le1\quad(1\le j\le N),\qquad 0<\eta<1/4,qquad N\eta\le1/4,$$
for fixed $a,b>0$. For every $w=(w_1,\ldots,w_N)$ in the probability
simplex, there are constants $c,C>0$ depending only on $a,b,m,\alpha(U_0)$
such that
$$\Pr\!\left\{\sum_{j=1}^N|F(U_j)-w_j|+F(U_0)\le3\eta,\quad
\min_{1\le j\le N}F(U_j)\ge\eta^2/2\right\}\ge C\exp\{-cN\log(e/\eta)\}.$$
For any compact $J\subset(0,m]$, the constants may instead depend only on
$a,b,m,J$ and are uniform over $\alpha(U_0)\in J$.
When $\alpha(U_0)=0$, the zero-base cell has $F(U_0)=0$ almost surely and is
omitted from the Dirichlet vector.

Let $p,q$ be probability densities relative to one measure $\mu$, assume
$p\,d\mu\ll q\,d\mu$, let
$h^2:=\int(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2d\mu$, and suppose
$R:=\operatorname*{ess,sup}_{q\,d\mu}(p/q)<\infty$, with $p/q=0$ on
$\{q=0,p=0\}$. Then $p\ll q$ and for a universal constant $C$,
$$\mathrm{KL}(p\,d\mu\Vert q\,d\mu)\le C h^2(1+\log^+R),\qquad \int p\left[\log(p/q)\right]^2d\mu\le C h^2(1+\log^+R)^2.$$
The logarithm is assigned value zero on $\{p=0\}$; the moment integrand is
also set to zero there.

finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$

probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law

$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

draw $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ with joint law $G^{\otimes n}$, where $n\ge1$. Then
$$K(x_1,\ldots,x_n;\,\cdot)=DP\!\left(\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}\right)$$
is a measurable data-indexed posterior kernel version. It satisfies the
posterior disintegration identity on the evaluation sigma-algebra of
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ and $\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. On prior-predictive
null data sets its values are a version choice; the displayed formula is
well-defined there but is not asserted to be uniquely forced.

$x_{1:n}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ has one-step predictive probability

for every measurable $A$ and every data vector. The formula is a
data-indexed version on prior-predictive null data sets; those pointwise
values are not uniquely determined by the disintegration identity.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. $$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$

$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

derivations.claim: The latent representation is $\theta_i\mid F\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}\sim F$ and $X_i\mid\theta_i,\sigma\sim N(\theta_i,\sigma^2)$ independently. Use the test $\varphi_n=\mathbf1\{\text{some }X_i\notin I\}$. Its type-I error is zero. For fixed $\theta$ and $\sigma$, set $g(\theta)=P(\theta+\sigma Z\in I)=\Phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)-\Phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)$. Then $g'(\theta)=\sigma^{-1}\left[\phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)-\phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)\right].$ For $\theta\le(L+U)/2$, $|L-\theta|\le|U-\theta|$, so $g'(\theta)\ge0$ because the standard normal density decreases with absolute value; for $\theta\ge(L+U)/2$ the inequality reverses and $g'(\theta)\le0$. Thus $g$ is maximized at the midpoint, where the component leakage is $2\Phi(-R/\sigma)$. Every component with $\sigma>s_n$ therefore puts probability at least $q_n=2\Phi(-R/s_n)$ outside $I$, and $P_{F,\sigma}^n(\varphi_n=0)\le(1-q_n)^n\le e^{-nq_n}$.

By [F8] the latent DP model is a measurable prior law. Introduce the latent locations $\theta_{1:n}$. Given these locations, $X_{1:n}$ and $\sigma$, the observation likelihood is independent of $F$, so [F1] gives the conditional law $DP(\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{\theta_i})$. Given this updated $F$, the next latent location has conditional law $F$; applying [F3] to that predictive draw gives $E[F(A)\mid\theta_{1:n},X_{1:n},\sigma]=\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_i\mathbf1_A(\theta_i)}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n}$ for every Borel set $A$. With $A=I_d^c$, conditional Markov inequality yields $\Pi_n(F(A)>\epsilon_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})\le\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_iP(\theta_i\in A,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})}{\epsilon_n^2(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)}.$

Fix an index $i$ and condition on $\theta_{-i},X_{1:n},\sigma$. The latent vector is exchangeable because its conditional law given $F$ is IID. Reordering $\theta_i$ last and applying [F2] shows its prior predictive law given $\theta_{-i}$ is $H_i=(\alpha+\sum_{k\ne i}\delta_{\theta_k})/(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1)$. Bayes' formula multiplies this measure by the likelihood $\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)$. Almost surely $X_i\in I$. On $A=I_d^c$, $|X_i-t|\ge d$, so the likelihood numerator is at most $C\sigma^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. For $\sigma\le s_n$, the denominator is at least the base-measure contribution $\frac{1}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1}\int_{X_i-\sigma}^{X_i+\sigma}\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)\,\alpha(dt)\ge\frac{c}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1},$ because the base density is bounded below near $I$ and $[X_i-\sigma,X_i+\sigma]$ lies there for all sufficiently large $n$. Consequently $P(\theta_i\in A\mid\theta_{-i},X_{1:n},\sigma)\le Cn\sigma^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2\sigma^2)}\le Cn s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)},$ where $s^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s^2)}$ is increasing on $0<s<d$.

Let $N_n^H$ be the likelihood-ratio numerator integrated over $\{\sigma>s_n\}$. By change of density and [F6], $E_0[(1-\varphi_n)N_n^H]\le e^{-nq_n}$. On the denominator event, [F7] therefore gives, for every $\zeta>0$, $P_0^n\{\Pi_n(\sigma>s_n\mid X_{1:n})>\zeta\}\le o(1)+\zeta^{-1}e^{(C_0+2)n\delta_n^2-nq_n}\longrightarrow0.$

Substitute the step 1.3 bound into step 1.2 and use $\alpha(A)\le\alpha(\mathbb R)$. The resulting upper bound is $\frac{\alpha(\mathbb R)}{\epsilon_n^2(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)}+Cn\epsilon_n^{-2}s_n^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2s_n^2)}+\Pi_n(\sigma>s_n\mid X_{1:n}),$ which tends to zero by $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, the second premise, and step 2.1. Thus the posterior probability of $F(I_d^c)>\epsilon_n^2$ tends to zero. Combining with step 2.1 proves the sieve-complement claim.

derivations.claim: The latent representation is $\theta_i\mid F\stackrel{\mathrm{iid}}\sim F$ and $X_i\mid\theta_i,\sigma\sim N(\theta_i,\sigma^2)$ independently. Use the test $\varphi_n=\mathbf1\{\text{some }X_i\notin I\}$. Its type-I error is zero. For fixed $\theta$ and $\sigma$, set $g(\theta)=P(\theta+\sigma Z\in I)=\Phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)-\Phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)$. Then $g'(\theta)=\sigma^{-1}\left[\phi((L-\theta)/\sigma)-\phi((U-\theta)/\sigma)\right].$ For $\theta\le(L+U)/2$, $|L-\theta|\le|U-\theta|$, so $g'(\theta)\ge0$ because the standard normal density decreases with absolute value; for $\theta\ge(L+U)/2$ the inequality reverses and $g'(\theta)\le0$. Thus $g$ is maximized at the midpoint, where the component leakage is $2\Phi(-R/\sigma)$. Every component with $\sigma>s_n$ therefore puts probability at least $q_n=2\Phi(-R/s_n)$ outside $I$, and $P_{F,\sigma}^n(\varphi_n=0)\le(1-q_n)^n\le e^{-nq_n}$.

By [F8] the latent DP model is a measurable prior law. Introduce the latent locations $\theta_{1:n}$. Given these locations, $X_{1:n}$ and $\sigma$, the observation likelihood is independent of $F$, so [F1] gives the conditional law $DP(\alpha+\sum_i\delta_{\theta_i})$. Given this updated $F$, the next latent location has conditional law $F$; applying [F3] to that predictive draw gives $E[F(A)\mid\theta_{1:n},X_{1:n},\sigma]=\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_i\mathbf1_A(\theta_i)}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n}$ for every Borel set $A$. With $A=I_d^c$, conditional Markov inequality yields $\Pi_n(F(A)>\epsilon_n^2,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})\le\frac{\alpha(A)+\sum_iP(\theta_i\in A,\sigma\le s_n\mid X_{1:n})}{\epsilon_n^2(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n)}.$

Fix an index $i$ and condition on $\theta_{-i},X_{1:n},\sigma$. The latent vector is exchangeable because its conditional law given $F$ is IID. Reordering $\theta_i$ last and applying [F2] shows its prior predictive law given $\theta_{-i}$ is $H_i=(\alpha+\sum_{k\ne i}\delta_{\theta_k})/(\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1)$. Bayes' formula multiplies this measure by the likelihood $\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)$. Almost surely $X_i\in I$. On $A=I_d^c$, $|X_i-t|\ge d$, so the likelihood numerator is at most $C\sigma^{-1}e^{-d^2/(2\sigma^2)}$. For $\sigma\le s_n$, the denominator is at least the base-measure contribution $\frac{1}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1}\int_{X_i-\sigma}^{X_i+\sigma}\phi_\sigma(X_i-t)\,\alpha(dt)\ge\frac{c}{\alpha(\mathbb R)+n-1},$ because the base density is bounded below near $I$ and $[X_i-\sigma,X_i+\sigma]$ lies there for all sufficiently large $n$. Let $N_n^H$ be the likelihood-ratio numerator integrated over $\{\sigma>s_n\}$. By change of density and [F6], $E_0[(1-\varphi_n)N_n^H]\le e^{-nq_n}$. Substitute the step 1.3 bound into step 1.2 and use $\alpha(A)\le\alpha(\mathbb R)$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

There is a universal constant $C$ such that, for $A,\sigma>0$,
$0<\eta<1/2$, and every probability measure $F$ supported on $[-A,A]$,
there is a discrete probability measure $F'$ on $[-A,A]$ with at most
$$C(A/\sigma\vee1)\log(e/\eta)$$
support points and
$$\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_1\le\eta,\qquad
\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F',\sigma}\|_\infty\le\eta/\sigma.$$

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

derivations.claim: Put $K:=\lceil C_0(A/\tau\vee1)\log(e/\epsilon)\rceil$. By [F1], every $p_{F,\sigma}\in\mathcal P_{A,\tau}$ is within $L^1$ distance $\epsilon^2/C_1$ of a mixture with at most $K$ atoms, for a fixed sufficiently large $C_1$. Pad shorter mixtures by zero-weight atoms.

Differentiating the density in [F3] gives $\|\partial_z\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)\|_1=\sigma^{-1}E|Z|\le\sigma^{-1}$, since $2|Z|\le1+Z^2$ and $E Z^2=1$, and $\|\partial_\sigma\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)\|_1=\sigma^{-1}E|Z^2-1|\le2\sigma^{-1}$ for $Z\sim N(0,1)$. Integrating these derivatives along the location and scale segments yields $\|\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z)-\phi_\sigma(\cdot-z')\|_1\le |z-z'|/\sigma$ and $\|\phi_\sigma-\phi_{\sigma'}\|_1\le2|\sigma-\sigma'|/(\sigma\wedge\sigma')$. Now choose a scale grid in $[\tau,2\tau]$ and a location grid in $[-A,A]$, each with mesh at most $c_2\tau\epsilon^2$, and an $L^1$ grid on the $K$-simplex of mesh at most $c_2\epsilon^2$. Replacing the scale, locations and weights changes the mixture density in $L^1$ by at most $C c_2\epsilon^2$; choose $c_2$ so this plus the approximation from step 1.1 is at most $\epsilon^2/4$. Thus the resulting finite set is an $L^1$ cover of radius $\epsilon^2/4$, hence an $h$-cover of radius $\epsilon/2$ by [F2].

The scale grid has at most $C\epsilon^{-2}$ points and the location grid at most $C(1+A/(\tau\epsilon^2))$ points. Rounding each of the first $K-1$ weights down to a mesh proportional to $\epsilon^2/K$ leaves the last weight nonnegative after setting it to make the sum one, gives at most $(CK/\epsilon^2)^K$ weight vectors, and changes their $L^1$ distance by at most $2c_2\epsilon^2$. Therefore the logarithm of the cover size is at most $C\log(e/\epsilon)+K\left[\log\!\left(\frac{C(A/\tau\vee1)}{\epsilon^2}\right)+\log\!\left(\frac{CK}{\epsilon^2}\right)\right]\le C(A/\tau\vee1)\left[\log\!\left(\frac{C(A/\tau\vee1)}{\epsilon}\right)\right]^2.$ The constructed finite set is an $h$-net of radius $\epsilon/2$, hence also a net of radius $\epsilon$; its cardinality therefore bounds the covering number and proves the first bound.

If $r:=F([-A,A]^c)=0$, then $F$ already belongs to the compact-location class. If $0<r\le\rho<1$, let $F_A$ and $F_{A^c}$ be the normalized restrictions to $[-A,A]$ and its complement. Then $p_{F,\sigma}=(1-r)p_{F_A,\sigma}+r p_{F_{A^c},\sigma}$, so $\|p_{F,\sigma}-p_{F_A,\sigma}\|_1\le2r$. By [F2], $h(p_{F,\sigma},p_{F_A,\sigma})\le\sqrt{2r}$; the triangle inequality in [F4] then transfers the compact cover to the tail-constrained class. For sufficiently small universal $c$, $\rho\le c\epsilon^2$ makes the truncation error at most $\epsilon/2$, so the radius-$\epsilon/2$ cover from steps 2.1–2.2 becomes a radius-$\epsilon$ cover after the constant rescaling used in the entropy bound.

Assume countable choice for the $L^2$-valued prior construction. Let the wavelet product prior have independent coefficients $\theta_{lk}=\sigma_l\xi_{lk}$, where the $\xi_{lk}$ are IID with density $\varphi$. Observe the independent Gaussian sequence

$$X_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}+n^{-1/2}Z_{lk},$$

where the $Z_{lk}$ have the standard normal density and are independent of the prior. Assume a data-indexed posterior kernel for the $L^2$-valued prior is supplied as part of this model. In the product white-noise model, for every finite set $J$ of coefficient indices its conditional law of $(\theta_j)_{j\in J}$ given the full data sequence $(X_j)$ is the product of the one-coordinate densities

$$p_{j,n}(t\mid X_j)=\frac{e^{-n(t-X_j)^2/2}\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t/\sigma_j)}{\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-n(s-X_j)^2/2}\,\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(s/\sigma_j)\,ds},\qquad j\in J.$$

Here $j$ abbreviates a pair $(l,k)$ and $\sigma_j=\sigma_l$. For $J=\varnothing$, the formula denotes the unit law on the zero-dimensional one-point space. Each denominator is strictly positive and finite: the Gaussian factor is everywhere positive and at most $1$, while the prior density integrates to $1$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix one coordinate $j=(l,k)$ and write $r=\theta_{0,j}/\sigma_j$. Under the true law, $X_j/\sigma_j=r+Z_j/(\sqrt n\sigma_j)\to r$ in probability, and $b_n=(\sqrt n\sigma_j)^{-1}\to0$. By [F1], under [A1], the posterior density of $U_n=\sqrt n(\theta_j-X_j)$ is $p_n(u\mid X_j)=\frac{e^{-u^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nu)}{c_n(X_j)},\qquad c_n(X_j)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-v^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nv)\,dv.$ For any deterministic sequence $x_n/\sigma_j\to r$, boundedness of $\varphi$ and [F2] give $c_n(x_n)\to\varphi(r)\sqrt{2\pi}>0$.

Along such a deterministic sequence, $p_n(u\mid x_n)\to(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}$ pointwise and is eventually bounded by a constant multiple of $e^{-u^2/2}$. A second application of [F2] gives convergence in $L^1(du)$, hence convergence in total variation. Since $X_j/\sigma_j\to r$ in probability, if the total-variation convergence in probability failed, some subsequence would have error probability bounded below. Select a further subsequence for which $\mathbb P(|X_j/\sigma_j-r|>2^{-q})\le2^{-q}$ at its $q$th term; [F3] bounds each union of tail events by the corresponding geometric tail, which tends to zero, so the further subsequence converges almost surely to $r$, contradicting the deterministic conclusion.

For finite nonempty $J$, [F1] makes the scaled posterior and its Gaussian target product measures. Telescope the difference of their product densities one coordinate at a time. Integrating the absolute value of each term gives the $L^1$ distance of that coordinate pair, since every other coordinate density integrates to $1$. Thus the joint $L^1$ distance is at most the sum of the finitely many coordinate $L^1$ distances, which tends to zero in probability by step 2.1. For each measurable event $A$, the absolute difference of its probabilities is at most this $L^1$ distance, so the total-variation conclusion follows.

derivations.claim: Fix one coordinate $j=(l,k)$ and write $r=\theta_{0,j}/\sigma_j$. Under the true law, $X_j/\sigma_j=r+Z_j/(\sqrt n\sigma_j)\to r$ in probability, and $b_n=(\sqrt n\sigma_j)^{-1}\to0$. By [F1], under [A1], the posterior density of $U_n=\sqrt n(\theta_j-X_j)$ is $p_n(u\mid X_j)=\frac{e^{-u^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nu)}{c_n(X_j)},\qquad c_n(X_j)=\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-v^2/2}\varphi(X_j/\sigma_j+b_nv)\,dv.$ For any deterministic sequence $x_n/\sigma_j\to r$, boundedness of $\varphi$ and [F2] give $c_n(x_n)\to\varphi(r)\sqrt{2\pi}>0$.

Along such a deterministic sequence, $p_n(u\mid x_n)\to(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-u^2/2}$ pointwise and is eventually bounded by a constant multiple of $e^{-u^2/2}$. A second application of [F2] gives convergence in $L^1(du)$, hence convergence in total variation. Since $X_j/\sigma_j\to r$ in probability, if the total-variation convergence in probability failed, some subsequence would have error probability bounded below. Select a further subsequence for which $\mathbb P(|X_j/\sigma_j-r|>2^{-q})\le2^{-q}$ at its $q$th term; [F3] bounds each union of tail events by the corresponding geometric tail, which tends to zero, so the further subsequence converges almost surely to $r$, contradicting the deterministic conclusion.

For finite nonempty $J$, [F1] makes the scaled posterior and its Gaussian target product measures. Telescope the difference of their product densities one coordinate at a time. Integrating the absolute value of each term gives the $L^1$ distance of that coordinate pair, since every other coordinate density integrates to $1$. Thus the joint $L^1$ distance is at most the sum of the finitely many coordinate $L^1$ distances, which tends to zero in probability by step 2.1. For each measurable event $A$, the absolute difference of its probabilities is at most this $L^1$ distance, so the total-variation conclusion follows.

Assume AC. Let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m>0$, $B=\sum_j\beta_j$, and let $Z_j$ be independent $\operatorname{Gamma}(\beta_j,1)$ variables. Put $S=\sum_j Z_j$. Then $\omega=(Z_j/S)_j$ is $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$, and $S$ is $\operatorname{Gamma}(B,1)$, with mean $B$ and variance $B$. Each $Z_j$ has mean $\beta_j$, variance $\beta_j$, and moment-generating function $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=(1-u)^{-\beta_j}$ for every real $u<1$. For real $q_j$ satisfying $|q_j|\le b$, put $T(q)=\sum_jq_j(Z_j-\beta_j)$ and $V=\sum_j\beta_jq_j^2$. If $V>0$, then for $x>0$,
$$\Pr\{|T(q)|>x\}\le2\exp\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2(V+bx)}\right\}.$$
If $V=0$, $T(q)=0$ almost surely. Sums of disjoint groups of the $Z_j$ are independent Gamma variables with their respective summed shapes.

Assume Countable Choice. For shape $a>0$ and rate $b>0$, the **shape-rate Gamma distribution**
$\operatorname{Gamma}(a,b)$ is the probability measure on $(0,\infty)$ with
density
$$f_{a,b}(\lambda)=\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}\lambda^{a-1}e^{-b\lambda}$$
relative to Lebesgue measure. Its normalization is proved in
[[lem-gamma-density-normalization]]. The second argument is a rate, not a scale.

Assume Countable Choice. For $a,b>0$,
$$\int_{(0,\infty)}\frac{b^a}{\Gamma(a)}x^{a-1}e^{-bx}\,d\lambda_1(x)=1.$$

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$, the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ is the probability law
on the open probability simplex with density
$$\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$$
relative to $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$, with $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. Its
normalization is [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]]. For $k=1$, define
the law to be the point mass at $p_1=1$. All coordinates of the parameter
vector must be strictly positive.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

$$ \int_V f(y)\,d\lambda_n(y) = \int_U f(T(x))\,|\det DT(x)|\,d\lambda_n(x). $$

derivations.claim: The product Gamma law exists by [F3]. In its density make the substitution $z_j=s\omega_j$, $\omega_m=1-\sum_{j<m}\omega_j$. Its Jacobian is $s^{m-1}$: factor $s$ from the proportion columns of the derivative matrix and add its first $m-1$ rows to the last; the remaining last row has first entry one and all other entries zero. The resulting density factors as $s^{B-1}e^{-s}/\Gamma(B)$ times the simplex density in [F2]. Integrating either normalized factor proves both distributional assertions. For $m=1$, $\omega_1=1$ directly.

Substituting $y=(1-u)z$ in the Euler Gamma density gives $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=(1-u)^{-\beta_j}$ for $u<1$. Its first two derivatives at zero yield mean $\beta_j$ and variance $\beta_j$; differentiation is justified by an exponential majorant with any fixed parameter in $(0,1)$. Independence makes the joint transform of disjoint group sums the product $\prod_h(1-u_h)^{-\sum_{j\in I_h}\beta_j}$, which is the transform of the corresponding product Gamma law. By [F5], these are the same laws. In particular $S$ has the asserted mean and variance, also following from step 1.1.

For $|\lambda|b<1$, independence and step 1.2 give $\log\mathbb E e^{\lambda T(q)}=\sum_j\beta_j[-\log(1-\lambda q_j)-\lambda q_j]\le\lambda^2 V/[2(1-|\lambda|b)]$. Indeed the convergent logarithm series gives $-\log(1-u)-u\le\sum_{r\ge2}|u|^r/r\le u^2/[2(1-|u|)]$ for $|u|<1$. If $V>0$, set $\lambda=x/(V+bx)$; exponential Markov then bounds the upper tail by $\exp[-x^2/(2(V+bx))]$. Apply the same calculation to $-q$ and sum the bounds. If $V=0$, positivity of all $\beta_j$ forces every $q_j=0$, so $T(q)=0$.

Assume AC. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma>0$, the normal law $N(m,\sigma^2)$
of [[def-standard-normal-and-normal-laws]] has Lebesgue density
$$g_{m,\sigma}(y)=\frac1\sigma\frac{e^{-((y-m)/\sigma)^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^2}}e^{-(y-m)^2/(2\sigma^2)}.$$

If $f,g\in\mathcal L^2(\mu)$, then

$$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_2\|g\|_2.$$

Equality holds if and only if at least one of $f,g$ is zero almost everywhere,
or there is a constant $c>0$ with

$$|f|^2=c\,|g|^2\qquad\mu\text{-almost everywhere}.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

derivations.claim: At every zero of the nonnegative differentiable function $p$, $p'=0$. At each accumulation point of its zero set, differentiation along zeros of $p'$ gives $p''=0$; isolated zeros form a countable set. Thus $p''=0$ almost everywhere on $\{p=0\}$. Put $r=p''/p$ on $\{p>0\}$ and zero elsewhere. Then $p''=rp$ almost everywhere, $\int r^2p=J$, and [F2] gives $\int|p''|\le\sqrt J$. Both $p$ and $p''$ are continuous and compactly supported.

Let $P_t f=f*\phi_{\sqrt t}$ for $t>0$. Direct differentiation of [F1] gives $\partial_t\phi_{\sqrt t}=\tfrac12\partial_x^2\phi_{\sqrt t}$. Differentiation under the compactly supported $p$ integral and two integrations by parts therefore give $\partial_tP_t p=\tfrac12P_t p''$. The boundary terms vanish because $p,p'$ have compact support. Gaussian approximate identities converge uniformly on continuous compactly supported functions: split their convolution integral at $|z|\le\delta$, where uniform continuity controls the integrand difference, and its complement, whose normal mass tends to zero by scaling and integrability of [F1]. Integrating the derivative from a positive $\varepsilon$ to $t$ and letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ consequently yields $p-P_t p=-\tfrac12\int_0^tP_s p''\,ds$ pointwise.

Fix $t>0$ and put $q=P_t p$, which is positive everywhere. For $0<s\le t$, the Gaussian formula gives $\phi_{\sqrt t}(z)\ge\sqrt{s/t}\,\phi_{\sqrt s}(z)$ for every $z$, hence $q\ge\sqrt{s/t}P_s p$. Applying [F2] inside the convolution and then [F3] gives $|P_s p''|^2\le(P_s p)P_s(r^2p)$ and therefore $\int |P_s p''|^2/q\le\sqrt{t/s}\int P_s(r^2p)=\sqrt{t/s}J$. These inequalities remain valid if one of the pointwise nonnegative integrals is infinite.

Apply [F2] to the time integral in step 1.2 with weights $w(s)=(t/s)^{1/4}$. Since $\int_0^t w(s)ds=4t/3$, it gives $|p-q|^2\le\tfrac14(4t/3)\int_0^t w(s)^{-1}|P_s p''|^2ds$. Divide by $q$, integrate and use [F3] and step 2.1. The result is $\int(p-q)^2/q\le\tfrac14(4t/3)J\int_0^t(t/s)^{1/4}ds=(4/9)t^2J$. In particular all these weighted integrals are finite.

For $u>0$, $\log u\le u-1$ gives $u\log u-u+1\le(u-1)^2$. Also write $u=e^{2v}$. The inequality $|v|\le|\sinh v|$, obtained by integrating $\cosh v\ge1$, gives $u(\log u)^2\le(u-1)^2$. At $u=0$, both inequalities extend by their finite limits, with $u\log u=u(\log u)^2=0$. Apply these pointwise bounds to $u=p/q$ and integrate against $q$. Since $p,q$ integrate to one, [F4] identifies the first integral as KL; its negative part is integrable because $u\log u\ge-e^{-1}$. Both requested logarithmic quantities are at most the chi-square integral from step 2.2. Taking $t=\sigma^2$ proves the Statement.

derivations.claim: At every zero of the nonnegative differentiable function $p$, $p'=0$. At each accumulation point of its zero set, differentiation along zeros of $p'$ gives $p''=0$; isolated zeros form a countable set. Thus $p''=0$ almost everywhere on $\{p=0\}$. Put $r=p''/p$ on $\{p>0\}$ and zero elsewhere. Then $p''=rp$ almost everywhere, $\int r^2p=J$, and [F2] gives $\int|p''|\le\sqrt J$. Both $p$ and $p''$ are continuous and compactly supported.

Let $P_t f=f*\phi_{\sqrt t}$ for $t>0$. Direct differentiation of [F1] gives $\partial_t\phi_{\sqrt t}=\tfrac12\partial_x^2\phi_{\sqrt t}$. Differentiation under the compactly supported $p$ integral and two integrations by parts therefore give $\partial_tP_t p=\tfrac12P_t p''$. The boundary terms vanish because $p,p'$ have compact support. Gaussian approximate identities converge uniformly on continuous compactly supported functions: split their convolution integral at $|z|\le\delta$, where uniform continuity controls the integrand difference, and its complement, whose normal mass tends to zero by scaling and integrability of [F1]. Integrating the derivative from a positive $\varepsilon$ to $t$ and letting $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ consequently yields $p-P_t p=-\tfrac12\int_0^tP_s p''\,ds$ pointwise.

Fix $t>0$ and put $q=P_t p$, which is positive everywhere. For $0<s\le t$, the Gaussian formula gives $\phi_{\sqrt t}(z)\ge\sqrt{s/t}\,\phi_{\sqrt s}(z)$ for every $z$, hence $q\ge\sqrt{s/t}P_s p$. Applying [F2] inside the convolution and then [F3] gives $|P_s p''|^2\le(P_s p)P_s(r^2p)$ and therefore $\int |P_s p''|^2/q\le\sqrt{t/s}\int P_s(r^2p)=\sqrt{t/s}J$. These inequalities remain valid if one of the pointwise nonnegative integrals is infinite.

Apply [F2] to the time integral in step 1.2 with weights $w(s)=(t/s)^{1/4}$. Since $\int_0^t w(s)ds=4t/3$, it gives $|p-q|^2\le\tfrac14(4t/3)\int_0^t w(s)^{-1}|P_s p''|^2ds$. Divide by $q$, integrate and use [F3] and step 2.1. The result is $\int(p-q)^2/q\le\tfrac14(4t/3)J\int_0^t(t/s)^{1/4}ds=(4/9)t^2J$. In particular all these weighted integrals are finite.

For $u>0$, $\log u\le u-1$ gives $u\log u-u+1\le(u-1)^2$. Also write $u=e^{2v}$. The inequality $|v|\le|\sinh v|$, obtained by integrating $\cosh v\ge1$, gives $u(\log u)^2\le(u-1)^2$. derivations.claim: Put $u=p/q$ on $\{q>0\}$. The explicit absolute-continuity premise gives $p=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{q=0\}$. Define $g(u)=(\sqrt u-1)^2$ and $a(u)=(u\log u-u+1)/g(u)$, $b(u)=u(\log u)^2/g(u)$ for $u\ne1$, with their limiting values at $u=1$ and $u=0$. These limits are finite: at $u=1$ the Taylor expansions of $\sqrt u$ and $\log u$ give $a(1)=2$, $b(1)=4$, while $u\log u\to0$ and $u(\log u)^2\to0$ as $u\downarrow0$. Thus $a,b$ are continuous on $[0,2]$ and bounded there by [F3].

For $u\ge2$, $g(u)=u(1-u^{-1/2})^2\ge u(1-2^{-1/2})^2$, while $0\le u\log u-u+1\le u\log u$ and $u(\log u)^2$ retain their displayed forms. Hence $a(u)\le C\log u$ and $b(u)\le C(\log u)^2$ for a universal $C$. Combining with step 1.1, for every $0\le u\le R$, $u\log u-u+1\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R),\qquad u(\log u)^2\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R)^2.$

Integrating the first inequality in step 2.1 against $q\,d\mu$ gives the KL bound, since $\int q(u\log u-u+1)d\mu=\int p\log(p/q)d\mu$ by $\int p=\int q=1$ and [F2]. Integrating the second gives the log-square bound. Finally $\int qg,d\mu=h^2$ by [F1], so both right sides have the claimed factors of $h^2$.

For $x>0$, define $\log x$ to be the unique real $y$ such that $\exp(y)=x$. This is well-defined because [[cor-exponential-is-a-bijection-onto-positive-reals]] states that $\exp:\mathbb R\to(0,\infty)$ is a bijection.

The function $\log:(0,\infty)\to\mathbb R$ is continuous and strictly increasing, is onto $\mathbb R$, and satisfies, for $x,y>0$,

derivations.claim: Put $u=p/q$ on $\{q>0\}$. The explicit absolute-continuity premise gives $p=0$ $\mu$-almost everywhere on $\{q=0\}$. Define $g(u)=(\sqrt u-1)^2$ and $a(u)=(u\log u-u+1)/g(u)$, $b(u)=u(\log u)^2/g(u)$ for $u\ne1$, with their limiting values at $u=1$ and $u=0$. These limits are finite: at $u=1$ the Taylor expansions of $\sqrt u$ and $\log u$ give $a(1)=2$, $b(1)=4$, while $u\log u\to0$ and $u(\log u)^2\to0$ as $u\downarrow0$. Thus $a,b$ are continuous on $[0,2]$ and bounded there by [F3].

For $u\ge2$, $g(u)=u(1-u^{-1/2})^2\ge u(1-2^{-1/2})^2$, while $0\le u\log u-u+1\le u\log u$ and $u(\log u)^2$ retain their displayed forms. Hence $a(u)\le C\log u$ and $b(u)\le C(\log u)^2$ for a universal $C$. Combining with step 1.1, for every $0\le u\le R$, $u\log u-u+1\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R),\qquad u(\log u)^2\le Cg(u)(1+\log^+R)^2.$

Integrating the first inequality in step 2.1 against $q\,d\mu$ gives the KL bound, since $\int q(u\log u-u+1)d\mu=\int p\log(p/q)d\mu$ by $\int p=\int q=1$ and [F2]. Integrating the second gives the log-square bound. Finally $\int qg,d\mu=h^2$ by [F1], so both right sides have the claimed factors of $h^2$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and

([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).

$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$

applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.
