continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$ when the integral is finite, using the real-power convention, including $0^{1/r}=0$, of [[def-real-power]]. If the integral is $+\infty$, define $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=+\infty$ directly. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this nonnegative extended integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

derivations.claim: Put $x_n=n\epsilon_n^2$, $y_n=n\delta_n^2$, and let $D_n$ be the likelihood denominator relative to $p_0^n$. By [F1], on an event $\Omega_n$ with $P_0^n(\Omega_n^c)\le y_n^{-1}$, $D_n\ge e^{-(C_0+2)y_n}$.

Write $T_n=\sum_j\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}$ and $s_n=e^{-x_n}T_n$, so $s_n\to0$. Fix $K>2(C_0+3)$ and split indices into active $J_n^+=\{j:\pi_{n,j}\ge e^{-Kx_n}\}$ and small-mass $J_n^-$. Since $N_{n,j}\ge1$, $\sum_{J_n^-}\pi_{n,j}\le e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n=e^{(1-K/2)x_n}s_n$. For active $j$, $\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}\le T_n=e^{x_n}s_n$, hence $\log(N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j})\le(2+2K)x_n$ for all sufficiently large $n$.

Fix a sufficiently large constant $M$. If $M\epsilon_n\ge\sqrt2$, then the alternative is empty because Hellinger distance is at most $\sqrt2$, and the desired posterior mass is zero for this $n$. For the remaining $n$, choose, by [A1], a finite $\epsilon_n$-cover with centers in each active stratum's density image, as allowed by [F9]. For every center $q$ within $\epsilon_n$ of a density $p_\theta$ satisfying $h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n$, the triangle inequality gives $h(q,p_0)>(M-1)\epsilon_n$. Set $m_n=\left\lceil\frac{2\log 8}{(M-1)^2\epsilon_n^2}\right\rceil$. On a block of $m_n$ observations define $T_q=\mathbf1\{\prod_iq(X_i)>\prod_i p_0(X_i)\}$. On rejection, $p_0^{\otimes m_n}\le\sqrt{p_0^{\otimes m_n}q^{\otimes m_n}}$, so its type-I error is at most the product affinity; on acceptance, $q^{\otimes m_n}\le\sqrt{p_0^{\otimes m_n}q^{\otimes m_n}}$, so its type-II error under $q$ has the same bound. By [F2], this affinity is $(1-h^2(q,p_0)/2)^{m_n}\le e^{-m_nh^2(q,p_0)/2}\le1/8$.

If $h(p_\theta,q)\le\epsilon_n$, product affinity gives $h^2(P_\theta^{m_n},Q^{m_n})=2\left[1-\left(1-h^2(p_\theta,q)/2\right)^{m_n}\right]\le m_n\epsilon_n^2$, using $1-(1-u)^m\le mu$ for $u\in[0,1]$; [F3] bounds their total variation by $\sqrt{m_n}\epsilon_n$. Since $M\epsilon_n<\sqrt2$, $\epsilon_n^2<2/M^2$ and $m_n\epsilon_n^2\le\frac{2\log8}{(M-1)^2}+\frac{2}{M^2}\le1/64$ for sufficiently large $M$. The total variation is then at most $1/8$. Therefore the block test in step 1.3 rejects with probability at least $3/4$ under every $p_\theta$ in the alternative and at most $1/8$ under $p_0$.

Divide $L_n=\lfloor n/m_n\rfloor$ disjoint blocks and let $Y_k$ be their block-test indicators. Under each IID law the indicators are independent by [F6]; their means are at most $a=1/8$ under $P_0$ and at least $b=3/4$ under every alternative by step 2.1. For independent Bernoulli variables with means at most $a$, exponential Markov [F7] gives $P_0(L_n^{-1}\sum Y_k\ge t)\le e^{-L_nD(t\Vert a)}$; with means at least $b$, the negative-exponential bound gives $P_\theta(L_n^{-1}\sum Y_k<t)\le e^{-L_nD(t\Vert b)}$, where $D(t\Vert u)=t\log(t/u)+(1-t)\log((1-t)/(1-u))$. These bounds follow by bounding each moment generating function by $1-u+ue^\lambda$ (using $u=a$ for $\lambda>0$, $u=b$ for $\lambda<0$) and optimizing over $\lambda$.

The function $D(t\Vert a)-D(t\Vert b)$ is affine and strictly increasing on $[a,b]$, is negative at $a$, and equals $D(b\Vert a)>0$ at $b$. Let $t_*$ be its unique zero. By AC [A1], for each active $j$ choose $t_j\in[t_*,b]$ such that $L_n\{D(t_j\Vert a)-D(t_j\Vert b)\}=\log(N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j})$. This is possible after increasing $M$: writing $A=2\log 8$, $M\epsilon_n<\sqrt2$ implies $A/((M-1)^2\epsilon_n^2)>2$ for sufficiently large $M$, so the ceiling in $m_n$ costs at most a fixed factor; since $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, the floor in $L_n$ also costs at most a fixed factor eventually. Hence $L_n\ge cM^2x_n$ for a universal $c>0$, while step 1.2 bounds the right side by $(2+2K)x_n$. Define $\phi_{n,j}$ as the maximum of the block-majority tests over its $N_{n,j}$ centers, using threshold $t_j$. Continuity on $[t_*,b]$ and positivity of both divergences at $t_*$ give a constant $c_*>0$ such that $(D(t\Vert a)+D(t\Vert b))/2\ge c_*$ there. The null union bound and step 3.1 give $P_0^n(\phi_{n,j}=1)\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}$; the same Chernoff bound for a center within $\epsilon_n$ of each alternative gives $\sup_{\theta\in S_{n,j}:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n}P_\theta^n(\phi_{n,j}=0)\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}/\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}$ by step 2.1.

Let $\phi_n$ be one on the countable union of the rejection events of $\phi_{n,j}$ over $j\in J_n^+$ and zero otherwise; it is measurable as a countable union of measurable events. The union bound and step 4.1 give $P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. For the tested likelihood numerator on an active stratum, Tonelli [F4], the jointly measurable likelihood interface [F5] and change of density give $E_0[(1-\phi_n)\int_{\{\theta\in S_{n,j}:h(p_\theta,p_0)>M\epsilon_n\}}\prod_i\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi_n(d\theta)]\le\pi_{n,j}\sup_{\theta\text{ in the set}}P_\theta^n(1-\phi_{n,j})\le\sqrt{N_{n,j}\pi_{n,j}}e^{-c_*L_n}.$

Write $d_n=e^{-(C_0+2)y_n}$. For the active numerator $R_n^+$, step 5.1 gives $P_0^n(\phi_n=1)\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$ and $E_0[(1-\phi_n)R_n^+]\le T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. Thus, for every fixed $\zeta>0$, $P_0^n(R_n^+/D_n>\zeta)\le P_0^n(D_n<d_n)+T_ne^{-c_*L_n}+\zeta^{-1}d_n^{-1}T_ne^{-c_*L_n}$. This tends to zero for sufficiently large $M$, since $T_n=e^{x_n}s_n$, $y_n\le x_n$, $L_n\ge cM^2x_n$, and $s_n\to0$. For the small-mass numerator $R_n^-$, [F8] and Tonelli give $E_0[R_n^-]\le\sum_{J_n^-}\pi_{n,j}\le e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n$; hence its posterior mass tends to zero in probability by Markov and the denominator event, because $e^{(C_0+2)y_n}e^{-Kx_n/2}T_n\le s_ne^{(C_0+3-K/2)x_n}\to0$ when $K>2(C_0+3)$.

The posterior outside the $M\epsilon_n$-ball is the union of its active-stratum part, its small-mass-stratum part, and the sieve complement. Step 6.1 sends the first two parts to zero in probability, and the sieve-complement term tends to zero by hypothesis.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $P,Q$ be probability measures on the same measurable space
([[def-probability-measure]]). Absolute continuity $P\ll Q$ has the convention
of [[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]. If
$P\not\ll Q$, define $D(P\|Q)=+\infty$. If $P\ll Q$, assume AC
([[def-axiom-of-choice]]) as in [[def-likelihood-ratio-as-rn-derivative]] and
let $r=dP/dQ$ be a finite-valued nonnegative measurable representative of its
Radon–Nikodym class; such a representative exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].
On $\{r=0\}$ set $\ell=0$, and on $\{r>0\}$ set $\ell=\log r$. This
function is measurable: for $a\ge0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r>\exp(a)\}$, and for
$a<0$, $\{\ell>a\}=\{r=0\}\cup\{r>\exp(a)\}$, by the inverse and
monotonicity properties of the natural logarithm
([[def-natural-logarithm]], [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]]). These are
measurable sets by [[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Since
$P(\{r=0\})=\int_{\{r=0\}}r\,dQ=0$ by
[[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]], the value chosen there does not
affect $\int\ell\,dP$. Define
$$D(P\|Q):=\int \ell\,dP,$$
where $\log$ is the natural logarithm ([[def-natural-logarithm]]).

The definition is independent of the representative: two representatives
agree $Q$-almost everywhere, hence $P$-almost everywhere. Put
$$\psi(0):=0,\qquad \psi(t):=t\log t\quad(t>0).$$
The function $\psi$ is continuous at zero: for $s\ge1$,
$$0\le \frac{\log s}{s}=\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{u}\le\frac1s\int_1^s\frac{du}{\sqrt u}\le\frac2{\sqrt s}.$$
Thus $t\log t\to0$ as $t\downarrow0$; here $L=\log$ by
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]] and
[[def-integral-logarithm]]. On $(0,\infty)$, $\psi$ is a product of continuous
functions by [[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and
[[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]], so $\psi$ is continuous on
$[0,\infty)$ and $\psi(r)$ is measurable by
[[def-extended-real-valued-measurable-function]]. Its signed integral is
defined by the positive and negative parts
([[def-positive-and-negative-parts-of-a-function]],
[[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]).

For $0<t\le1$, the function $-t\log t$ has derivative $-\log t-1$ and
maximum $1/e$ at $t=1/e$: $e=\exp(1)>1$ by
[[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]] and
[[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]], $1/e=\exp(-1)$ by
[[cor-exponential-reciprocal-and-positivity]], and $\log(1/e)=-1$ by
[[thm-natural-logarithm-laws]] and the inverse definition. The mean value
theorem gives increase before and decrease after this point
([[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]], [[thm-integral-logarithm-derivative-and-normalisation]],
[[cor-integral-logarithm-agrees-with-natural-logarithm]], [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]).
At $t=0$ the negative part is zero. Since $Q$ is a probability measure,
$$\int \psi(r)^-\,dQ\le\frac1e.$$
The change-of-measure identity of [[thm-likelihood-ratio-change-of-measure]],
applied to $\ell^-$ gives $\int\ell^-\,dP=\int\psi(r)^-\,dQ\le1/e$,
so $\int\ell\,dP$ is well-defined; applying it to both positive and negative
parts gives
$$D(P\|Q)=\int\ell\,dP=\int\psi(r)\,dQ=\int r\log r\,dQ,$$
with $0\log0:=0$ and a finite negative part. Therefore the extended integral
is well-defined without an $\infty-\infty$ ambiguity.

This convention is directional: the first argument must be absolutely
continuous with respect to the second for the integral formula to apply.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space, $\Pi$ a prior probability measure on it, and $p_\theta$ a jointly measurable family of finite-valued probability densities relative to one fixed sigma-finite measure $\mu$. Let $P_0$ have finite-valued density $p_0$ relative to $\mu$, and let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID with law $P_0$. Assume the Axiom of Choice for the imported directional KL convention ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). The jointly measurable density family is explicit input, so no arbitrary-index selection of versions is used here. In the expression below, the weighted log terms are set to zero on $\{p_0=0\}$; on $\{p_0>0,p_\theta=0\}$ the log ratio is $-\infty$ and its square is $+\infty$. For $\epsilon_n>0$, define
$$K_n:=\left\{\theta:\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)\le\epsilon_n^2,\quad \int\left[\log\frac{p_\theta}{p_0}\right]^2p_0\,d\mu\le\epsilon_n^2\right\}.$$
Joint measurability and Tonelli make $K_n$ measurable, as verified below. If $\Pi(K_n)\ge e^{-Cn\epsilon_n^2}$ for $C>0$ and $\mathrm{KL}(P_0\Vert P_\theta)$ uses the direction in [[def-kullback-leibler-divergence]], then, defining the ratio to be zero on the $P_0$-null set where $p_0=0$, the likelihood denominator
$$D_n:=\int_\Theta\prod_{i=1}^n\frac{p_\theta(X_i)}{p_0(X_i)}\,\Pi(d\theta)$$
is finite and positive $P_0^n$-almost surely and
$$P_0^n\!\left\{D_n\ge e^{-(C+2)n\epsilon_n^2}\right\}\ge1-\frac1{n\epsilon_n^2}.$$

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let $p,q:\mathsf X\to[0,\infty)$ be measurable densities with $\int p\,d\mu=\int q\,d\mu=1$. They define probability laws $P(B)=\int_Bp\,d\mu$ and $Q(B)=\int_Bq\,d\mu$ ([[def-probability-measure]]). Their **root-L2 Hellinger distance**, with the root-L2 normalization, is
$$h(P,Q):=\left(\int_{\mathsf X}(\sqrt p-\sqrt q)^2\,d\mu\right)^{1/2}.$$

The dominating measure $\mu$ is fixed throughout a use of this definition. Changing either density on a $\mu$-null set does not change the value, since the integrand changes only on a null set. This definition does not assert that separate choices of density versions are jointly measurable in an additional parameter.

For probability densities $p,q$ relative to one fixed measure $\mu$, define $h$ as in [[def-hellinger-distance-between-density-laws]] and set $d_1(P,Q):=\int|p-q|\,d\mu$. Then $h$ is a metric on the induced probability laws and
$$h(P,Q)^2\le d_1(P,Q)=2\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV},\qquad d_1(P,Q)\le2h(P,Q),$$
where library total variation is the event supremum $\lVert P-Q\rVert_{\rm TV}=\sup_{A\in\mathcal A}|P(A)-Q(A)|$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). It is
**dominated** by a supplied positive measure $\mu$ on
$(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ when $\mu$ is sigma-finite
([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]) and
$P_\theta\ll\mu$ for every $\theta\in\Theta$
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]]).
The dominating measure is part of the specified setup. This condition adds no
measurable structure on $\Theta$ and no measurability of
$\theta\mapsto P_\theta$.

Let $\mathcal E=((\mathcal X,\mathcal A),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$
be dominated by the fixed sigma-finite positive measure $\mu$. For each
$\theta$, the Radon–Nikodym theorem gives the almost-everywhere class
$dP_\theta/d\mu$; a sigma-finite exhaustion for $\mu$ is also finite for the
probability measure $P_\theta$. Under AC, select simultaneously a
finite-valued measurable nonnegative representative $p_\theta$ from each
class. The nonnegative version exists by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

For fixed observed $x\in\mathcal X$, the function
$$L_x:\Theta\to[0,+\infty),\qquad L_x(\theta):=p_\theta(x),$$
is the **likelihood at $x$**. This is a function on the parameter labels, not
a probability distribution on $\Theta$. No sigma-algebra on $\Theta$ or
measurability of $L_x$ is implied. Each density is determined only
$\mu$-almost everywhere; there is no canonical pointwise version and, for
arbitrary uncountable $\Theta$, no common exceptional null set is asserted.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $n\ge1$, let $X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}$ be independent real random variables on a
common probability space, and let $g_i:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ be Borel
measurable for each $i<n$.

1. If every $g_i$ is nonnegative, then
   $$\mathbb E\left[\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)\right]=\prod_{i<n}\mathbb E[g_i(X_i)]$$
   in $[0,+\infty]$. In this finite product of expectations, a zero factor
   makes the product zero even when another factor is $+\infty$; otherwise
   multiplication has its usual extended nonnegative meaning.
2. If every $g_i(X_i)$ is integrable, then $\prod_{i<n}g_i(X_i)$ is integrable
   and the same factorization holds in $\mathbb R$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

A **probability measure** on a measurable space $(X,\mathcal A)$ is a measure $\mathbb P$ with $\mathbb P(X)=1$ ([[def-measure]]). The triple $(X,\mathcal A,\mathbb P)$ is a **probability space** ([[def-measure-space]]); $X$ is its sample space and the members of $\mathcal A$ are its events.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

A pseudometric $d$ on a set $T$ is a nonnegative symmetric function $d:T\times T\to[0,\infty)$ with $d(t,t)=0$ and $d(s,t)\le d(s,u)+d(u,t)$; distinct points may have distance zero. For a nonempty subset $\mathcal F\subseteq T$ and $\epsilon>0$, the covering number $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the least finite $k$ for which there are centers $f_1,\ldots,f_k\in\mathcal F$ such that every $f\in\mathcal F$ satisfies $d(f,f_j)\le\epsilon$ for some $j$. It is $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists. Set $N(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=1$.

The packing number $D(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ is the largest size of a finite subset $\{f_1,\ldots,f_k\}\subseteq\mathcal F$ whose distinct members have pairwise distance strictly greater than $\epsilon$. If the sizes of such finite subsets are unbounded, put $D=+\infty$; put $D(\epsilon,\varnothing,d)=0$. These conventions give the radius comparison proved in [[lem-packing-covering-number-comparison]]. The metric entropy is $H(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d):=\log N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,d)$ for nonempty classes, with $\log(+\infty)=+\infty$.

For a probability measure $Q$ on $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ and a measurable real function $g$, set $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=(\int |g|^r\,dQ)^{1/r}$ for $1\le r<\infty$ when the integral is finite, using the real-power convention, including $0^{1/r}=0$, of [[def-real-power]]. If the integral is $+\infty$, define $\|g\|_{Q,r}:=+\infty$ directly. The function $|g|$ is measurable by [[thm-arithmetic-and-lattice-operations-preserve-measurability]], and [[lem-real-power-preserves-measurability]] makes $|g|^r$ measurable, so this nonnegative extended integral is well-defined. On a class of functions with finite such norms, $d_{Q,r}(f,g):=\|f-g\|_{Q,r}$ is a pseudometric: nonnegativity, symmetry, and zero diagonal follow from the absolute value, and the triangle inequality is [[thm-minkowski-inequality-for-integrals]]. Functions that agree $Q$-almost everywhere have distance zero. We write $N(\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ for this covering number.

For measurable real endpoints $\ell\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere, the bracket $[\ell,u]$ is the set of measurable functions $f$ satisfying $\ell\le f\le u$ $Q$-almost everywhere. Its $L^r(Q)$ width is $\|u-\ell\|_{Q,r}$. The bracketing number $N_{[]} (\epsilon,\mathcal F,L^r(Q))$ is the least number of such brackets of width at most $\epsilon$ that cover $\mathcal F$, or $+\infty$ if no finite cover exists; for the empty class set it equal to $1$. Centers of metric covers are in $\mathcal F$; bracket endpoints need not be.

This is possible after increasing $M$: writing $A=2\log 8$, $M\epsilon_n<\sqrt2$ implies $A/((M-1)^2\epsilon_n^2)>2$ for sufficiently large $M$, so the ceiling in $m_n$ costs at most a fixed factor; since $n\epsilon_n^2\to\infty$, the floor in $L_n$ also costs at most a fixed factor eventually. Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

derivations.claim: For any probability measure $Q$ on $M_0(w)$ and any bounded $1$-Lipschitz function $h$, $|h(x)-h(P_Jx)|\le\min(2,\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)})$. Splitting at $\varepsilon>0$ and taking the supremum over such $h$ gives $\beta_{BL}(Q,Q\circ P_J^{-1})\le\varepsilon+2Q(\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon)$. Applying this to $Q_n$ and $G$, then using the triangle inequality, bounds $\beta_{BL}(Q_n,G)$ by the two projection errors and the fixed-$J$ distance between projected laws.

For each $x\in M_0(w)$, [F2] gives $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$. Thus the events $\{x:\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon\}$ decrease to the empty set, and [F3] makes their $G$-probabilities tend to zero. Given any target error, first choose $\varepsilon$ small, then choose $J$ large so this $G$-tail and the limiting posterior-tail probability are small; for that fixed $J$, the projected-law distance tends to zero in probability by assumption. Step 1.1 then implies $\beta_{BL}(Q_n,G)\to0$ in probability.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

Only supports meeting $t$ can contribute. Uniformly bounded overlap bounds their number by a constant, and each coefficient has magnitude at most $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C_0 2^{-l/2}$. Thus $\sup_t\sum_k|\langle1_{[0,t]},\psi_{lk}\rangle|\le C_1 2^{-l/2}$. The finitely many coarsest levels have a finite uniform sum as well.

By [F1] and step 1.1, the absolute sum of all terms at levels $l\ge l_0$ is at most $C_1\|x\|_{M(w)}\sum_{l\ge l_0}w_l2^{-l/2}$, uniformly over $t$. Its tails tend uniformly to zero because $S_w<\infty$. Each finite-level sum is continuous in $t$, since $t\mapsto\int_0^t\psi_{lk}(u)du$ is continuous for an $L^1$ function. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

citations.quote: Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$. Then the following are
equivalent:

1. the family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent;
2. for every natural number $n\ge1$, every choice of distinct indices
   $i_0,\dots,i_{n-1}\in I$, and every choice of measurable sets
   $B_k\in\Sigma_{i_k}$,
   $$\mathbb P\bigl(X_{i_0}\in B_0,\dots,X_{i_{n-1}}\in B_{n-1}\bigr)=\prod_{k<n}\mathbb P(X_{i_k}\in B_k).$$

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $H$ be a real Hilbert space with a countable orthonormal basis $(\psi_{lk})$, where $K_l$ is the level-$l$ index set and $|K_l|=2^l$ for each $l\ge0$ ([[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Such an $H$ is separable because finite rational linear combinations of the countable basis are dense. Let $\xi_{lk}$ be IID real random variables with common density $\varphi$ and finite second moment $m_2=\int x^2\varphi(x)\,dx<\infty$ ([[def-identically-distributed-and-iid-random-variables]]). For $\alpha>0$, set $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ and form the partial wavelet sums

$$f_N=\sum_{0\le l\le N}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}.$$

Assume countable choice, denoted $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, when specializing to $H=L^2([0,1])$. Then $f_N$ converges almost surely in $H$ to a Borel $H$-valued random element $f$, and

$$\mathbb E\|f\|_H^2=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^l\sigma_l^2=m_2\sum_{l\ge0}2^{-2\alpha l}<\infty.$$

The abstract Hilbert-space assertion is choice-free; for $H=L^2([0,1])$, completeness follows from the Riesz–Fischer theorem under countable choice ([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]], [[thm-riesz-fischer-completeness-of-l-p]]). More generally, finitely many additional coarsest orthogonal coordinates with fixed scales and finite coefficient second moments may be added; they contribute only a finite expectation to the displayed sum.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For each coordinate $j$, the pair $(\theta_j,X_j)$ is a measurable function of the independent pair $(\xi_j,Z_j)$. Thus the coordinate pairs are independent: finite rectangle probabilities factor by [F1] and [F2]. Fix finite $J$. For any cylinder event $B$ depending on finitely many observations outside $J$, the random vector $(\theta_J,X_J)$ is independent of $B$ by that same factorization. The events in $\sigma(X_{J^c})$ for which this independence identity holds form a lambda-system containing the outside-coordinate cylinder pi-system; [F3] extends it to all outside-data events. Hence conditioning on $X_{J^c}$ adds no information about $\theta_J$ once $X_J$ is known.

For finite $J$, the joint prior density of $\theta_J$ is the product of $\sigma_j^{-1}\varphi(t_j/\sigma_j)$, and the likelihood of $X_J=x_J$ is proportional to $\prod_{j\in J}e^{-n(x_j-t_j)^2/2}$. Each one-dimensional normalizer is at most $1$ and is positive: the Gaussian factor is bounded by $1$, is strictly positive everywhere, and the prior density integrates to $1$. Thus the normalized product density is $\prod_{j\in J}p_{j,n}(t_j\mid x_j)$. Integrating it over rectangles in $\theta_J$ and $X_J$ verifies the conditional-law identity for these coordinates. The prior is a Borel probability on $L^2$ by [L1] under [A1], and [A2] supplies the full posterior kernel; step 1.1 extends the finite-coordinate identity to the full observation sequence.

The product of the one-coordinate conditional densities in step 2.1 is exactly the stated finite-dimensional posterior marginal, so the posterior factors by coordinates for every finite index set $J$.

Let $y\mapsto\Pi_y$ be a probability kernel on $\mathbb R$. For $u\in(0,1)$ put
$$F_y(t)=\Pi_y((-\infty,t]),\qquad q_u(y)=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:F_y(r)\ge u\}.$$The infimum is taken in $\mathbb R$; [[thm-infimum-property]] supplies it once the defining set is shown nonempty and bounded below. Then $q_u:\mathsf Y\to\mathbb R$ is measurable, and$$\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)))\le u\le\Pi_y((-\infty,q_u(y)]).$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

derivations.claim: Fix $x\in\mathbb R$ and $\eta>0$. Choose $0<\delta<\min(1,\eta)$. The piecewise-linear ramps that fall from $1$ to $0$ on $[x-\delta,x]$ and on $[x,x+\delta]$ bound $1_{(-\infty,x]}$ below and above. Multiplying each ramp by $\delta$ makes its sup norm and Lipschitz constant at most $1$. Comparing the lower and upper ramps under $Q_n$ with their integrals under $Q$ gives $|Q_n((-\infty,x])-F(x)|\le\delta^{-1}\beta_{BL}(Q_n,Q)+Q([x-\delta,x+\delta])$. By [A1], $Q(\{x\})=0$; [F2] then gives $Q([x-\delta,x+\delta])\to0$ as $\delta\downarrow0$. First choose $\delta$ small and then let $n\to\infty$; this proves $Q_n((-\infty,x])\to F(x)$ in probability.

Write $q=q_u(Q)$ as in [F1]. Since [A1] makes $F$ continuous, the CDF bracket in [F1] gives $F(q)=u$. For every sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$, strict increase near $q$ then gives $F(q-\varepsilon)<u<F(q+\varepsilon)$. Step 1.1 at these two points implies, with probability tending to one, $Q_n((-\infty,q-\varepsilon])<u<Q_n((-\infty,q+\varepsilon])$. By monotonicity, no rational at or below $q-\varepsilon$ is in the defining set for $q_u(Q_n)$, while every rational above $q+\varepsilon$ belongs to it. Its infimum therefore lies in $[q-\varepsilon,q+\varepsilon]$. Since arbitrarily small such $\varepsilon$ are available, the quantiles converge in probability.

Fix the real orthonormal wavelet basis and level weights $a_l$ of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. For $0\le s<S$, define the basis Sobolev space
$$H^s_2=\left\{g\in L^2([0,1]):\sum_{l,k}a_l^{2s}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|^2<\infty\right\}.$$
For $g\in H^s_2$, $s>1/2$, and $f\in L^2([0,1])$, define $L_g(f)=\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}$. For $x=(x_{lk})\in H(\delta)$, the intended extension is the coefficient pairing $L_g(x)=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle$; [[lem-smooth-functional-extends-to-negative-sobolev-space]] proves that this series is absolutely convergent and defines a continuous linear functional on $H(\delta)$ for every $\delta>0$.

In the white-noise experiment $X^{(n)}=f_0+n^{-1/2}W$, $L_g(X^{(n)})$ means this continuous pairing with the $H(\delta)$-valued observation. It does not assert that $X^{(n)}$ is an $L^2$ function. The representer is nonzero when $g\ne0$; the corresponding white-noise variance is $\|g\|_2^2$.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

derivations.claim: Since $s>1/2$, the level factor $a_l^{1-2s}(\log a_l)^{2\delta}$ is bounded: it tends to zero as $a_l\to\infty$, because a positive power of $a_l$ dominates every fixed power of $\log a_l$, and the finitely many coarsest levels have finite weights. Thus $w_l^{-1}\le C_{s,\delta}^2a_l^{2s}$ after increasing a finite constant.

Weighted Cauchy–Schwarz gives $\sum_{l,k}|x_{lk}g_{lk}|\le(\sum_{l,k}w_l|x_{lk}|^2)^{1/2}(\sum_{l,k}w_l^{-1}|g_{lk}|^2)^{1/2}\le C_{s,\delta}\|x\|_{H(\delta)}\|g\|_{H^s_2}$. The same bound applied to $x-y$ proves continuity and absolute convergence of the series.

If $x$ is the coefficient sequence of $f\in L^2$, its finite orthonormal projections converge to $f$ in $L^2$ because $(\psi_{lk})$ is a complete orthonormal basis. Their inner products with $g$ are the finite partial sums of the displayed pairing, and converge to $\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}$ by continuity of the inner product. Step 2.1 identifies the same limit with $L_g(x)$.

citations.quote:
For type S use a fixed sufficiently regular compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution wavelet basis $(\psi_{lk})$ on $[0,1]$ as in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with boundary correction, regularity greater than the truth smoothness $\alpha$, and $|K_l|=2^l$. The spaces $V_L$ spanned by the retained levels $l\le L$ contain constants and have orthonormal scaling bases with uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-L}$, and suprema at most $C2^{L/2}$; a fixed shift of the scaling-resolution index is absorbed in $C$. The wavelets likewise have uniformly bounded overlap, support diameters at most $C2^{-l}$, and suprema at most $C2^{l/2}$. For an integer $m>\alpha$, the detail wavelets have vanishing moments through degree $m-1$, and derivatives through order $m$ satisfy $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$, with uniformly bounded overlap of their supports; the fixed low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the sufficiently regular compact multiresolution basis conditions in the source density theorem. For the density-model source results, every truth $f_0$ is a probability density satisfying $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$ for constants $\rho_0,D_0$. For $n\ge3$ and smoothness index $\alpha>0$, let $j_n$ and $\ell_n$ be the largest integers satisfying
$$2^{j_n}\le n^{1/(2\alpha+1)},\qquad 2^{\ell_n}\le(n/\log n)^{1/(2\alpha+1)}.$$
Choose one cutoff sequence $L_n\in\{j_n,\ell_n\}$ for all $n\ge3$; set any finite $L_n$ for $n=1,2$, which does not change asymptotic claims.

For a finite wavelet series $T_n=\sum_{l\le L_n}\sum_{k\in K_l}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$, define $c(T_n)=\log\int_0^1e^{T_n(x)}dx$ and the normalized log-density $f_n(x)=e^{T_n(x)-c(T_n)}$.

The **type-S1 family** takes IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with a continuous density $\varphi_H$ for which $\log\varphi_H$ is Lipschitz, and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$. Its source theorem assumes $\log f_0$ has coefficient Hölder regularity $\alpha>1$ and $f_0$ is bounded above and bounded away from zero.

The **type-S2 family** takes IID standard-normal coefficients and uses $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$, where $0<r<\alpha-1/4$; its source theorem uses $\log f_0\in C^\alpha$, $\alpha>1/2$, and positive finite density bounds.

For the **type-H family**, use the Haar basis instead of the regular type-S wavelets: its scaling function is $1$ and $\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}})$ for $l\ge0$ and $0\le k<2^l$. The histogram space at resolution $L$ consists of the scaling coordinate and detail levels $l<L$; all detail coefficients at $l\ge L$ vanish. Partition $[0,1]$ into dyadic cells $I_{L_n,k}$ of length $2^{-L_n}$, draw $\omega=(\omega_k)_{k<2^{L_n}}\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(a_{0,L_n},\ldots,a_{2^{L_n}-1,L_n})$, and set $f_n=2^{L_n}\omega_k$ on cell $I_{L_n,k}$. The source assumptions are $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$, and $f_0\in C^\alpha$ for $1/2<\alpha\le1$, together with the common positive finite density bounds above. The posterior asymptotic conclusions for these families are separate results.

Here $C^\alpha_\psi$ denotes the coefficient class with norm $\|g\|_{C^\alpha_\psi}:=\sup_{l,k}2^{l(\alpha+1/2)}|\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle|$. For sufficiently regular standard wavelets this is the usual Hölder scale (with the usual Zygmund interpretation at integer smoothness).

derivations.claim: For a type-S draw, boundedness of the finite wavelet sum gives $M=\|T\|_\infty<\infty$, hence $e^{-M}\le e^{T(x)}\le e^M$ on $[0,1]$. Therefore $0<e^{-M}\le\int_0^1e^{T(x)}dx\le e^M<\infty$, so $c(T)$ is finite and $f=e^{T-c(T)}$ is positive and integrates to one. The same bounds make $f$ bounded, so $f\in L^2([0,1])$.

For type H, each dyadic cell has length $2^{-L}$, so $\int_0^1 f(x)dx=\sum_{k<2^L}2^L\omega_k2^{-L}=\sum_k\omega_k=1$. Also $\|f\|_2^2=2^L\sum_k\omega_k^2\le2^L(\sum_k\omega_k)^2=2^L<\infty$, since all weights are nonnegative. Thus every type-H draw is a nonnegative $L^2$ probability density.

Let $V_L$ be the span of wavelets through level $L$ in a compactly supported orthonormal multiresolution basis on $[0,1]$, either boundary corrected or periodized. Assume constants belong to $V_L$, its dimension $d_L\asymp2^L$, and its orthonormal scaling functions $\phi_{Lk}$ have supremum norm at most $C2^{L/2}$, support diameter at most $C2^{-L}$, and uniformly bounded overlap. Periodized supports and distances are interpreted on the circle. Assume also $\sum_k|\psi_{lk}(x)|\le C2^{l/2}$ and $\|\psi_{lk}\|_1\le C2^{-l/2}$. Let $P_L$ denote the orthogonal projection onto $V_L$.

Then $P_L$ has a kernel $K_L$ satisfying $\sup_x\int|K_L(x,y)|dy\le C'$ and $K_L(x,y)=0$ when $\operatorname{dist}(x,y)>C'2^{-L}$. If $a$ is $\beta$-Hölder for $0<\beta\le1$, then
$$\|P_L(ah)-ah\|_\infty\le C'\|a\|_{C^\beta}2^{-\beta L}\|h\|_\infty,\qquad h\in V_L.$$
For the composition assertion, assume additionally an integer $m>\alpha$ such that $\|\psi_{lk}^{(q)}\|_\infty\le C_q2^{l(q+1/2)}$ for $0\le q\le m$, bounded overlap also for their derivatives, and vanishing moments through degree $m-1$ for the detail wavelets, including boundary wavelets; the finite low scaling functions are $C^m$. These are the usual sufficiently regular compact wavelet hypotheses. If a bounded function $g$ has coefficients bounded by $C_g2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, with $\alpha>0$, and its wavelet expansion represents $g$ in $L^2$, then $\|g-P_Lg\|_\infty\le C''C_g2^{-\alpha L}$, up to equality of the continuous representatives. Under these additional derivative and cancellation hypotheses, $e^g$ also has coefficients bounded by $C_g^\prime2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$, including integer $\alpha$, and $g,e^g$ are $\beta$-Hölder for every $0<\beta<\min(\alpha,1)$. Moreover $\|h\|_\infty\le C''\sqrt{d_L}\|h\|_2$ for $h\in V_L$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

derivations.claim: Quotient out constants before using likelihood curvature. Constants belong to the fixed low scaling space. An orthogonal change within that finite space separates $T=\theta+c1$; integrate $c$ out of the prior and write $q_L$ for the resulting Lebesgue density on $E_L$. The likelihood depends only on $\theta$. In S1 its product density before integration obeys $p(\theta+u,c)/p(\theta,c)\in[e^{-B_L\|u\|_2},e^{B_L\|u\|_2}]$, where $B_L^2\le C\sum_{l\le L}2^l\sigma_l^{-2}\le Cd^{2\alpha+2}$. Integrating preserves both inequalities for $q_L$; it is positive, finite almost everywhere, and the log-Lipschitz inequality supplies its positive continuous finite version everywhere. In S2 the marginal is a nondegenerate Gaussian on $E_L$, with precision $Q_L$ equal to $\sigma_l^{-2}$ on high wavelets and a fixed positive definite low block; hence $\|Q_L\|\le Cd^{2r+1}$.

Let $f_*=e^{\theta_*}/\int e^{\theta_*}$. [F1] gives $\|f_*-f_0\|_\infty\le Cd^{-\alpha}$. For $\ell(\theta)=n(P_n\theta-\log\int e^\theta)$, the centered score at $\theta_*$ has expected squared Euclidean norm at most $Cnd$: sum the coordinate variances, each bounded by $D_0$ by orthonormality. The score's deterministic mean is the coefficient vector of $n(f_0-f_*)$, with norm at most $Cnd^{-\alpha}$. Consequently [F3] gives $\|\nabla\ell(\theta_*)\|_2=O_P(ne_n)$. On every ball $\|u\|_2\le Re_n$ with fixed $R$, [F1] and $\sqrt d e_n\to0$ make $f_{\theta_*+u}$ bounded uniformly above and away from zero. For $v\in E_L$, $\operatorname{Var}_f(v)=\inf_a\int(v-a)^2f$ lies between $c\|v\|_2^2$ and $C\|v\|_2^2$, using $\int v=0$. Thus $-\nabla^2\ell$ is between $cnI$ and $CnI$ on these balls. Convexity of $-\ell$ holds globally.

In S1, $B_L\le Cne_n$ by either cutoff. In S2 the Hölder coefficient bound gives $G_L^2:=\|Q_L\theta_*\|_2^2\le C[1+\sum_{l\le L}2^{l(4r+2-2\alpha)}]$, so $G_L\le Cne_n$, and $\|Q_L\|/n\to0$ because $r<\alpha$. The Gaussian log-density increment is exactly $-\langle Q_L\theta_*,u\rangle-\langle Q_Lu,u\rangle/2$. In particular its radial upper slope is at most $G_L$, and on the $e_n$ ball it is bounded below by $-G_Le_n-\|Q_L\|e_n^2/2$.

Fix a score event $\|\nabla\ell(\theta_*)\|_2\le Ane_n$. Put $r_0=Re_n$, with $R$ a large fixed constant. Taylor's formula on the $r_0$ ball bounds $\ell(\theta_*+r_0\omega)-\ell(\theta_*)$ above by $Ane_nr_0-cnr_0^2/2$ and its radial derivative above by $Ane_n-cnr_0$. Global convexity of $-\ell$ extends this derivative bound to every $r\ge r_0$. Add the prior bound $B_Lr$ in S1, or $G_Lr$ with its nonpositive quadratic term in S2. For $R$ large enough the log unnormalized posterior ratio $H(r\omega)$ relative to $\theta_*$ is at most $-c'nr_0r$ for all $r\ge r_0$. On $r\le e_n$, the lower Taylor bound and the prior lower bounds instead give $H\ge-C_Ane_n^2$.

Polar integration in dimension $m=d-1$ bounds the tail/normalizer ratio by $e^{C_Ane_n^2}m\int_R^\infty t^{m-1}e^{-c'nRe_n^2t}dt$. Here $ne_n^2\ge d>m$. Choose $R$ so large that $\log t\le c'Rt/4$ for $t\ge R$ and $C_A\le c'R^2/4$. The integral is then at most $[m/(c''nRe_n^2)]e^{-c''nR^2e_n^2}$ after decreasing $c''>0$, and tends to zero. The denominator used here is the integral on the $e_n$ ball, at least its volume times $e^{-C_Ane_n^2}$ times the positive unnormalized value at $\theta_*$. First increase $A$ to make its score event arbitrarily probable, then increase $R$. This proves tightness. For any $b_n\to\infty$, eventual containment of every fixed $Re_n$ ball in the $b_ne_n$ ball yields the stated equivalent formulation.

Every modeled density is everywhere positive. Its prior predictive product density is positive and integrates to one by [F2], so it is finite Lebesgue-almost everywhere on the sample cube. The law $P_0^n$ has a bounded Lebesgue density, hence the same exceptional set is $P_0^n$-null. This proves finite positive evidence on the asserted fibers independently of the score event.

before_contract.claim:
Assume AC for the imported measure and Gaussian interfaces. Use Type-S priors and either cutoff of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]] with the compact multiresolution basis of [[lem-compact-wavelet-projection-kernel-and-commutator]], regular enough for the truth's Hölder approximation. Suppose $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0$, $g_0=\log f_0\in C^\alpha$, and $\alpha>1/2$. In S1 take $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ and any probability density whose logarithm is Lipschitz on all of $\mathbb R$. In S2 take Gaussian coefficients with $\sigma_l=2^{-l(r+1/2)}$ and $0<r<\alpha-1/4$.

Write $d=\dim V_{L_n}\asymp2^{L_n}$, $E_{L_n}=V_{L_n}\cap\{h:\int h=0\}$, $\theta=T-\int T$, $\theta_*=P_{L_n}g_0-\int g_0$, and $e_n=\sqrt{d/n}+d^{-\alpha}$. Under IID data of density $f_0$, the posterior distributions of $\|\theta-\theta_*\|_2/e_n$ are tight in probability. Equivalently, for every deterministic $b_n\to\infty$,
$$\Pi(\|\theta-\theta_*\|_2>b_ne_n\mid X^n)\to0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability. The normalizer defining the posterior is positive and finite $P_0^n$-almost surely. The quotient prior has a positive continuous Lebesgue density $q_L$ on $E_L$. In S1 it obeys
$$|\log q_L(\theta+u)-\log q_L(\theta)|\le B_L\|u\|_2,\qquad B_L^2\le C\sum_{l\le L}2^l\sigma_l^{-2},$$
and a shift in a single high wavelet coordinate obeys the sharper bound $C|u_{lk}|/\sigma_l$. The low scaling block has a fixed finite collection of analogous weighted bounds. In S2 the quotient prior is centered Gaussian, with precision $Q_L$ diagonal on high wavelets with entries $\sigma_l^{-2}$ and a fixed positive definite low scaling block. Its log-density increment is $-\langle Q_L\theta,u\rangle-\langle Q_Lu,u\rangle/2$.

citations.quote:
A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be a countable complete orthonormal basis of the real Hilbert space $L^2([0,1])$ ([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]], [[def-hilbert-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]). For a wavelet basis, index levels by $l\ge0$, let $K_l$ have $2^l$ indices, and put $a_l=2^l$ for $l\ge1$ and $a_0=2$ for the finite coarsest level. This finite-level convention only prevents a zero logarithmic weight and does not change any convergence criterion below. For a trigonometric basis, use its integer frequency index $l$, bounded multiplicities, and $a_l=\max(2,|l|)$.

Here an **$S$-regular wavelet basis** means a wavelet orthonormal basis whose members are $S$ times differentiable, with each derivative through order $S$ in $L^2([0,1])$, following the source convention. The weak BvM theorem below only uses the basis's completeness, orthonormality, and level counts.

For $\delta>0$, define $H(\delta)=H^{-1/2,\delta}_2$ to be the space of coefficient sequences $c=(c_{lk})$ with norm

$$\|c\|_{H(\delta)}^2:=\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}|c_{lk}|^2<\infty.$$

Its inner product is the corresponding weighted coefficient inner product. Multiplying each coordinate by $a_l^{-1/2}(\log a_l)^{-\delta}$ identifies it isometrically with $\ell^2(I)$, where $I=\{(l,k):k\in K_l\}$ (or the corresponding trigonometric index set). This sequence space is complete: if $x^{(m)}$ is Cauchy, each coordinate converges to a scalar $x_i$; for every finite $F\subset I$, the Cauchy bound passes to the limit in $\sum_{i\in F}|x_i^{(m)}-x_i^{(n)}|^2$, so the supremum over finite $F$ shows $x^{(m)}\to x$ in $\ell^2(I)$. It is separable because finite-support sequences with rational coordinates form a countable dense set. Thus $H(\delta)$ is a separable Hilbert space without an additional choice assumption.

A function $f\in L^2([0,1])$ is identified with its coefficient sequence $c_{lk}=\langle f,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. For each finite set $F$ of indices, orthonormality makes $\sum_{(l,k)\in F}c_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ orthogonal to its residual in $L^2$, so the Pythagorean identity gives $\sum_F|c_{lk}|^2\le\|f\|_2^2$. Taking the supremum over finite $F$ and using the boundedness of the weights proves continuity of the coefficient map. If all coefficients of $f$ vanish, then $f$ is orthogonal to the linear span of the basis. Completeness makes this span dense, and continuity of $g\mapsto\langle f,g\rangle$ gives $\langle f,f\rangle=0$, hence $f=0$ in $L^2$. Applying this to the difference of two functions proves injectivity. Thus the coefficient map is a continuous linear embedding $L^2([0,1])\hookrightarrow H(\delta)$.

The weight trace $\sum_{l,k}a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$ is finite exactly when $\delta>1/2$: for wavelets its tail is a constant multiple of $\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$, while for a trigonometric basis it is comparable to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The product-prior theorem below uses the wavelet case.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

$$\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Assume countable choice. Put $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Then $\gamma(E)=\int_Eg(x)\,dx$ is a Borel probability on $\mathbb R$. In this item and its applications, write $N(m,v)$ for its pushforward under $x\mapsto m+\sqrt v\,x$, where $v\ge0$; thus $N(m,0)=\delta_m$. This density convention requires no full axiom of choice. For $v>0$ the law has density
$$g_{m,v}(x)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp\{- (x-m)^2/(2v)\},$$
and its CDF is continuous and strictly increasing. Its mean and variance are $m$ and $v$.

If $Z_j$ are mutually independent with density $g$ and $\sum_{j\ge1}c_j^2=v<\infty$, and the finite sums $S_m=\sum_{j\le m}c_jZ_j$ converge in probability to a supplied real random variable $S$, then $S$ has law $N(0,v)$. In particular, this applies whenever the sums converge almost surely or in $L^2$.

derivations.claim: Write $w_l=a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$. In the wavelet case, the trace sum is a finite coarsest term plus $\sum_{l\ge1}2^lw_l=(\log2)^{-2\delta}\sum_{l\ge1}l^{-2\delta}$. On each block $2^m\le l<2^{m+1}$, the sum of $l^{-r}$ is between $2^m2^{-r(m+1)}$ and $2^m2^{-rm}$; hence these blocks form a convergent geometric series when $r>1$, while for $r\le1$ their contributions are bounded below by a fixed positive constant and the series diverges. For trigonometric coefficients with bounded multiplicities, the block $2^m\le |l|<2^{m+1}$ contributes between constant multiples of $m^{-2\delta}$ to $\sum_{l\ge2}[l(\log l)^{2\delta}]^{-1}$. The same comparison therefore gives finiteness exactly when $\delta>1/2$. Thus the trace $T_\delta:=\sum_{l,k}w_l$ is finite in either case.

Let $S_m$ be the sum of $w_lZ_{lk}^2$ over the first $m$ coordinates in the fixed countable enumeration. These nonnegative partial sums increase to $S=\sum_{l,k}w_lZ_{lk}^2$, and [F3] gives $\mathbb ES=\lim_m\mathbb ES_m=\sum_{l,k}w_l=T_\delta$. The mean and second moment of each coordinate are $0$ and $1$ by [F5]. If $S=\infty$ on a set of probability $p>0$, then $\mathbb ES\ge Rp$ for every $R>0$, impossible; hence $S<\infty$ almost surely.

On that probability-one event, the finite-coordinate sums of $W$ are Cauchy in $H(\delta)$ because the squared norm of every tail is the corresponding tail of the convergent series $S$. Completeness gives a limit in $H(\delta)$. The Cauchy event is measurable, and the partial sums are measurable; their pointwise limit on that event is measurable as an $H(\delta)$-valued map because the space is separable. Setting it to zero on the measurable complement gives a Borel random element.

Let $e_j$ be the unit vector of the weighted sequence Hilbert space supported on coordinate $j$ and let $b_j=L(e_j)$ for a continuous real linear functional $L$. For each finite set $F$, boundedness applied to $\sum_{j\in F}b_je_j$ gives $\sum_{j\in F}b_j^2\le\|L\|^2$, so $\sum_jb_j^2<\infty$. Since the weights $w_j$ are bounded, $v:=\sum_jw_jb_j^2<\infty$. The finite-coordinate projections of $W$ converge almost surely in $H(\delta)$ by step 3.1, so continuity gives $L(W)=\lim_m\sum_{j\le m}\sqrt{w_j}b_jZ_j$ almost surely. By [F5] this limit has exactly the density normal law $N(0,v)$. Thus $W$ is centered Gaussian. For a continuous coefficient pairing $L(c)=\sum_jd_jc_j$, one has $b_j=d_j/\sqrt{w_j}$, giving $v=\sum_jd_j^2$.

Enumerate the infinite basis as $(\psi_j)_{j\ge1}$, write its white-noise coordinates as $Z_j$, and let $A_j=\{|Z_j|\ge1\}$. The displayed normal density is positive on $[1,2]$, so $p:=\mathbb P(A_j)>0$; independence gives $\mathbb P(\bigcap_{j=m}^{m+q}A_j^c)=(1-p)^{q+1}$. By [F4], $\mathbb P(\bigcap_{j\ge m}A_j^c)=0$ for each $m$, so the event that only finitely many $A_j$ occur, a countable union of these intersections, has probability zero: disjointify that union by replacing its $m$th event $E_m$ with $E_m\setminus\bigcup_{i<m}E_i$, and use countable additivity and monotonicity to sum zero probabilities. Therefore $\sum_{j\le n}Z_j^2$ is unbounded almost surely. If the same $H(\delta)$ element were represented by an $L^2$ function, the coefficient embedding in [F1] would identify its $L^2$ coefficients with $Z_j$. The finite Pythagorean identity, applied to the projection onto $\psi_1,\dots,\psi_n$, would then give $\sum_{j\le n}Z_j^2\le\|W\|_2^2$ for every $n$, a contradiction.
