citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel
space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

The construction uses the Poisson random measure with intensity
$$\mu(dx,dt)=\alpha(dx)t^{-1}e^{-t}\,dt\quad\text{on }\mathsf X\times(0,\infty),$$
and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a
gamma-process existence theorem.

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of
[[def-independent-sigma-algebras-and-events]].

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$
For $n=0$, the target is the empty-product singleton and $K$ is its point
mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. More generally, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X:\Omega\to\Theta$ and $Y:\Omega\to\mathsf Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). A **posterior regular conditional distribution (posterior RCD)** is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, in the sense of [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. It is a kernel indexed by the sample point $\omega\in\Omega$. The canonical realization is $\Omega=\Theta\times\mathsf Y$ with $Q=J$ and coordinate maps $X(\theta,y)=\theta$, $Y(\theta,y)=y$.

A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

The definition asserts no existence of either conditional kernel. Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,
\alpha_k)$, with each $\alpha_j>0$. Conditional on $p$, observe a
Multinomial$(n,p)$ count vector $y\in\mathbb N_0^k$ with $\sum_jy_j=n$.
For $k\ge2$, the data space is equipped with counting measure on its finite
set of admissible counts. The evidence is
$$m(y)=\frac{n!}{\prod_jy_j!} \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \frac{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_++n)} \in(0,\infty),$$
where $\alpha_+=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and the posterior is
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+y_1,\ldots,\alpha_k+y_k)$.
For $k=1$, the parameter and count are both deterministic and the posterior
equals the prior point mass.

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$, the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ is the probability law
on the open probability simplex with density
$$\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$$
relative to $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$, with $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. Its
normalization is [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]]. For $k=1$, define
the law to be the point mass at $p_1=1$. All coordinates of the parameter
vector must be strictly positive.

Assume AC. Let $P=(P_1,\ldots,P_k)$ have the Dirichlet distribution with
positive parameters $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$. If
$I_1,\ldots,I_r$ is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ into nonempty groups,
then
$$\left(\sum_{j\in I_1}P_j,\ldots,\sum_{j\in I_r}P_j\right)\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(b_1,\ldots,b_r),\qquad b_\ell=\sum_{j\in I_\ell}a_j.$$
When $r=1$, the grouped vector is the point mass at $1$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ put $\beta_x=\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. This is a finite nonzero measure because its total mass is $\alpha(\mathsf X)+n$ by [F8]. The existence theorem [F1] therefore defines $DP(\beta_x)$ for every $x$.

Fix a finite evaluation cylinder $C=\{G:(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_s))\in H\}$ with Borel $H$, and form the finite Boolean partition generated by $A_1,\ldots,A_s$. On each cell $P_j$, the updated parameter is $\beta_x(P_j)=\alpha(P_j)+\sum_i\mathbf1_{P_j}(x_i)$. Each count is a measurable finite-valued function of $x$ by [F9], so $x\mapsto DP(\beta_x)(C)$ is measurable: it is constant on each of finitely many count-pattern preimages.

For each $G\in\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$, the map $A\mapsto G(A)$ is a probability kernel from the evaluation-measurable space $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ to $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$. Its finite product $G^{\otimes n}$ is a probability kernel by [F2]; on rectangles $D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$ it has value $\prod_iG(D_i)$, which is evaluation-measurable. The proper model in [F3] therefore gives a joint probability $J$ for $(G,X_{1:n})$ and its data marginal $M$.

Fix a finite-partition cylinder $C$ and a data rectangle $D=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$. Refine the partition defining $C$ by all $D_i$ to obtain a finite measurable partition $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ of $\mathsf X$. The data rectangle is a disjoint union of ordered cell-pattern blocks $P_{j_1}\times\cdots\times P_{j_n}$. For one such block let $y_j=\#\{i:j_i=j\}$. If $y_j>0$ for a cell with $\alpha(P_j)=0$, then $G(P_j)=0$ almost surely by [F1], so the block has prior-predictive mass zero.

The finite evaluation cylinders form a generating pi-system. The class of sets $C$ for which $x\mapsto DP(\beta_x)(C)$ is measurable contains this pi-system, contains the whole space, is closed under complements, and is closed under countable disjoint unions by pointwise limits of partial sums. Dynkin's theorem [F7] gives measurability on the full evaluation sigma-algebra. Each section is a probability measure by [F1], so $K$ is a probability kernel.

Otherwise omit cells with $\alpha(P_j)=0$ (their counts are zero). On the remaining cells the prior vector is Dirichlet with positive parameters $a_j=\alpha(P_j)$. Given that vector, the likelihood of this particular ordered pattern is $\prod_jG(P_j)^{y_j}$, a constant multiple $\prod_jy_j!/n!$ of the multinomial count likelihood. By [A2] and [F5], its posterior vector is Dirichlet$(a_1+y_1,\ldots,a_m+y_m)$ with positive finite evidence. Coarsening to the cells defining $C$ gives the same cylinder probability as $DP(\beta_x)$ by [F6]. This probability is constant over the ordered block because its cell counts are fixed.

Summing step 2.2 over the ordered blocks contained in $D$ gives $J(C\times D)=\int_DK(x,C)\,M(dx)$ for every finite-partition cylinder $C$ and data rectangle $D$. For fixed such $C$, the two sides define finite measures of $D$; their total masses agree by taking $D=\mathsf X^n$. Finite-measure uniqueness [F7] extends the identity to every $D\in\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$.

Now fix any $D\in\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. The set functions $C\mapsto J(C\times D)$ and $C\mapsto\int_DK(x,C)\,M(dx)$ are finite measures on the evaluation sigma-algebra; the second is a measure because $K$ is a probability kernel. They have common total mass $M(D)$ and agree on every finite-partition cylinder by step 3.1. These cylinders form a generating pi-system, so [F7] extends equality to every measurable $C$. By [F4], $K(x;\cdot)$ is the claimed posterior version. Null data blocks contribute zero to both sides, so the proof imposes no pointwise uniqueness there.

boundaries.reason: The theorem assumes n>=1; the prior-only case is handled separately by the predictive theorem.

boundaries.evidence: Proof steps 1.4 and 2.2 show positive counts in zero-base cells have zero prior-predictive mass.
Proof step 2.2 applies the one-cell finite Dirichlet update under the supplier convention.
Proof step 1.4 isolates prior-predictive null blocks and step 4.1 extends the identity across them.
Statement and proof step 4.1 state that kernel values on predictive-null data are version choices.
Statement assumes full AC; no additional point is selected by the proof.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

A measurable space $(E,\mathcal E)$ is **standard Borel** if there are a Polish space $P$ and a bijection $h:E\to P$ such that $A\in\mathcal E$ exactly when $h[A]$ is Borel in $P$. Thus the measurable structure is part of the datum; no particular compatible Polish topology on $E$ is selected.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$ be a standard Borel space and let $\alpha$ be a
finite nonzero measure on it. Write $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ for the set of
probability measures on $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$, equipped with the
**evaluation sigma-algebra**
$$\sigma\bigl(\{G\mapsto G(A):A\in\mathcal A\}\bigr).$$
For a probability law $P$ on this space, let $G$ be the coordinate random
probability measure $G(\omega)=\omega$. Call $P$ a **Dirichlet-process law
with base measure** $\alpha$ if, for every finite measurable partition
$(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$ of $\mathsf X$, the vector
$(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_k))$ has the Dirichlet distribution with parameters
$(\alpha(A_1),\ldots,\alpha(A_k))$ after zero-parameter cells are omitted;
each omitted zero-base cell has mass zero. If the partition has one
positive-parameter cell, its mass is one. The finite-partition specification
determines at most one law on the evaluation sigma-algebra. When such a law
exists, denote it by $DP(\alpha)$; the construction theorem on this page
proves existence.

The Dirichlet distribution here has the positive-parameter density and
one-category convention of [[def-dirichlet-distribution]]. The definition
asserts no weak topology, support statement, or density-contraction result.

space and let $\alpha$ be a finite nonzero measure on it. Then there is a
measurable random probability measure $G$ whose law on the evaluation
sigma-algebra of $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ is $DP(\alpha)$. For every finite
measurable partition $(A_1,\ldots,A_k)$, the unnormalized increments are
independent with
$\Gamma(A_j)\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(\alpha(A_j),1)$ when
$\alpha(A_j)>0$, and $\Gamma(A_j)=0$ almost surely when $\alpha(A_j)=0$.
Consequently the normalized masses have the finite-partition Dirichlet laws
in [[def-dirichlet-process]]. These laws determine the probability law on
$\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ uniquely.

and normalizes its weighted projection onto $\mathsf X$. It does not assume a

They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. Independence means mutual independence, not merely pairwise independence. No moment assumption is part of either definition. The empty family satisfies these universal conditions vacuously.

Let $X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ be random elements on a
common probability space. For each $i$, write

$$\sigma(X_i):=\{X_i^{-1}(B):B\in\Sigma_i\}\subseteq\mathcal F.$$

The family $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ is **independent** when the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(X_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent in the sense of

When $\Sigma_i$ is a Borel sigma-algebra, this agrees with the notation
$\sigma(X_i)$ from [[def-sigma-algebra-generated-by-a-function]].

Let $n\ge1$, and let
$X_i:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to(S_i,\Sigma_i)$ for $i<n$ be independent
random elements. Define

$$X=(X_0,\dots,X_{n-1}):\Omega\to\prod_{i<n}S_i.$$

Then $X$ is a random element of
$\left(\prod_{i<n}S_i,\bigotimes_{i<n}\Sigma_i\right)$, and its law is the
finite product of the marginal laws:

$$\mathbb P_X=\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathbb P_{X_i}.$$

Let $(S,\Sigma)$ and $(T_i,\Tau_i)$ for $i<n$ be measurable spaces, with
$n<\infty$, and let $K_i:S\to T_i$ be probability kernels with the same
source. There is a unique probability kernel
$$K:S\to\prod_{i<n}T_i$$
whose evaluation on every measurable rectangle is
$$K(s,\prod_{i<n}B_i)=\prod_{i<n}K_i(s,B_i).$$

mass. For $n>0$, the product sigma-algebra is the recursive finite product
sigma-algebra.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let
$$\mathsf E=((\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y),\Theta,(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta})$$
be a statistical experiment ([[def-statistical-experiment]]). Equip the parameter set with a specified measurable structure $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measurable-space]]). A **proper Bayesian model** based on this experiment consists of a prior probability measure $\Pi$ on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-probability-measure]]) and a probability kernel $K$ from $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ to $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) that represents the experiment:
$$K(\theta,B)=P_\theta(B)\qquad(\theta\in\Theta,\ B\in\mathcal Y).$$
Thus $\theta\mapsto K(\theta,B)$ is $\mathcal T$-measurable for every data event $B$, as required for a parameter-measurable model ([[def-parameter-measurable-statistical-model-as-markov-kernel]]). The family of measures in a parametric model alone does not supply this parameter sigma-algebra or measurability condition ([[def-parametric-statistical-model]]).

The word **proper** means that the prior is a probability measure. A sigma-finite improper prior is not a proper Bayesian model in this definition; fixed-data posterior normalizers for such priors are handled separately.

A **measure kernel** from $(S,\Sigma)$ to $(T,\Tau)$ is a map $K:S\times\Tau\to[0,\infty]$ such that, for every $s\in S$, $A\mapsto K(s,A)$ is a measure on $(T,\Tau)$, and for every $A\in\Tau$, $s\mapsto K(s,A)$ is $\Sigma$-measurable. Measures and measurability have the meanings in [[def-measure]] and [[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]; the evaluation functions use the Borel sigma-algebra on $[0,\infty]$.

A **probability kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)=1$ for every s. A **finite kernel** satisfies $K(s,T)<\infty$ for every s; there need not be a common bound on these masses. A **uniformly sigma-finite kernel**, in the convention of this page, comes with a specified sequence $T_n\in\Tau$ increasing to T such that $K(s,T_n)<\infty$ for every s and n. This is a common measurable exhaustion, not a bound uniform in s. A finite kernel has the constant exhaustion $T_n=T$. An arbitrary measure kernel is not assumed to have such an exhaustion.

All these requirements are pointwise in s, not merely almost everywhere for an unspecified measure on S. If T is empty, its only measure is zero, so a probability kernel into T can exist only when S is empty. If S is empty, the kernel requirements are vacuous. The zero kernel is finite. This definition selects no versions and uses no choice axiom.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and $(\mathcal X,\mathcal A)$ be measurable spaces,
let $\pi$ be a probability measure on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$, and let
$K:\Theta\times\mathcal A\to[0,1]$ be a probability kernel. For
$C\in\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal A$, write
$C_\theta=\{x\in\mathcal X:(\theta,x)\in C\}$ and set
$$J(C)=\int_\Theta K(\theta,C_\theta)\,\pi(d\theta).$$
Then $J$ is a probability measure on the product sigma-algebra, and for every
nonnegative product-measurable $h$,
$$\int_{\Theta\times\mathcal X}h(\theta,x)\,J(d\theta,dx)=\int_\Theta\left(\int_\mathcal Xh(\theta,x)\,K(\theta,dx)\right)\pi(d\theta).$$
In particular, $J(A\times B)=\int_AK(\theta,B)\,\pi(d\theta)$ for
$A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal A$.

Let a proper Bayesian model be given, and let $J$ be its joint prior-predictive probability on $(\Theta\times\mathsf Y,\mathcal T\otimes\mathcal Y)$, supplied by [[lem-prior-and-model-kernel-define-joint-law]]. More generally, let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,Q)$ be any probability space carrying parameter and data random elements $X:\Omega\to\Theta$ and $Y:\Omega\to\mathsf Y$ whose joint law is $J$ ([[def-probability-measure]], [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]], [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]]). A **posterior regular conditional distribution (posterior RCD)** is a regular conditional distribution of $X$ given $\sigma(Y)$, in the sense of [[def-regular-conditional-distribution]]. It is a kernel indexed by the sample point $\omega\in\Omega$. The canonical realization is $\Omega=\Theta\times\mathsf Y$ with $Q=J$ and coordinate maps $X(\theta,y)=\theta$, $Y(\theta,y)=y$.

A **data-indexed posterior kernel** is a probability kernel $\Pi_{\cdot}$ from $(\mathsf Y,\mathcal Y)$ to $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ ([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]]) for which $\omega\mapsto\Pi_{Y(\omega)}$ is a conditional law of $X$ given $Y$ ([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]). Equivalently, for every $A\in\mathcal T$ and $B\in\mathcal Y$,
$$Q(X\in A,\ Y\in B)=\int_B\Pi_y(A)\,Q_Y(dy),$$
where $Q_Y$ is the data marginal (equal to $J_Y$). This kernel is indexed by data values, not sample points.

The definition asserts no existence of either conditional kernel. Values of a data-indexed version on a measurable $J_Y$-null set are not fixed by the conditional-law identities; replacing them there by a fixed probability preserves those identities. A dominated-density construction is a separate route: [[thm-bayes-formula-for-dominated-kernels]] requires a proper prior, a sigma-finite data measure, and a specified jointly measurable sampling density, and fills fibres whose marginal density is zero or infinite with the prior. It does not require the data space to be standard Borel.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,
\alpha_k)$, with each $\alpha_j>0$. Conditional on $p$, observe a
Multinomial$(n,p)$ count vector $y\in\mathbb N_0^k$ with $\sum_jy_j=n$.
For $k\ge2$, the data space is equipped with counting measure on its finite
set of admissible counts. The evidence is
$$m(y)=\frac{n!}{\prod_jy_j!} \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \frac{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_++n)} \in(0,\infty),$$
where $\alpha_+=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and the posterior is
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+y_1,\ldots,\alpha_k+y_k)$.
For $k=1$, the parameter and count are both deterministic and the posterior
equals the prior point mass.

Assume Countable Choice. For $k\ge2$ and $\alpha_j>0$, the **Dirichlet distribution**
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,\alpha_k)$ is the probability law
on the open probability simplex with density
$$\frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \prod_jp_j^{\alpha_j-1}$$
relative to $dp_1\cdots dp_{k-1}$, with $p_k=1-\sum_{j<k}p_j$. Its
normalization is [[thm-dirichlet-density-normalization]]. For $k=1$, define
the law to be the point mass at $p_1=1$. All coordinates of the parameter
vector must be strictly positive.

Assume AC. Let $P=(P_1,\ldots,P_k)$ have the Dirichlet distribution with
positive parameters $(a_1,\ldots,a_k)$. If
$I_1,\ldots,I_r$ is a partition of $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ into nonempty groups,
then
$$\left(\sum_{j\in I_1}P_j,\ldots,\sum_{j\in I_r}P_j\right)\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(b_1,\ldots,b_r),\qquad b_\ell=\sum_{j\in I_\ell}a_j.$$
When $r=1$, the grouped vector is the point mass at $1$.

Let $X$ be a set. A **pi-system on $X$** is a nonempty family
$\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal P(X)$ closed under binary intersections: if
$A,B\in\mathcal P$, then $A\cap B\in\mathcal P$.

The nonempty-family requirement is the convention used here. It does not require
$X\in\mathcal P$ and it does not add an empty-intersection axiom.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$ and let $\mathcal A=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. If finite measures $\mu$ and $
u$ on $(X,\mathcal A)$ agree on $\mathcal P$ and satisfy $\mu(X)=
u(X)$, then $\mu=
u$ on $\mathcal A$.

The total-mass equality is separate because this library's pi-system convention does not require $X\in\mathcal P$.

Let $\mathcal P$ be a pi-system on $X$. Then
$\lambda_X(\mathcal P)=\sigma_X(\mathcal P)$. Consequently, if $\mathcal D$ is
any lambda-system on $X$ with $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal D$, then
$\sigma_X(\mathcal P)\subseteq\mathcal D$.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space ([[def-measure-space]]).

- The measure $\mu$ is **finite** if $\mu(X)<+\infty$.
- It is **sigma-finite** if there is a sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in $\mathcal A$ such that $X=\bigcup_nE_n$ and $\mu(E_n)<+\infty$ for every $n$.
- It is **semifinite** if, whenever $E\in\mathcal A$ and $\mu(E)>0$, there is $F\in\mathcal A$ with $F\subseteq E$ and $0<\mu(F)<+\infty$.

The last condition is automatic when $0<\mu(E)<+\infty$, by taking $F=E$; its substantive case is $\mu(E)=+\infty$.

Let $(X,\mathcal{A})$ and $(Y,\mathcal{B})$ be measurable spaces
([[def-measurable-space]]). A function $f : X \to Y$ is **measurable** when

$$f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \qquad \text{for every } B \in \mathcal{B}.$$

Equivalently, the family

$$\mathcal{C}_f := \{\, B \subseteq Y : f^{-1}(B) \in \mathcal{A} \,\}$$

is a sigma-algebra on $Y$ containing $\mathcal{B}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B)$ be measurable spaces. Their
**product sigma-algebra** is

$$\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B := \sigma(\{A \times B : A \in \mathcal A,\ B \in \mathcal B\}),$$

the sigma-algebra on $X \times Y$ generated by the measurable rectangles of
[[def-measurable-rectangle]].

For the empty family, put $\prod_{i<0}X_i:=\{()\}$ and define its **empty
product sigma-algebra** by

$$\bigotimes_{i<0}\mathcal A_i:=\{\varnothing,\{()\}\}.$$

For a nonempty finite family of measurable spaces $(X_i,\mathcal A_i)$ with
$i<n$, the **finite product sigma-algebra** is defined recursively by

$$\bigotimes_{i<1}\mathcal A_i := \mathcal A_0,\qquad \bigotimes_{i<n+1}\mathcal A_i := \left(\bigotimes_{i<n}\mathcal A_i\right)\otimes\mathcal A_n.$$

This recursive definition is the finite base case used later when the library
passes to countable product constructions.

derivations.claim: For $x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$ put $\beta_x=\alpha+\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. This is a finite nonzero measure because its total mass is $\alpha(\mathsf X)+n$ by [F8]. The existence theorem [F1] therefore defines $DP(\beta_x)$ for every $x$.

Fix a finite evaluation cylinder $C=\{G:(G(A_1),\ldots,G(A_s))\in H\}$ with Borel $H$, and form the finite Boolean partition generated by $A_1,\ldots,A_s$. On each cell $P_j$, the updated parameter is $\beta_x(P_j)=\alpha(P_j)+\sum_i\mathbf1_{P_j}(x_i)$. Each count is a measurable finite-valued function of $x$ by [F9], so $x\mapsto DP(\beta_x)(C)$ is measurable: it is constant on each of finitely many count-pattern preimages.

For each $G\in\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$, the map $A\mapsto G(A)$ is a probability kernel from the evaluation-measurable space $\mathcal P(\mathsf X)$ to $(\mathsf X,\mathcal A)$. Its finite product $G^{\otimes n}$ is a probability kernel by [F2]; on rectangles $D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$ it has value $\prod_iG(D_i)$, which is evaluation-measurable. The proper model in [F3] therefore gives a joint probability $J$ for $(G,X_{1:n})$ and its data marginal $M$.

Fix a finite-partition cylinder $C$ and a data rectangle $D=D_1\times\cdots\times D_n$. Refine the partition defining $C$ by all $D_i$ to obtain a finite measurable partition $P_1,\ldots,P_m$ of $\mathsf X$. The data rectangle is a disjoint union of ordered cell-pattern blocks $P_{j_1}\times\cdots\times P_{j_n}$. For one such block let $y_j=\#\{i:j_i=j\}$. If $y_j>0$ for a cell with $\alpha(P_j)=0$, then $G(P_j)=0$ almost surely by [F1], so the block has prior-predictive mass zero.

The finite evaluation cylinders form a generating pi-system. The class of sets $C$ for which $x\mapsto DP(\beta_x)(C)$ is measurable contains this pi-system, contains the whole space, is closed under complements, and is closed under countable disjoint unions by pointwise limits of partial sums. Dynkin's theorem [F7] gives measurability on the full evaluation sigma-algebra. Each section is a probability measure by [F1], so $K$ is a probability kernel.

Otherwise omit cells with $\alpha(P_j)=0$ (their counts are zero). On the remaining cells the prior vector is Dirichlet with positive parameters $a_j=\alpha(P_j)$. Given that vector, the likelihood of this particular ordered pattern is $\prod_jG(P_j)^{y_j}$, a constant multiple $\prod_jy_j!/n!$ of the multinomial count likelihood. By [A2] and [F5], its posterior vector is Dirichlet$(a_1+y_1,\ldots,a_m+y_m)$ with positive finite evidence. Coarsening to the cells defining $C$ gives the same cylinder probability as $DP(\beta_x)$ by [F6]. This probability is constant over the ordered block because its cell counts are fixed.

Summing step 2.2 over the ordered blocks contained in $D$ gives $J(C\times D)=\int_DK(x,C)\,M(dx)$ for every finite-partition cylinder $C$ and data rectangle $D$. For fixed such $C$, the two sides define finite measures of $D$; their total masses agree by taking $D=\mathsf X^n$. Finite-measure uniqueness [F7] extends the identity to every $D\in\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$.

Now fix any $D\in\mathcal A^{\otimes n}$. The set functions $C\mapsto J(C\times D)$ and $C\mapsto\int_DK(x,C)\,M(dx)$ are finite measures on the evaluation sigma-algebra; the second is a measure because $K$ is a probability kernel. They have common total mass $M(D)$ and agree on every finite-partition cylinder by step 3.1. These cylinders form a generating pi-system, so [F7] extends equality to every measurable $C$. By [F4], $K(x;\cdot)$ is the claimed posterior version. Null data blocks contribute zero to both sides, so the proof imposes no pointwise uniqueness there.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the S-regular wavelet basis in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with $2^l$ coefficients at each level $l\ge0$. For $\alpha>0$, put $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ and let the prior on $f=\sum_{l,k}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ have IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with density $\varphi$. Assume countable choice for the $L^2$ prior construction supplied by [[lem-wavelet-product-prior-is-l2-valued]], and take the full posterior kernel as the supplied model input of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Let $f_0\in L^2([0,1])$, write $\theta_{0,lk}=\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ and $r_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}/\sigma_l$, and suppose

$$\sup_{l,k}|r_{lk}|\le M<\tau,$$

where $\varphi$ is a probability density satisfying $\varphi(u)\le C_\varphi$ for every $u$, $\varphi(u)\ge c_\varphi>0$ for $|u|<\tau$, $\int u^2\varphi(u)\,du<\infty$, and $\varphi$ is continuous at each $r_{lk}$. The observation model is

$$dX^{(n)}(t)=f_0(t)\,dt+n^{-1/2}dW(t),\qquad 0\le t\le1,$$

with standard white noise $W$; in the stated basis this is the sequence experiment $X_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}+n^{-1/2}Z_{lk}$ with independent standard normal coordinates. Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X)$ be the product-coordinate posterior of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Let $N$ be the law of the canonical white noise in $H(\delta)$ and define

$$\widetilde\Pi_n:=\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X)\circ[f\mapsto\sqrt n(f-X)]^{-1},\qquad \beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\mu,\nu):=\sup_{\substack{\|g\|_\infty\le1\\ \operatorname{Lip}_{H(\delta)}(g)\le1}}\left|\int g\,d\mu-\int g\,d\nu\right|.$$

For every $\delta>1/2$,

$$\beta_{BL,H(\delta)}(\widetilde\Pi_n,N)\longrightarrow0$$

in probability under the true white-noise law $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$. This is a bounded-Lipschitz weak BvM conclusion; it asserts neither total-variation convergence on all Borel subsets nor an $L^2$-valued Gaussian limit.

Let $H(\delta)$ be the coefficient Hilbert space of [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with weights $w_l=a_l^{-1}(\log a_l)^{-2\delta}$. If $g\in H^s_2$ for some $s>1/2$, then the pairing $L_g(x)=\sum_{l,k}x_{lk}g_{lk}$, where $g_{lk}=\langle g,\psi_{lk}\rangle$, converges absolutely for every $x\in H(\delta)$ and is continuous, with
$$|L_g(x)|\le C_{s,\delta}\|g\|_{H^s_2}\|x\|_{H(\delta)}.$$
On $L^2([0,1])$ this extension agrees with the usual inner product $\langle f,g\rangle_{L^2}$.

Assume countable choice. Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the wavelet or trigonometric basis from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. Let $Z_{lk}$ be mutually independent real random variables with density $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Define the formal white-noise coefficient sequence $W=(Z_{lk})$. For every $\delta>1/2$, this sequence is almost surely an element of $H(\delta)$ and is a Borel Gaussian random element there. Its law $N$ is a Borel probability on $H(\delta)$. For an infinite-dimensional basis, white noise is not an $L^2([0,1])$-valued random element. Here Gaussian means that each continuous real linear functional has a centered law $N(0,v)$ in the density convention of [[lem-density-normal-laws-and-square-summable-gaussian-series]]; in particular, for $L(c)=\sum_jd_jc_j$ its variance is $\sum_jd_j^2$ whenever this pairing is continuous on $H(\delta)$.

Let $Q_n(y,\cdot)$ be data-indexed probability kernels on $\mathbb R$, let $Q$ be a fixed law with continuous CDF $F$, and suppose $\beta_{BL}(Q_n(y,\cdot),Q)\to0$ in probability. Fix $0<u<1$ and let $q=q_u(Q):=\inf\{r\in\mathbb Q:Q((-∞,r])\ge u\}$, using the canonical rational embedding. Assume $F$ is strictly increasing on some open interval containing $q$. Define $q_u(Q_n(y,\cdot))$ by the same convention. Then $q_u(Q_n)\to q$ in probability. The local strict-increase hypothesis permits CDFs, such as norms of nonnegative random elements, that are constant on part of $\mathbb R$.

Let $\Pi_y$ be a posterior probability kernel on $\mathbb R$ and let $0<\alpha<1$. Define $C_\alpha(y)=[q_{\alpha/2}(y),q_{1-\alpha/2}(y)]$ using the quantiles from [[lem-measurable-posterior-quantile-and-cdf-bracketing]]. Then $C_\alpha$ is graph-measurable and $\Pi_y(C_\alpha(y))\ge1-\alpha$ for every $y$. Thus equal-tailed posterior quantile intervals are one kind of credible set.

Assume countable choice. Put $g(x)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}$. Then $\gamma(E)=\int_Eg(x)\,dx$ is a Borel probability on $\mathbb R$. In this item and its applications, write $N(m,v)$ for its pushforward under $x\mapsto m+\sqrt v\,x$, where $v\ge0$; thus $N(m,0)=\delta_m$. This density convention requires no full axiom of choice. For $v>0$ the law has density
$$g_{m,v}(x)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp\{- (x-m)^2/(2v)\},$$
and its CDF is continuous and strictly increasing. Its mean and variance are $m$ and $v$.

If $Z_j$ are mutually independent with density $g$ and $\sum_{j\ge1}c_j^2=v<\infty$, and the finite sums $S_m=\sum_{j\le m}c_jZ_j$ converge in probability to a supplied real random variable $S$, then $S$ has law $N(0,v)$. In particular, this applies whenever the sums converge almost surely or in $L^2$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix $\delta>1/2$. For every bounded $1$-Lipschitz function $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the composition $h\circ L_g$ is bounded by $1$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $\|L_g\|_{H(\delta)^*}$. Rescaling by $c_g=\max(1,\|L_g\|_{H(\delta)^*})$ makes it an admissible bounded-Lipschitz test on $H(\delta)$. Hence the scalar pushforward distance is at most $c_g$ times the distance in [F1]. The pushforward of $N$ is $N(0,\sigma_g^2)$ by [F3], proving the asserted scalar BvM limit.

Translate the posterior law of $L_g(f)$ by $L_g(X^{(n)})$ and scale by $\sqrt n$. By [F4] and the continuous strictly increasing normal CDF from [F6], the two quantiles of this scaled law converge in probability to $\sigma_g z_{\alpha/2}$ and $\sigma_g z_{1-\alpha/2}$, where $z_u$ is the $u$-quantile of $N(0,1)$. Since the affine map is increasing, these are exactly the scaled endpoints of $C_{n,\alpha}-L_g(X^{(n)})$. The interval is credible by [F5].

Under the true white-noise law, $\sqrt n\{L_g(X^{(n)})-L_g(f_0)\}=L_g(W)$ has exactly the centered normal law $N(0,\sigma_g^2)$ by [F3]. On the event that both random scaled endpoints in step 2.1 lie within $\varepsilon$ of their limits, the event $L_g(f_0)\in C_{n,\alpha}$ is bounded between the corresponding deterministic normal-interval events with endpoints enlarged or contracted by $\varepsilon$. This sandwich uses no independence between the endpoints and the observation. The endpoint event has probability tending to one, and [F6] makes the normal mass of shrinking neighborhoods of the two endpoints tend to zero.

Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in the sandwich of step 3.1 gives limiting coverage $\Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2})-\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$ by the definition of the normal quantiles and CDF in [F6].

before_contract.claim:
Use the product-prior white-noise model and supplied posterior kernel of [[thm-weak-nonparametric-bernstein-von-mises-for-product-priors]], including its wavelet-basis, coefficient-density, truth, and countable-choice hypotheses. Let $g\in H^s_2$ for some $s>1/2$, with $g\ne0$, and put $\sigma_g=\|g\|_2$. Let $Q_n$ be the posterior law of $L_g(f)$ and let
$$C_{n,\alpha}=\left[q_{\alpha/2}(Q_n),q_{1-\alpha/2}(Q_n)\right],\qquad 0<\alpha<1.$$
Then
$$\beta_{BL,\mathbb R}\!\left(Q_n\circ[u\mapsto\sqrt n(u-L_g(X^{(n)}))]^{-1},N(0,\sigma_g^2)\right)\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_{f_0}^{(n)}$-probability. The interval $C_{n,\alpha}$ is posterior credible at level $1-\alpha$, and its frequentist coverage satisfies
$$P_{f_0}^{(n)}\{L_g(f_0)\in C_{n,\alpha}\}\longrightarrow1-\alpha.$$

$$g_{m,v}(x)=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\exp\{- (x-m)^2/(2v)\},$$

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: Fix $\delta>1/2$. For every bounded $1$-Lipschitz function $h:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$, the composition $h\circ L_g$ is bounded by $1$ and has Lipschitz constant at most $\|L_g\|_{H(\delta)^*}$. Rescaling by $c_g=\max(1,\|L_g\|_{H(\delta)^*})$ makes it an admissible bounded-Lipschitz test on $H(\delta)$. Hence the scalar pushforward distance is at most $c_g$ times the distance in [F1]. The pushforward of $N$ is $N(0,\sigma_g^2)$ by [F3], proving the asserted scalar BvM limit.

Translate the posterior law of $L_g(f)$ by $L_g(X^{(n)})$ and scale by $\sqrt n$. By [F4] and the continuous strictly increasing normal CDF from [F6], the two quantiles of this scaled law converge in probability to $\sigma_g z_{\alpha/2}$ and $\sigma_g z_{1-\alpha/2}$, where $z_u$ is the $u$-quantile of $N(0,1)$. Since the affine map is increasing, these are exactly the scaled endpoints of $C_{n,\alpha}-L_g(X^{(n)})$. The interval is credible by [F5].

Under the true white-noise law, $\sqrt n\{L_g(X^{(n)})-L_g(f_0)\}=L_g(W)$ has exactly the centered normal law $N(0,\sigma_g^2)$ by [F3]. On the event that both random scaled endpoints in step 2.1 lie within $\varepsilon$ of their limits, the event $L_g(f_0)\in C_{n,\alpha}$ is bounded between the corresponding deterministic normal-interval events with endpoints enlarged or contracted by $\varepsilon$. This sandwich uses no independence between the endpoints and the observation. The endpoint event has probability tending to one, and [F6] makes the normal mass of shrinking neighborhoods of the two endpoints tend to zero.

Letting $n\to\infty$ and then $\varepsilon\downarrow0$ in the sandwich of step 3.1 gives limiting coverage $\Phi(z_{1-\alpha/2})-\Phi(z_{\alpha/2})=1-\alpha$ by the definition of the normal quantiles and CDF in [F6].

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

Let $P_0$ have a density $f_0$ on $[0,1]$ bounded above and bounded away from zero, and put $F_0(t)=\int_0^t f_0(x)dx$. Use the wavelet basis and $M_0(w)$ of [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], and assume the wavelet conditions and summability condition $\sum_lw_l2^{-l/2}<\infty$ of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Let $T_n$ be a measurable $L^2$-valued center, let $\Pi_n$ be a posterior kernel supported on $L^2$ densities, and define $Q_n$ to be the conditional law on $M_0(w)$ of $\sqrt n(f-T_n)$ under $f\sim\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$.

Assume under $P_0^n$ that (i) $Q_n$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance in probability to the centered Gaussian bridge coefficient law $G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$, whose finite coefficient covariances are $P_0[(h-P_0h)(g-P_0g)]$, and (ii) $\sqrt n(T_n-f_0)\Rightarrow G_{P_0}$ in $M_0(w)$. For $u=1-\alpha$, let $q_M$ and $q_C$ be the lower $u$-quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|JG_{P_0}\|_\infty$. Assume both CDFs are continuous on $\mathbb R$ and strictly increasing on open neighborhoods of their respective quantiles, and that $q_M,q_C>0$. These local quantile conditions allow the CDFs to be constant on the negative half-line. In the projected empirical-center case $T_n=P_n(L_n)$, [[thm-projected-empirical-process-clt-in-m0w]] supplies premise (ii) under its stated smoothness and cutoff conditions. For the source-specific type-S and type-H priors, the posterior BvM premise (i) is established in [[thm-type-s-density-weak-bvm-on-m0w]] and [[thm-type-h-histogram-posterior-weak-bvm-in-m0w]], respectively.

For a posterior draw $f$, write $F_f=Jf$ and $F_{T_n}=JT_n$, where $J$ is the primitive map of [[lem-multiscale-primitive-map-to-continuous-cdfs]]. Then the posterior law of $\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})$ converges in bounded-Lipschitz distance on $C([0,1])$ to the $P_0$-Brownian bridge $B_{P_0}(t)$, with covariance $F_0(s\wedge t)-F_0(s)F_0(t)$.

For $0<\alpha<1$, let $R_n^M$ and $R_n^C$ be the posterior lower $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|\sqrt n(f-T_n)\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|\sqrt n(F_f-F_{T_n})\|_\infty$, respectively. The corresponding posterior balls
$$C_n^M=\{f:\|f-T_n\|_{M(w)}\le R_n^M/\sqrt n\},\qquad C_n^C=\{F:\|F-F_{T_n}\|_\infty\le R_n^C/\sqrt n\}$$
are measurable credible sets of posterior mass at least $1-\alpha$. Their frequentist coverage tends to $1-\alpha$, and the scaled radii converge to the respective $1-\alpha$ quantiles of $\|G_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|B_{P_0}\|_\infty$.

derivations.claim: Since $\|f_0\|_{C^\gamma_\psi}<\infty$ and $u_n\to\infty$, [L1] implies the truth belongs to the coefficient smoothness ball for all sufficiently large $n$. For those $n$, $\{f_0\in\overline C_n\}=\{f_0\in C_n^M\}$, so the asserted coverage follows from [F2].

Let $f,g\in\overline C_n$. For $l\le j_n$, [F1] gives $\max_k|f_{lk}-g_{lk}|\le2R_n^Mw_l/\sqrt n$. For $l>j_n$, [L1] and membership in the coefficient smoothness ball give $\max_k|f_{lk}-g_{lk}|\le2u_n2^{-l(\gamma+1/2)}$. At each point, only a uniformly bounded number of level-$l$ wavelets are nonzero, each bounded by $C2^{l/2}$. Therefore the low-frequency contribution to $\|f-g\|_\infty$ is at most $C R_n^M n^{-1/2}\sum_{l\le j_n}2^{l/2}w_l$, and the high-frequency contribution is at most $C u_n\sum_{l>j_n}2^{-l\gamma}$. These series also give uniformly convergent representatives because $\gamma>0$.

Since $w_l$ is nondecreasing, $\sum_{l\le j_n}2^{l/2}w_l\le C2^{j_n/2}w_{j_n}$ by summing a geometric series. Also $\sum_{l>j_n}2^{-l\gamma}\le C_\gamma2^{-j_n\gamma}$. The first bound in step 1.2 is thus at most $C R_n^M w_{j_n}2^{j_n/2}/\sqrt n=C R_n^M u_n\sqrt{j_n}2^{j_n/2}/\sqrt n$.

The relation $2^{j_n}\asymp(n/\log n)^{1/(2\gamma+1)}$ implies both $2^{-j_n\gamma}\asymp(n/\log n)^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+1)}$ and $\sqrt{j_n}2^{j_n/2}/\sqrt n\le C_\gamma(n/\log n)^{-\gamma/(2\gamma+1)}$. Combining the low- and high-frequency bounds in steps 1.2 and 2.1 and using $R_n^M=O_P(1)$ from [F2] yields the stated diameter bound.

Let $(\psi_{lk})$ be the S-regular wavelet basis in [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]], with $2^l$ coefficients at each level $l\ge0$. For $\alpha>0$, put $\sigma_l=2^{-l(\alpha+1/2)}$ and let the prior on $f=\sum_{l,k}\sigma_l\xi_{lk}\psi_{lk}$ have IID coefficients $\xi_{lk}$ with density $\varphi$. Assume countable choice for the $L^2$ prior construction supplied by [[lem-wavelet-product-prior-is-l2-valued]], and take the full posterior kernel as the supplied model input of [[lem-product-prior-coordinate-posterior-law]]. Let $f_0\in L^2([0,1])$, write $\theta_{0,lk}=\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle$ and $r_{lk}=\theta_{0,lk}/\sigma_l$, and suppose

$$\sup_{l,k}|r_{lk}|\le M<\tau,$$

where $\varphi$ is a probability density satisfying $\varphi(u)\le C_\varphi$ for every $u$, $\varphi(u)\ge c_\varphi>0$ for $|u|<\tau$, $\int u^2\varphi(u)\,du<\infty$, and $\varphi$ is continuous at each $r_{lk}$. The observation model is

$$dX^{(n)}(t)=f_0(t)\,dt+n^{-1/2}dW(t),\qquad 0\le t\le1,$$

citations.quote:
Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. The same coefficient-space definition applies to the Haar system used for type-H histograms: detail levels $l\ge0$ have $2^l$ coefficients, and the single scaling coefficient is an additional finite coarsest coordinate, included in the norm with weight $1$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

For every weight sequence in [[def-multiscale-coefficient-space-m0w]], $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space. If $P_J$ retains exactly the coefficients at levels $l\le J$, then $\|P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\le\|x\|_{M(w)}$ and $\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}\to0$ for each $x\in M_0(w)$. Every square-summable coefficient sequence belongs to $M_0(w)$.

Let $Q_n$ be data-indexed probability measures on $M_0(w)$ and let $G$ be a fixed probability measure on this space. For the projections $P_J$ of [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]], suppose that for every fixed $J$,
$$\beta_{BL}(Q_n\circ P_J^{-1},G\circ P_J^{-1})\to0$$
in probability, and that for every $\varepsilon,\eta>0$,
$$\lim_{J\to\infty}\limsup_{n\to\infty}P\left\{Q_n(\|x-P_Jx\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon)>\eta\right\}=0.$$
Then $\beta_{BL}(Q_n,G)\to0$ in probability.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be a finite integer. Let $(X_k)_{k\ge1}$ be iid $\mathbb R^d$-valued random vectors with $\mathbb E\|X_1\|^2<\infty$, mean m and covariance Sigma. Then $$n^{-1/2}\sum_{k=1}^n(X_k-m)\Rightarrow N_d(0,\Sigma).$$ The covariance may be singular.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(S,d)$ be a Polish space, and let $\mu_n,\mu$ be Borel probability measures on $S$. Define

$$\beta_{BL}(\nu,\rho):=\sup\left\{\left|\int g\,d\nu-\int g\,d\rho\right|:g:S\to\mathbb R,\ \|g\|_\infty\le1,\ \operatorname{Lip}_d(g)\le1\right\},$$

where $\operatorname{Lip}_d(g):=\sup_{x\ne y}|g(x)-g(y)|/d(x,y)$, with value $0$ when $S$ has at most one point. Then

$$\mu_n\Rightarrow\mu\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\beta_{BL}(\mu_n,\mu)\longrightarrow0,$$

where $\Rightarrow$ is weak convergence of Borel probabilities ([[def-weak-convergence-of-borel-probability-measures]]). The implication from bounded-Lipschitz convergence to weak convergence is choice-free; the reverse implication below uses AC through Prokhorov's theorem.

Let $\mu$ be a measure and let $(E_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}$ be measurable. Then

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb N}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\mu(E_k).$$

For every $m\in\mathbb N$ one also has

$$\mu\left(\bigcup_{k<m}E_k\right)\le\sum_{k<m}\mu(E_k),$$

including $m=0$, where both sides are $0$.

If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is a nonnegative random variable on a probability
space and $a>0$, then
$$\mathbb P(X\ge a)\le\frac{\mathbb E[X]}{a}.$$

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

Let $(X_i)_{i\in I}$ be random elements with the same measurable target $(E,\mathcal E)$. They are **identically distributed** if $\mathbb P(X_i\in B)=\mathbb P(X_j\in B)$ for all $i,j\in I$ and $B\in\mathcal E$, that is, their laws in [[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]] agree. They are **independent and identically distributed (IID)** if, in addition, the whole family is independent in [[def-independent-random-elements]]. derivations.claim: $P_n(L_n)$ has finitely many nonzero coefficients, so it is in $M_0(w)$. The coefficient sequence of $f_0$ is square-summable by Parseval, so [F2] places it in $M_0(w)$. Thus $U_n=\sqrt n\{P_n(L_n)-f_0\}$ is a well-defined $M_0(w)$-valued random element.

Fix $J$. For all sufficiently large $n$, $L_n\ge J$, so the coordinates of $P_JU_n$ are $n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^n(\psi_{lk}(X_i)-P_0\psi_{lk})$ for the finitely many indices through level $J$. The vector summand is bounded by [A2], has finite second moment, and is IID by [F9]; its covariance is the displayed covariance of $G_{P_0}$. By [F4] these finite-dimensional vectors converge weakly to the corresponding Gaussian projection. The projection space is finite-dimensional Euclidean with an equivalent weighted maximum norm, so [F5] gives convergence in bounded-Lipschitz distance for every fixed $J$.

Let $Y_i=\psi_{lk}(X_i)-P_0\psi_{lk}$. Then $\mathbb EY_i=0$, $\mathbb EY_i^2\le P_0\psi_{lk}^2\le B$, and $|Y_i|\le2C_0 2^{l/2}=:b_l$ by [A2]. For $m\ge2$, $\mathbb E|Y_i|^m\le b_l^{m-2}\mathbb EY_i^2$. Since $m!\ge2\,3^{m-2}$, expansion of the exponential gives, for $0<\lambda b_l<3\sqrt n$, $\mathbb E\exp(\lambda n^{-1/2}\sum_{i=1}^nY_i)\le\exp(\lambda^2B/[2(1-\lambda b_l/(3\sqrt n))])$. Applying [F7] to this exponential and optimizing at $\lambda=t/(B+b_lt/(3\sqrt n))$ yields $P_0^n\{|\sqrt n(P_n-P_0)\psi_{lk}|>t\}\le2\exp(-t^2/[2(B+b_lt/(3\sqrt n))])$. Applying the same argument to $-Y_i$ supplies the lower-tail bound.

Above the cutoff, $U_n$ has only the deterministic bias coefficients $-\sqrt n\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle$. By [A3] and monotonicity of $w_l$, $\sup_{l>L_n,k}\sqrt n|\langle f_0,\psi_{lk}\rangle|/w_l\le C_f\sqrt n\,2^{-L_n(\gamma+1/2)}/w_{L_n}$. For the first cutoff regime the numerator is bounded, while $w_{L_n}\to\infty$. For the second, the numerator is $O(\sqrt{\log n})$ and $\sqrt{L_n}\asymp\sqrt{\log n}$; admissibility $w_{L_n}/\sqrt{L_n}\to\infty$ again makes the ratio vanish.

Fix $\varepsilon>0$. By [F6] and step 1.3, $P_0^n\{\max_{J<l\le L_n,k}|\sqrt n(P_n-P_0)\psi_{lk}|/w_l>\varepsilon\}\le\sum_{J<l\le L_n}2^{l+1}\exp(-\varepsilon^2w_l^2/[2(B+(2C_0\varepsilon/3)2^{l/2}w_l/\sqrt n)])$. For levels with $2^{l/2}w_l/\sqrt n\le1$, the denominator is bounded by a constant depending only on $B,C_0,\varepsilon$. Their sum is bounded by $\sum_{l>J}2^{l+1}e^{-c_\varepsilon w_l^2}$, which tends to zero as $J\to\infty$: admissibility gives $w_l^2/l\to\infty$, so the summand is eventually bounded by $2^{-l}$.

For the fixed Gaussian law $G_{P_0}$, [F2] gives $\|G_{P_0}-P_JG_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}\to0$ pointwise. Hence the events $\{\|G_{P_0}-P_JG_{P_0}\|_{M(w)}>\varepsilon\}$ decrease to the empty set; [F8] makes their probabilities tend to zero. Steps 4.1 and 1.4 give the matching posterior-tail condition for the laws of $U_n$.

For each fixed $J$, step 1.2 gives convergence of the projected laws in bounded-Lipschitz distance; steps 4.1 and 1.4 give vanishing tails for $U_n$, and step 5.1 gives vanishing tails for $G_{P_0}$. Finite projections always retain that scaling coordinate; this finite convention does not alter any tail assertion. Let $w=(w_l)$ be nondecreasing with $w_l\ge1$. Define
$$M(w)=\left\{x=(x_{lk}):\|x\|_{M(w)}:=\sup_l\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}<\infty\right\}$$
and its closed little-o subspace
$$M_0(w)=\left\{x\in M(w):\frac{\max_{k\in K_l}|x_{lk}|}{w_l}\longrightarrow0\text{ as }l\to\infty\right\},$$
with the same norm. Call $w$ admissible when $w_l/\sqrt l\to\infty$. The finite coarsest level is included in the norm and does not affect this limit. Elements are coefficient sequences; in particular, they need not be $L^2$ functions. [[lem-m0w-separable-and-projection-tails]] proves that $M_0(w)$ is a separable Banach space, that $L^2$ coefficient sequences embed in it, and that finite-level projections converge in its norm.

Assume AC. Use the type-H prior of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], retaining its original conditions: $1/2<\alpha\le1$, $f_0\in C^\alpha([0,1])$, $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, either original cutoff $L_n=j_n$ or $L_n=\ell_n$, and $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$. $$\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}}),\qquad l\ge0,\quad 0\le k<2^l,$$
and a histogram at resolution $L_n$ has only the scaling coordinate and levels $l<L_n$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID from $f_0$, let $N_{nk}=\sum_i\mathbf1_{I_{L_n,k}}(X_i)$, and define the empirical histogram
$$h_n(x)=m_n N_{nk}/n\quad\text{on }I_{L_n,k}.$$
Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$ be the density posterior for the stated histogram prior. For every nondecreasing $w_l\ge1$ with $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, its conditional law $Q_n$ of $\sqrt n(f-h_n)$ satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}(Q_n,\mathcal L(G_{P_0}))\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where the Borel centered Gaussian bridge $G_{P_0}$ is supplied by [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]] and has covariance $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Assume AC. Let $\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m>0$, $B=\sum_j\beta_j$, and let $Z_j$ be independent $\operatorname{Gamma}(\beta_j,1)$ variables. Put $S=\sum_j Z_j$. Then $\omega=(Z_j/S)_j$ is $\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\beta_1,\ldots,\beta_m)$, and $S$ is $\operatorname{Gamma}(B,1)$, with mean $B$ and variance $B$. Each $Z_j$ has mean $\beta_j$, variance $\beta_j$, and moment-generating function $\mathbb E e^{uZ_j}=(1-u)^{-\beta_j}$ for every real $u<1$. For real $q_j$ satisfying $|q_j|\le b$, put $T(q)=\sum_jq_j(Z_j-\beta_j)$ and $V=\sum_j\beta_jq_j^2$. If $V>0$, then for $x>0$,
$$\Pr\{|T(q)|>x\}\le2\exp\left\{-\frac{x^2}{2(V+bx)}\right\}.$$
If $V=0$, $T(q)=0$ almost surely. Sums of disjoint groups of the $Z_j$ are independent Gamma variables with their respective summed shapes.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $p\sim\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1,\ldots,
\alpha_k)$, with each $\alpha_j>0$. Conditional on $p$, observe a
Multinomial$(n,p)$ count vector $y\in\mathbb N_0^k$ with $\sum_jy_j=n$.
For $k\ge2$, the data space is equipped with counting measure on its finite
set of admissible counts. The evidence is
$$m(y)=\frac{n!}{\prod_jy_j!} \frac{\Gamma(\alpha_+)}{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j)} \frac{\prod_j\Gamma(\alpha_j+y_j)}{\Gamma(\alpha_++n)} \in(0,\infty),$$
where $\alpha_+=\sum_j\alpha_j$, and the posterior is
$\operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha_1+y_1,\ldots,\alpha_k+y_k)$.
For $k=1$, the parameter and count are both deterministic and the posterior
equals the prior point mass.

$$Q(\theta,B)=\int_B\ell(\theta,y)\,\nu(dy)\quad\text{for every }\theta\in E,\ B\in\mathcal T.$$

Define $m(y)=\int_E\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)$. Under the joint law with density $\ell$ relative to $\pi\times\nu$, a conditional law of the parameter given the observation is
$$K(y,A)=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{\int_A\ell(\theta,y)\,\pi(d\theta)}{m(y)},&0<m(y)<\infty,\\ \pi(A),&m(y)=0\text{ or }m(y)=\infty.\end{cases}$$

The observation marginal is $m\,d\nu$, and the filled fibres have marginal mass zero. This is a choice-free assertion about the explicit kernel and event identities.

Use the wavelet coefficient levels $(l,k)$ and multiplicities $|K_l|=2^l$ from [[def-negative-sobolev-space-for-white-noise]]. derivations.claim: Abbreviate $m=m_n$, $a_k=a_{k,L_n}$, $A=\sum_ka_k$, $\beta_k=N_{nk}+a_k$, and $B=n+A$. The original cutoff conditions and $\alpha>1/2$ give $m/\sqrt n\to0$ and $m\log n/n\to0$, and $A\le c_2m$. On the positive simplex, the full-data histogram likelihood is $m^n\prod_k\omega_k^{N_{nk}}$. Multiplication by the prior density yields a constant times $\prod_k\omega_k^{\beta_k-1}$, with every shape positive; its normalization is finite positive by [F2]. Therefore the full-data posterior is Dirichlet$(\beta_k)_k$, regardless of whether the actual sampling truth is itself a histogram. By [F1] realize it by $\omega_k=Z_k/S$. Write $R_n$ for the posterior mean histogram measure, identified with its density in coefficient differences, with cell masses $\beta_k/B$. For a cell-constant function $q$, set $T(q)=\sum_kq_k(Z_k-\beta_k)$. Direct subtraction gives $\sqrt n(\omega q-R_nq)=(\sqrt n/S)T(q-R_nq)$.

Fix constants $t>0$ and $C$ large enough that $c:=tC-D_0(e^t-1)>0$. Since $N_{nk}$ is Binomial$(n,p_k)$ with $p_k=P_0I_{L_n,k}\le D_0/m$, independence of the observations gives $\mathbb E e^{tN_{nk}}=(1+p_k(e^t-1))^n\le e^{nD_0(e^t-1)/m}$. Hence $E_n=\{\max_kN_{nk}\le Cn/m\}$ satisfies $P_0^n(E_n^c)\le m e^{-cn/m}\to0$, by exponential Markov and the union bound. On $E_n$, for all sufficiently large $n$, $\beta_k\le C'n/m$, $B\le2n$, and both the empirical histogram density and the mean histogram density are bounded by a fixed constant $C'$ independent of $n$.

On $E_n$, take any Haar detail $\psi=\psi_{lk}$ with $l<L_n$ and put $q=\psi-R_n\psi$. Then $|q|\le2\,2^{l/2}$ and $V=\sum_k\beta_kq_k^2=B\operatorname{Var}_{R_n}(\psi)\le B R_n\psi^2\le C'n$, using $\int\psi^2=1$ and the density bound. By [F1] and [F7], $\Pr(S<B/2\mid X^n)\le4/B$, because $\operatorname{Var}(S)=B$. On the complement, step 1.1 yields $|\sqrt n(\omega\psi-R_n\psi)|\le2|T(q)|/\sqrt n$. Thus, apart from the single event $\{S<B/2\}$, the conditional probability that this absolute coefficient exceeds $x$ is at most $2\exp\{-c_0x^2/(1+2^{l/2}x/\sqrt n)\}$ for a fixed $c_0>0$. The zero-variance case has no such failure event, by [F1].

Choose a fixed $K>0$ sufficiently large. Uniformly over $l<L_n$, $2^{l/2}K\sqrt{l+1}/\sqrt n\le K\sqrt{m(L_n+1)/n}\to0$. Summing the exponential bounds of step 2.1 over levels $J<l<L_n$ and their $2^l$ coefficients therefore gives, for all large $n$, $\Pi_n\{\max_{J<l<L_n,k}|\sqrt n(f-R_n)_{lk}|/\sqrt{l+1}>K\mid X^n\}\le4/B+\sum_{l>J}2^{l+1}e^{-c_1K^2(l+1)}$ on $E_n$, with fixed $c_1>0$. The probability $4/B$ is counted only once, since the same $S$ normalizes every coordinate. Choose $K$ with $c_1K^2>2\log2$; the displayed series tail then tends to zero with $J$. For any $\varepsilon>0$, admissibility gives $K\sqrt{l+1}\le\varepsilon w_l$ for all sufficiently large $l$. Both $f$ and $R_n$ are histograms, so all their detail coordinates at $l\ge L_n$ vanish. Consequently their conditional $M(w)$ tails vanish in the iterated limit of [F4], first $n\to\infty$, then $J\to\infty$, since $P_0^n(E_n^c)\to0$.

For a Haar detail $\psi=\psi_{lk}$, exact subtraction gives $\sqrt n(R_n\psi-P_n\psi)=\sqrt n[\sum_ka_k\psi_k-A P_n\psi]/B$. Haar cell values satisfy $m^{-1}\sum_k|\psi_k|=\int|\psi|=2^{-l/2}\le1$. Hence $|\sum_ka_k\psi_k|\le c_2m$, while on $E_n$, $|P_n\psi|\le C\int|\psi|\le C$. This bounds every such mean shift by $C''m/\sqrt n\to0$. The scaling-coordinate shift is exactly zero, and all coordinates at $l\ge L_n$ vanish for both centers. Since $w_l\ge1$, $\|\sqrt n(R_n-h_n)\|_{M(w)}\to0$ uniformly on $E_n$. In particular step 2.2 also supplies the required posterior tails about $h_n$.

Fix finitely many Haar coordinates. Choose a fixed coarse dyadic partition of $r$ cells on which all their functions are constant. For large $n$ its cells are unions of level-$L_n$ cells. By [F1], the corresponding grouped Gamma variables $Z_{nj}$ are independent Gamma$(b_{nj},1)$ with $b_{nj}=N_n(J_j)+\sum_{I_{L_n,k}\subset J_j}a_k$. Their summed shape is still $B$. Markov applied to squared deviations, together with $A/n\to0$, proves $b_{nj}/n\to p_j$ in $P_0^n$-probability simultaneously for the fixed finite partition.

Consider any deterministic data sequence along which $b_{nj}/n\to p_j$ for every $j$. Under its conditional Gamma product laws put $Y_{nj}=(Z_{nj}-b_{nj})/\sqrt n$. For every fixed $t\in\mathbb R^r$, [F1] and the logarithm series give $\log\mathbb E e^{t\cdot Y_n}=\sum_j b_{nj}[-\log(1-t_j/\sqrt n)-t_j/\sqrt n]\to\tfrac12\sum_jp_jt_j^2$. By [F5], any subsequence has a further weak limit. For any fixed $t$, the same expansion at $2t$ uniformly bounds $\mathbb E e^{2t\cdot Y_n}$; hence $e^{t\cdot Y_n}$ is uniformly integrable. Truncation of this continuous exponential therefore passes its expectation through each weakly convergent subsequence. The limit law has transform $\exp(\tfrac12\sum_jp_jt_j^2)$ and an exponential moment on a neighborhood of zero: $e^{\delta\sum_j|y_j|}\le\sum_{\epsilon\in\{-1,1\}^r}e^{\delta\epsilon\cdot y}$ and the corresponding transforms are finite. The independent centered normal vector with variances $p_j$ has this same transform, by completing the square in each normal density. Here $(S-B)/\sqrt n=\sum_jY_{nj}$, $S/n\to1$ in conditional probability by its variance $B/n^2\to0$ and mean $B/n\to1$. Exact algebra gives $\sqrt n(Z_{nj}/S-b_{nj}/B)=(n/S)[Y_{nj}-(b_{nj}/B)\sum_hY_{nh}]$. By [F6] and step 3.2, this vector converges to $(U_j-p_j\sum_hU_h)_j$, with $U_j$ independent $N(0,p_j)$. Its covariance is $\operatorname{diag}(p)-pp^T$. Applying the fixed linear map from coarse-cell masses to the chosen Haar coordinates yields covariance exactly $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Step 2.3 removes the mean shift from $R_n$ to $h_n$ on $E_n$. The posterior histogram construction [F8] and its finite-dimensional simplex kernel make $Q_n$ a data-indexed Borel probability on $M_0(w)$: each draw and $h_n$ has only finitely many Haar coefficients, and its map from simplex coordinates is continuous. Apply [F4] to obtain the stated $M_0(w)$ BL convergence. Every original type-H assumption has been retained; in particular the lower parameter bound is compatible with, but is not needed beyond, positivity in this conjugate proof.

proposed_contract.claim:
Assume AC. Use the type-H prior of [[def-type-s-and-h-multiscale-density-priors]], retaining its original conditions: $1/2<\alpha\le1$, $f_0\in C^\alpha([0,1])$, $0<\rho_0\le f_0\le D_0<\infty$, either original cutoff $L_n=j_n$ or $L_n=\ell_n$, and $c_1 2^{-L_na}\le a_{k,L_n}\le c_2$ for fixed positive $a,c_1,c_2$. Write $m_n=2^{L_n}$. In the Haar convention, the scaling function is $1$, the detail functions are
$$\psi_{lk}=2^{l/2}(\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k}}-\mathbf1_{I_{l+1,2k+1}}),\qquad l\ge0,\quad 0\le k<2^l,$$
and a histogram at resolution $L_n$ has only the scaling coordinate and levels $l<L_n$. Let $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ be IID from $f_0$, let $N_{nk}=\sum_i\mathbf1_{I_{L_n,k}}(X_i)$, and define the empirical histogram
$$h_n(x)=m_n N_{nk}/n\quad\text{on }I_{L_n,k}.$$
Let $\Pi_n(\cdot\mid X^n)$ be the density posterior for the stated histogram prior. For every nondecreasing $w_l\ge1$ with $w_l/\sqrt{l+1}\to\infty$, its conditional law $Q_n$ of $\sqrt n(f-h_n)$ satisfies
$$\beta_{BL,M_0(w)}(Q_n,\mathcal L(G_{P_0}))\longrightarrow0$$
in $P_0^n$-probability, where the Borel centered Gaussian bridge $G_{P_0}$ is supplied by [[lem-density-gaussian-bridge-is-borel-on-m0w]] and has covariance $P_0[(\psi-P_0\psi)(\psi'-P_0\psi')]$. Its scaling coordinate is zero. This proves the type-H source-specific posterior BvM with the empirical projection center; no additional contraction, bias, or Dirichlet-parameter condition is imposed.
